en: He whose sovereignty over the worlds created at the beginning is innate, who thereafter provides protection, brings about their development, and effects the possibility of enjoining what is beneficial and prohibiting what is harmful;
Homage to that father, the supreme primordial teacher of the worlds and their Lord, whose speech is truth, whose compassion is innate, and whose effort for their sake is untiring and selfless.

[ĀtmaViv (B: 10. 7–14 = C: 9. –15. 2)] Here, indeed, all people who desire to abandon suffering—which is established by the common experience of all as being by nature inherently disagreeable—and who, while ignorant of the means to its abandonment, nevertheless pursue it, hear from the unanimous testimony of all those who know the inner self that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) alone is the means to that end, and nothing else. Furthermore, because of the relationship between the subject and the object of inquiry, it is the self (*ātman*) itself that must be known in its true nature. For instance, whether there is no-self (*nairātmya*) or whether the self exists as a real entity, in both cases, the knowledge of the self is innate.
Since the disputants are in complete agreement even on this point—that it is simply a lack of knowledge of reality—the true nature of the self (*ātmatattva*) is here analyzed.

In that regard, the subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) are as follows: either the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), or the denial of external objects (*bāhyārthabhaṅga*), or the denial of the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality (*guṇaguṇibhedabhaṅga*), or non-perception (*anupalambha*).
Among these, the first [position] is not tenable due to a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued: "Whatever exists is momentary, like a jar; and sound and other such things under dispute exist," [we reply: no, because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is unestablished.

If it is argued that their difference is established through the connection with contradictory properties characterized by capacity and incapacity, [we reply: no, because the connection with contradictory properties is not established. If it is argued that this is established through *prasaṅga* and its reversal (*viparyaya*), [we reply: no; for capacity is either the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) or fitness (*yogyatā*).
The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it would entail the fallacy of being non-different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatva*).
If it is argued that this is not a fault because of a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛttibheda*), we say no, because that is untenable;
for contradiction is rooted in a difference between the things to be excluded (*vyāvartyabheda*).

Furthermore, that [non-existence] cannot be established through mutual exclusion, like "cowness" and "horseness," because if that were the case, there would be a contradiction; consequently, upon the disappearance of one, it would follow that either the sublation (*bādha*) or the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the other would necessarily occur.
Nor can it be [the case that one is] the subsumer and [the other] the subsumed, like "tree-ness" and "śiṃśapā-ness," because we do not admit a relationship of priority and posteriority between them;
for if such a relationship were admitted, it would follow that either that which is capable would fail to act, or that which is incapable would act.
Nor can it be due to a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as in the case of being an effect or impermanence, because such an adjunct is absent here.
Furthermore, a mere word cannot be the limiting adjunct, for that would entail the consequence of the cessation of synonymous terms.

Nor can the difference in conceptual construction (*vikalpabheda*) be the cause of that [difference in exclusion], for if it were to differentiate the exclusion based on its own nature (*svarūpa*), it would follow that even an ineffective exclusion would possess difference. If, on the other hand, that [conceptual construction] differentiates it based on its object (*viṣaya*), there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, this conventional usage of the difference in exclusion cannot be without a cause, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable. For that [capacity] must be either the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārisākalya*) or something intrinsic (*prātisvikī*).

First, it is not the first position, because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*), and because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) since it is not accepted by the opponent.

Indeed, who would not accept that "whatever possesses the conjunction of auxiliary conditions necessarily performs [the action]"—it is precisely for such a person that this is being proved? Furthermore, we do not admit that there is a possession of the conjunction of auxiliary conditions at the time when [the cause] does not act, such that a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) could be applied.

6–8)] But specific capacity (*prātisvikī yogyatā*) must be either seedhood (*bījatva*) as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), or a sub-classification (*avāntara-jāti-bheda*) thereof, or the state of possessing an absence of effect due to the deficiency of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-vaikalya-prayukta-kāryābhāva-vattva*).

The first alternative is not tenable, because even that which does not act is established by perception as belonging to the class of seeds; for you, too, there is no disagreement on this point. The second alternative is not tenable either, because since I do not admit that it acts, the illustrative example lacks the probans (*sādhanavikala*). For what person of sound mind would accept something devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaśūnya*)?
For that [difference] is not perceived through direct perception, because it is not so determined;
nor is it known through inference, due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
If there is no distinction whatsoever, then how can there be performance and non-performance? If this is asked, who says "no"? [Indeed, there is a difference.]
Furthermore, as we search for a determining proof—whether [the difference] consists in a distinction of genus or in the presence or absence of auxiliary causes—we see none.

Nevertheless, if it is argued: "This entity which, situated in the midst of its auxiliaries, has the nature of acting without delay, must necessarily produce its effect even if it existed previously; this cannot be set aside even by a hundred divine curses," then this is correct. However, we do not understand how that very nature of acting without delay could be established for the entity if it were not within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that [this is established] through reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its converse (*tadviparyaya*), we say no, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

For the application of those two [arguments] depends upon the establishment of such an intrinsic nature (*evaṃsvabhāvatva*), and the establishment of such an intrinsic nature depends upon the application of those two.
It might be argued:

"In this matter, the very production of the effect is the proof; for if its nature were to persist in acting with delay, there would be no production of the effect at all, [and thus it would follow that] it never acts. To this we say: No, because if that which has a nature characterized by delayed action were never to produce [the effect], its very essence would be contradicted.
Consequently, the meaning of the term "delayed producer" (*vilambakārī*) is that it does not act as long as its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are not present.
And thus, the production of an effect can be used as a proof for the existence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), but not for a difference in genus (*jātibheda*).

As for whether those [causes] produced the effect by being mutually proximate while possessing a delayed-producing nature according to experience, or whether they possessed a rapid-producing nature according to your own conceptualization, in either case, the production of the effect remains unestablished.
Nor is the third [alternative] possible, because it is contradictory:
for it is a contradiction to claim that something possesses the absence of an effect due to the absence of auxiliary causes, and yet possesses the effect when those auxiliary causes are absent.
Therefore, it must be the case that whatever [an agent] does not do only in the absence of something X, he necessarily does that very thing when X is present.
And this is the supreme seed, the very essence, for establishing stability.

By this, the argument that "being the object of the conventional usage of 'capacity' (*samartha-vyavahāra-gocaratva*) is the logical reason" is refuted. For even a seed, though it is the object of such a conventional usage, is observed not to produce a sprout. If it is argued that this conventional usage is not the primary cause (*mukha*), because it is based on the fact of production (*janana-nimittakatvāt*), and that otherwise there would follow the consequence of lack of restriction (*aniyama-prasaṅga*); then what kind of production is the cause for the conventional usage of "capacity"? It cannot be "unimpeded production," because that is unestablished; rather, restriction consists precisely in production occurring only when all auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) are present.

Since it is also logically consistent that the instrument itself possesses such an intrinsic nature, this conventional usage is therefore based solely on the occasion of production, and not on the establishment of a pervasion (*vyāpti*).

8)] It might be argued: "Even by this much, what nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity has been established? For there is no other mode besides [the two]—delaying and not delaying. To this we say: No, because at the time of stating the refutation, since the mere absence of certainty establishes the "unestablished due to doubt" (*saṃdigdhāsiddhi*), the preliminary stage of the debate reaches its conclusion.
But on the occasion of the rejoinder, even that is not difficult to state.
5)] For instance, what is the meaning of "non-delay with respect to acting"? (65) Does it mean that acting occurs immediately after arising, or immediately after the convergence of auxiliary causes?
And what is the meaning of "delay"? (66) Does it mean that there is no acting as long as there is no convergence of auxiliary causes, or that there is no acting at all? (67)
In that regard, although there is no certainty regarding the first and fourth [alternatives] due to a lack of evidence, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself is the proof for the second and third.

For it is established by direct perception that a thing belonging to the class of seeds produces [its effect] immediately after the convergence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), and indeed only then; likewise, it is established that what lacks the convergence of auxiliary conditions does not produce [the effect].

And here, even with respect to the cultivation [of the cause], there is no disagreement at all, because it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and because there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary view.

To explain: if that which does not act in the absence of auxiliary causes were also not to act in their presence, then things of that same kind would never act at all, since they would not act in either case—whether there is the presence or the absence of the auxiliaries.
Likewise, if it were to act even in the absence of those auxiliaries, then the auxiliaries would not be causes, since the action would occur even without them.

And likewise, if those things which possess positive and negative concomitance that are not established otherwise were not causes, it would follow that the effect is causeless; and thus, its occasional nature would be contradicted.
And thus, when the second position is intended, the very nature of an entity is its non-delayed activity;
whereas, when the third position is intended, the very essence of an entity is its delayed activity. Therefore, there is no cessation of both modes.

Nevertheless, one might ask: what is the determining factor as to whether the lack of auxiliary causes belongs only to that which is incapable, or whether the presence of auxiliary causes belongs only to that which is already capable of acting immediately after acquiring its own nature, or otherwise? To this it is said: if there were no specific distinction in a seed situated in a granary from a fragment of stone in terms of its suitability for producing a sprout, then that which seeks such a result would never engage with the former and would always desist from the latter. This is not the case. Therefore, a distinction must exist.

If it is argued that [the seed] certainly exists because it produces, through a succession, a momentary seed capable of generating a sprout, then when will it produce such [a result] even through a succession?

If you say there is doubt in this regard, what is the nature of that doubt? Is it whether it will produce [the result] when the auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) are assembled, or whether it will produce it even when they are not assembled?
Now, as for the claim that it will act precisely when there is the conjunction of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), this merely gives rise to the doubt: "When, then, will their conjunction occur?

This [doubt] cannot arise in the first case, because once the cause-ness has been determined in a general sense, there is no room for such a doubt; or, if there were room for it, the cause-ness would not have been determined.

Nor can it arise in the second case, because once the true nature of the auxiliaries has been determined, there is no room for such a doubt; or, if there were room for it, their true nature would not have been determined.

In the third case, however, all the seed-moments included within that continuum would acquire identical capacities (*samānaśīla*), because there is a restriction regarding the production [of the effect] whenever the collection of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-samavadhāna*) occurs, and because such a collection of auxiliaries is possible everywhere. If it is argued that the collection of earth and other factors occurs only at a moment that is already capable, [we ask]: Is it the case that there is no collection of auxiliaries whatsoever for what is incapable? Or, even if the collection exists, does the production of the effect not arise from that [incapable moment]?
The first [alternative] is not tenable, because the conjunction of earth, water, fire, and air is observed even in fragments of stone and the like.

Nor is the second, for it would follow that a sprout might never arise from a seed—even when it possesses the full complement of auxiliary conditions—just as it does not arise from a fragment of stone.
[ĀtmaViv (B: 74. 7–11 = C: 76. 1–6)] Even so, it might be argued: "What is the fault? We reply: this has not yet been observed.
If it is argued that it is merely suspected, we say no; for just as one does not act when those [causes] are present, one would likewise have to suspect action even in their absence.

If it is argued that [the cause] must be suspected [to exist], then one would have to suspect it even in the absence of a seed. This being the case, the purification of perception and non-perception remains to be proven.

It might be argued as follows: this objection is not raised by assuming that seeds and other factors produce their effect only when they are in mutual conjunction—such that, because of the necessity of such conjunction, one could conclude that all things of that same class possess a single uniform nature; nor is it raised by assuming the production of a capable entity here or there—such that, since even from incomplete causes the occasional arising of an effect would be possible, there would be a contradiction with perception and non-perception.

What is it that makes one suppose that, even when seeds and other factors are present together, the production of an effect is possible by depending on some intermediate specific class (*avāntarajātiviśeṣa*)? It is not so; for when the phenomenon is established by the mere presence of the observed factors, there is no evidence for postulating such a class, as that would entail the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanāgaurava*). Furthermore, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of abolishing supersensible faculties and the like, because such a distinction cannot be logically justified, and because a specific property can only serve as a causal factor for another specific property.

For instance, from its production until the final blow of the hammer, the jar is experienced as never having been overtaken by another genus; rather, through the diversity of successive auxiliary causes, it produces various effects—both similar and dissimilar. Since everything is thus perfectly accounted for by this alone, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or for what purpose would one postulate a multitude of unperceived genera, such that the fault of the consequence of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*) would not arise?
As you yourself have stated: "When something is postulated for a certain purpose, the very fact that it can be established otherwise constitutes its non-existence."

Furthermore, having set aside observed differences in genus (*jāti*), since auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are also observed to produce an effect through the mere postulation of a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are accepted in some way; however, the postulation of supersensible faculties (*indriya*) and so forth would collapse due to a lack of evidence and because such conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are untenable.
1)] That specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*) must either be that which subsumes "rice-ness" (*śālitva*) or that which excludes it.
In the first case, why would even rice remaining in a granary not possess that nature? In the second case, however, how could even the rice intended [as rice] possess that nature?
In this way, "rice-ness" (*śālitva*) as well would be either inclusive of or exclusive of it.

In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence that what is not rice would be that [the universal]; in the second case, however, there would be the undesirable consequence that rice itself would not be that [the universal].
Nor can it be said that "neither [is the case]," because there exists no third alternative between contradiction and non-contradiction.

If it is argued that inclusion and exclusion based on a difference in individuals are not contradictory, then the distinction between "belonging to that class" and "not belonging to that class" would now collapse; for even when a few observed individuals are excluded, a mutual commingling might still occur in some cases, such as between a horse and a bird.

If a particular genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*) were to deviate from that which it characterizes, then even a *śiṃśapā* tree would deviate from being a tree, because there is no distinction [between them]. Thus, the case is already settled by the *svabhāva-hetu*.

If it is argued that there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the contrary [of the pervasion]—namely, that "it is a specific property"—we say no, because such a subverting proof exists here as well; for in the absence of that [specificity], the status of being an essential nature (*svabhāvatva*) is untenable.

Or rather, what is the point of this obsession with seeking a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) regarding the arising [of the effect]? For a particular [cause] is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of a particular [effect].

To illustrate: if the nature of being a seed (*bījatva*) were not the motivator for the sprout-nature (*aṅkurātva*) residing in the effect, it would follow that the sprout could arise even from what is not a seed (*abīja*).

If it is argued, "How can there be a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) of a seed in that which is not a seed? then one might ask, "How could there be a specific quality of rice (*śāli*) in that which is not rice? In that case, it would follow that a rice sprout could not arise. If it is further argued, "Let this specific quality exist even in that which is not a seed, just as it does in non-rice; nevertheless, it is only when co-inherent (*ekārthasamaveta*) with the nature of being a seed (*bījatva*) that it acts as the cause for the sprout," we reply: No. For if the nature of being rice (*śālitva*) is subject to deviation [in non-rice], then just as it cannot be restricted by co-inherence with the nature of being rice, so too—since there is no difference—it cannot be restricted by co-inherence with the nature of being a seed when that nature is subject to deviation [in non-seeds]. Thus, there is no distinction between the two cases.

Therefore, we consider it logical that whatever reproduces its own positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) exactly as they are, possesses causal capacity for that very effect in that same manner;
however, it is the specific differences within that [cause] which bring about the specific differences in the effect, just as in the case of rice and other grains.

If it is asked, "Of which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this collection of operations? we reply: "It belongs to that which consists of perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*), serving as the cause for the ascertainment of origination from that. Now, if you are not satisfied without formal reasoning (*nyāya*), listen to that as well: "In that case, whatever is not a causal factor (*aprayojaka*) with respect to a sprout is not of the same kind as a seed (*bījajātīya*), just like a stone fragment; and the seed placed in a granary is accepted by others as being a non-causal factor with respect to a sprout. This is a *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅga*) based on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

If it is asked, "What is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) even in the case of the opposite [position]?"—it has been stated that it would follow that the specific determination of the sprout’s genus (*jāti-pratiniyama*) is accidental (*āka-smikatva*). If it is argued, "Its being a seed (*bījatva*) is established by perception (*pratyakṣa-siddha*) and cannot be denied," then let the opposite be the case. Whatever is a seed is the efficient cause (*prayojaka*) for a sprout, just like a seed situated within the final causal complex (*antya-sāmagrī*); and this subject of dispute is a seed. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).
For the specific restriction regarding the birth of a sprout cannot be without a cause, as that would entail the consequence of its occurring everywhere;
nor can it have another cause, because no such cause exists.

This very possession of a causal sign (*nimittavattā*), by excluding itself from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), rests precisely upon the status of being a necessary factor (*prayojakatā*) for its own pervaded [effect]; thus, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established. Alternatively, enough with the mention of the sprout: is the nature of being a seed (*bījasvabhāvatva*) a necessary factor for some effect or not?

If it were not so, the seed would not possess that intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because it would be of no utility whatsoever in that form. Thus, the nature of being a seed, which is established by direct perception, would not exist; yet there would still be a particularity (viśeṣa) that lies beyond the scope of all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). This is the purified understanding: even if there is utility for one [particular] in that form, there is no distinction among all [seeds], since they all share that same nature. And if that were the case, how could only a certain seed produce its own effect and not others? Furthermore, the effect would not be produced from the mere thing-in-itself (vastumātra), because it would follow that the effect could arise even from what is not a seed.
Nor is it merely the seed, for that would entail the production of the sprout even by something other than its cause;
nor is it merely any one of the factors such as the sprout, for that would entail the production of that very thing even prior to its arising.

If it is argued that whenever a thing has arisen and rests within a collection of auxiliary causes conducive to a particular effect, at that time it alone possesses the status of being the producer (*prayojaka*) with respect to that effect—then does this occur by virtue of a distinct intermediate genus (*avāntarajāti*), or rather by its very nature as a seed (*bījasvabhāva*)?

In the first case, that very difference in genus (*jātibheda*) is the operative factor; what, then, has come of the "seed-ness" (*bījatva*)? In the second case, however, it follows that even those things possessing identical natures do not produce an effect due to a deficiency in auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri*). This is because, when accompanied by their respective auxiliaries, the seed-nature—which is the operative factor toward each respective effect—is common to all of them. Regarding this as well, there is the following formal argument (*prayoga*):

Whatever form something does not employ in causal functions (arthakriyā), it does not possess that form. For example, a seed that performs no function whatsoever in its capacity as an elephant does not have the nature of an elephant; likewise, rice seeds and the like, having entered into the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), do not employ their form as seeds in causal functions. This is a *prasaṅga* reason based on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), because the state of possessing that form is pervaded by the fitness for causal functions; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

1–5)] If it is argued that its having that nature cannot be denied because it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then let the opposite be the case: whatever has a certain nature is employed for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in that very form, just as entities situated within a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) possess their own intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), such as seeds remaining in a granary. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), because capacity is invariably concomitant with that very nature.

Furthermore, there exists some effect for which the seed is employed as its causal factor (*bījatva*). If it is argued that the experience of the seed itself is the unique effect in which the nature of being a seed (*bījatva*) is the determining cause, and since that [experience] arises from every single seed, what is there that is untenable? We reply: no; because that experience in its technical sense (*yaugika*) can be accounted for even without that [seed].

If it is argued that it is the worldly experience (*laukika*), we say no; this is true, but it does not necessarily arise from every seed, because the proximity of the sense organs and other factors is neither constant nor universal.

1)] And therefore, if it is argued that even though [the seed] is capable, it does not produce [the effect] due to the non-proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), and thus by implication it will be an entirely different, supersensible effect (*kāryāntara*) that is invariably concomitant with all seeds—this is not so. First of all, it cannot be accepted as a material cause (*upādāna*), because that which is formless cannot have that which possesses form as its material cause; furthermore, since it would consist of a perceptible form, it is impossible for another form to occupy that same location. Nor can it be an auxiliary cause, because it is impossible for mutually exclusive auxiliary causes to be invariably concomitant.

Moreover, this being the case, the nature of the causal agent (*prayojaka*) is not within the scope of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); whereas that which is within their scope is not the causal agent. Furthermore, the entire range of perceptible effects is produced by an imperceptible nature, while the imperceptible is produced by the perceptible. This, then, is the subject matter of the principle "those things which are constant...

Alternatively, there is a formulation by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): The seed under dispute possesses a deficiency in its effects, such as the sprout, which is caused by a deficiency in auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), because it belongs to the same class as seeds that are the objects of the certainty regarding their production [of such effects]. Whatever does not possess a deficiency in its effects, such as the sprout, caused by a deficiency in auxiliary factors, does not belong to the class of seeds that have become such [i.e., productive], just like a piece of stone.

Nor should it be said that there is a doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—namely, whether the exclusion of the stated probandum follows from the exclusion of the stated probans directly, or whether it does so indirectly because of a lack of such generative capacity; for the seed of such a suspicion has already been refuted.
This might be argued as follows:

If it is argued: "Let there not be a conjunction of contradictory properties characterized by capacity and incapacity; let seed-ness alone be the determinant; and let the nature of the entity be that of an agent when there is a convergence of auxiliary causes. Thus, its non-agency in the absence of those [causes] is also logically consistent. Nevertheless, this restriction applies only to things of that same class, for it cannot be avoided in the case of a single individual, since the conjunction of contradictory properties—namely agency and non-agency—is established by direct perception. [We reply: No, because the nature of contradiction has not been correctly determined. (156)

Indeed, that [mutual exclusion] must either consist in the two properties being of the nature of mutual absence, like permanence and impermanence; or it must consist in their producing that [absence] in the substratum, like coldness and heat; and the possession of those [properties] is like being a staff-bearer or being a ring-wearer. Furthermore, [the opponent might argue]: "If the property of being a jar were not distinct from the property of being a cloth, then the cognition of 'jar' would arise even when a cloth is present, because the object of the cognition of 'jar' would be non-different from the cloth. Or else, the cognition of 'cloth' would arise even when a jar is present, because the object of the cognition of 'cloth' would be non-different from the jar. Moreover, since the objects of the cognitions of 'jar' and 'cloth' would be non-different, the two cognitions themselves would become identical. And if they were identical, there would be no distinction between them. To this we reply: This is not so. For the difference between the two cognitions is established by the difference in their causes. Just as the cognitions of blue and yellow are different due to the difference in their respective objects, so too are these two cognitions different due to the difference in their respective causes. Furthermore, the difference between the two cognitions is established by the difference in their objects, just as the cognitions of a pot and a cloth are different. Therefore, the objection is invalid. Moreover, if the property of being a jar were not distinct from the property of being a cloth, then the cognition of 'jar' would arise even when a cloth is present, because the object of the cognition of 'jar' would be non-different from the cloth. Or else, the cognition of 'cloth' would arise even when a jar is present, because the object of the cognition of 'cloth' would be non-different from the jar. Furthermore, since the objects of the cognitions of 'jar' and 'cloth' would be non-different, the two cognitions themselves would become identical. And if they were identical, there would be no distinction between them. To this we reply: This is not so. Just as the cognitions of blue and yellow are different due to the difference in their respective objects, so too are these two cognitions different due to the difference in their respective causes. Furthermore, the difference between the two cognitions is established by the difference in their objects, just as the cognitions of a pot and a cloth are different. Therefore, the objection is invalid. The first [alternative] is not tenable because that which is without qualification is unestablished; as for that which has qualifications—namely, that "as long as something exists, it performs some action"—even if a contradiction were established, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) would still be untenable.

For when there is non-performance of a certain thing at a certain time, there is an absence of its performance at that time, but not an absence of its performance at another time; nor do we maintain that these two [non-performance and performance] coexist in a single substratum.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because the performance and non-performance of an action distinct from existence and non-existence are unestablished. For performance and non-performance are designated as the presence or absence of auxiliary causes—which are synonymous with activity—or as the presence or absence of the effect. Even if such distinction were established, performance would entail the exclusion of non-performance at its own time, just as it excludes its own nature; but it does not entail this at another time. For that which does not exist at a certain time cannot, at that time, exclude its own nature, nor can it exclude the absence of its opposite.

If that were the case, it would never cease to be, nor would there ever be any contradiction regarding it; thus it follows that "there is no coming into being for the non-existent, nor is there non-existence for the existent," or else there is no contradiction.

Now, if this were the case, even a difference in magnitude would not be contradicted by a difference in time, for it would be equally easy to say that there too [time is the cause]. However, this is not so, because in that case, a difference in time is intended on the strength of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). For instance, a new substance is not produced by the constituent parts of a substance while those very parts are already engaged in producing another substance, because there is a contradiction between having a physical form (*mūrtatva*) and occupying the same location at the same time. Thus, according to the theory of production (*ārambhapakṣa*), the prior substance must cease; if it does not cease, there can be no production. This is the point therein.

If [the substance] has ceased, the difference in dimension occurs precisely because of the difference in its substratum; if it has not ceased, then in the absence of an addition of another conjoined substance, where could a difference in dimension be perceived that would bring about a contradiction? But if there were such an addition, how could another dimension arise, since the substratum itself has not arisen? For this very reason, even the cognition of an excellence in bulk (*sthailyātiśaya*) in that case is erroneous. Therefore, a difference in dimension cannot be attributed to a single substrate even through a difference in time; this should be investigated together with those who are skilled in the investigation of categories (*padārtha*).

[ĀtTaViv (B: 128. 4–12 = C: 142. 14–146. 2)] If it is argued: "Let there be a subverting force (*bādhaka-bala*) here as well, since the *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*tadviparyaya*) have already been stated," we say no. This is because those two have as their object capacity (*sāmarthya*) and incapacity (*asāmarthya*), and this has already been explained therein. Or, even if they were so, nevertheless, since capacity and incapacity are not intended [as the primary objects] by those two, it is only a contradiction regarding a difference in time that is established, for it is impossible to conclude [the argument] in that way. If it is argued: "Disregarding the temporal distinction of 'when' and 'then,' one can conclude that 'whatever is capable necessarily acts,'" we say no.

If there is no intention to specify a restriction regarding time, then that which is capable necessarily performs its function; thus, it might be the case that [the rule] is so. And in this way, for a rule of possibility (*sambhava-vidhi*), absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*) is what is contradicted, but not mere non-connection (*ayoga*), just as in the expression "a lotus is indeed blue" (*nīlaṃ sarojaṃ bhavaty eva*).
[Objection: But surely, if something was initially incapable, from where has its capacity come later? Or, if it was initially capable, where has that capacity gone later?

This is not so. For capacity (*sāmarthya*) is indeed the state of being a producer of this or that [effect] when associated with this or that auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*); the lack of capacity is the non-production of that [effect] when not possessing those [causes] or possessing something else. And this is its innate nature; furthermore, since those auxiliaries occur at different times due to the force of the causes for their own approach, it follows that the effects also occur at different times. If it is argued: "Even so, let the entity, while remaining at one and the same time, produce its respective effect at each respective moment once it has arisen and ceased, because as soon as it has arisen, it possesses that very nature, just like [an object] situated in one place."
This state of existing at a single time is either in relation to its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) or in relation to the proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri*).

In the first case, nothing is untenable, because even eternal things possess such a nature; for all entities have the single characteristic of being present (*vartamāna*) at one specific time. The distinction, however, is that in some cases this [existence] is limited by a temporal boundary, while in others it is without such a limit.
Even if there is a limit [to its duration], there is a distinction based on the excellence or deficiency in the stream of the results of its activity.

As for the second [alternative], it might occur if those [auxiliaries] were simultaneous; however, it has already been stated that they are successive auxiliaries (*kramiṇaḥ sahakāriṇaḥ*). But as for one who asserts that "the entity produces by its own nature when accompanied by auxiliaries," the consequence that "that which has already arisen and perished must produce" would follow, like the unrestrained prattle of a child. Enough of this.

Therefore, that very time belongs to the effect, while for the cause it is both that [time] and another; thus, in relation to the times of the related entities, there is the conventional usage of "prior time.

Furthermore, instead of the expressions "when" (*yadā*) and "then" (*tadā*), if one substitutes "where" (*yatra*) and "there" (*tatra*), what fault would there be in those same two cases—the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive?
If you say there is no fault, then either the non-duality of space or the plurality of causes would result.

If you say, "Let it fall; having taken that, we shall enter the city of the Yogācāra system," [we reply: no, for it is impossible to enter there without first repudiating the enemy—the doctrine of the existence of cause and effect.
Or, if you do repudiate that, then for you, who have laid down the weapon of the proof known as "existence" (*sattva*), how can there be any fear even on the battlefield of external debate?
