Not the third [alternative], because if the characteristic of contradiction is present, it is impossible to remove that contradiction even by a thousand refutations; or if it is not present, then that very point must be considered.

When there is a negation of one thing upon the affirmation of another, or an affirmation of one thing upon the negation of another, there is a contradiction between those two by virtue of their existing through mutual exclusion within a single locus (*dharmin*). However, such a contradiction does not exist here. For the capacity to perform a function in a particular place is indeed contradicted by the incapacity to perform that same function in that same place; this is because when the former is affirmed, the latter is necessarily negated. It is not, however, contradicted by the incapacity to perform that function in another place, since it is not negated therein. Indeed, the non-performance of a function elsewhere, or its performance of a different function, does not constitute the absence of its performance of that specific function in the first place; rather, it is [the absence] in that very place.

If it is argued that "there is no such production," then—alas!—you should reflect upon what has already been largely stated: that the exclusion of the characteristic of contradiction is likewise applicable even to capacities and incapacities belonging to different times.

Therefore, even though the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*) are established, the attribution of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) remains unproven.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that there is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) as follows: whatever performs a certain action at one time must perform that very action as long as it exists, just as a particular sound [produces] another sound? Conversely, the contrapositive is: whatever does not perform a certain action at one time never performs it at all, just as a stone fragment [never produces] a sprout? And a seed situated in a granary does not produce a sprout at one time. [Response: This [argument] would have to be intended either with reference to the genus (*jāti*) or with reference to the individual (*vyakti*). (208) [ĀtTaViv (B: 154. 13–16 = C: 176. 1–4)]
In the first case, both [reasons] are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because of the observation of non-restriction.

In the second case, both are established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*): because absolute non-performance is conditioned by an absolute incapacity, whereas the restriction to performance occurs when there is capacity, being conditioned by the presence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

By this, the following is refuted: "Whatever a thing does, it does immediately upon arising, just as motion does; and whatever a thing does not do immediately upon arising, it never does at all, just as a stone fragment does not produce a sprout.
Here too, as before, the defects of inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*) and being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*) remain.

Nor is it the third [alternative], because it would follow that even producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*), and so forth, would be contradictory merely by virtue of possessing mutual absence.
Let it be, then, that contradiction consists in a thing being both related and unrelated to that very same auxiliary cause; no, for such an alternative is untenable.

For instance, regarding one related entity in relation to another related entity, would its own absence or its own nature be contradicted? Or would it be its being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of that absence; or that very same thing accompanied by "at that time" (*tadaiti*); or that very same thing accompanied by "in that place" (*tatraitīti*); or both together; or that very same thing accompanied by "in that manner" (*tathaiveti*)? [216] It is not the first, because it is not admitted.
The second [alternative] is not tenable, because of the refutation of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
Nor is the third, because we do not admit that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) are simultaneous with the entity.

Nor is the fourth; for that [contradiction] cannot first be established by a rule of coexistence, since such a relation is unproven. If its establishment were derived from this very [rule], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): for the contradiction is established only when the rule is established, and the rule is established only when there is a difference [between the two] once the contradiction is established.

Nor is it established from anything else, because that [other cause] does not exist; and because connection and non-connection are governed by causes for approaching and departing that are not fixed. Nor does this contradiction [of coexistence and non-coexistence] follow from the fact that destruction is causeless, since that too is unestablished. As for the necessity of its occurrence, we shall address that later. Nor is there a fifth [alternative], for we do not admit that the very same thing is both present and absent at the very same time with respect to the same auxiliary cause.

Now, is it not the case that you maintain that "conjunction" (*samavadhāna*), which is the property of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), is indeed contact (*saṃyoga*), and that it is both distinct from those causes and non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*)? If so, then it follows that the very same thing exists and does not exist in that very place at that very time. If it were not distinct [from the causes], then for one who maintains the permanence [of things], the seed, water, earth, and the locus—even when separate—would be identical to those [combined] causes; consequently, the production of the effect would follow even from them individually. Furthermore, if it were pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), there would be the error of seeing redness and so forth everywhere, and the production of effects such as sound would follow everywhere.
Therefore, it is better to maintain that atoms possessing a conjoined nature have arisen as something entirely distinct from those that are unconjoined.
This is not so, however, because this very contradiction is unavoidable even in the case of momentary atoms.

For instance, just as an atom situated in the eastern direction has arisen with a form that is occluded by the atom situated in the western direction with respect to the western spatial division (*digavaccheda*), is it likewise [occluded] with respect to the eastern spatial division, or not, or both? In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-perception from both sides. In the second case, however, there would be the undesirable consequence of perception from both sides. In the third case, moreover, there is that same wretched contradiction: that very same [atom] is both occluded and non-occluded by that very same [atom] at that very same time.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the distinction is based on a difference in mode (*prakāra*), then what is this "delimitation by another direction" (*digantarāvaccheda*)? For if there were a contradiction, it would have to be the case that by the very same delimitation of direction by which something is conjoined, it is also not conjoined; but here, that is not so. Alas! Even in the view that the conjunction and the conjoined object are distinct, if such were the established position (*siddhāntavṛttānta*), what kind of fault could there be?
By this, the position of absolute difference (*vyatirekapakṣa*) is also refuted.

Furthermore, there is an additional deficiency: there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the locus, the reason, and the example, because valid means of cognition do not operate upon a non-entity (*avastu*), and if they were to operate, its unreality (*alīkatva*) would be untenable.

If it is argued that, in such a case, there would be a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) regarding non-conventional usage (*avyavahāra*), then does this contradiction with one's own words serve to demonstrate a valid means of cognition for those [entities], or is the very practice of negating conventional usage being refuted, or is it being asserted that this non-authoritative practice must necessarily be accepted?

Not the first [alternative], for it is impossible to demonstrate—by even a thousand contradictions—either perception or inference regarding a permanent entity (which lacks succession and so forth), or regarding a rabbit’s horn; if that were possible, enough with this quarreling of fools. As for the second, however, it is indeed accepted by those who uphold valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*). "In that case, silence is obtained," [you might say]. What can we do? Where speech is altogether untenable, silence is indeed better. You too should consider this: between one who speaks like a mute and one who remains silent regarding a matter lacking any means of valid cognition (*niṣprāmāṇika*), which is superior?

[ĀtmaViv (B: 172. 5–12 = C: 197. 14–200. 3)] If you say: "Even though you are a learned man, you have not remained silent; rather, you have indeed refuted worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*) regarding what is non-existent (*asat*)," that is true. Just as you, thinking that an unauthentic (*aprāmāṇika*) meaning contradictory to your own words must not follow as a consequence, have accepted an unauthentic discourse regarding the non-existent, so too we, thinking that an unauthentic discourse must not follow as a consequence when investigating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), accept an unauthentic contradiction with our own words.
If, however, you were to maintain an equal view toward both cases, then we too would have nothing further to say.
But regarding the third case, since it is both unauthenticated and yet necessarily to be accepted, you yourself must be asked: whose command is this?

If it is argued that this is because conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is firmly established (*suddṛḍhanirūḍhatvāt*), there is a contradiction: to be without a basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*) and yet be firmly established. If it is argued that it is so because it is established in some way (*kathañcid api vyavasthitatvāt*), then if it lacks a basis in valid cognition, it is not established in any way at all; whereas if it has a basis in valid cognition, let that very thing be stated. Thus is the resolution in debate.

However, in the case of *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), for one who engages merely in questioning the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the thesis and other elements, there is no contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*). In that context, an answer given by means of a *pramāṇa* would be undesirable and impossible; rather, if an answer is given by means of what is not a *pramāṇa*, there is defeat (*bhaṅga*) by one's own words alone, because one has personally accepted that "there is no *pramāṇa* for the thesis and other elements stated by me. On the other hand, if no answer is given, it is simply a lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*).

If the adoption of conventional usage were to eliminate contradiction, then it might indeed be accepted; however, this is not the case, for the statement that "it is both the locus of all conventional usage and the locus of the convention of its negation" is certainly not mutually consistent.

If it is asked, "What contradiction is there in the doctrine that [the self] is not a fit object [for treatment], if this is intended merely as a conventional usage of a rule?"—alas! If it is not a fit object for any conventional usage of injunctions or prohibitions, is it then treated as something at all, or is it not? In either case, there is a contradiction with one's own words; for in both cases, it must be a non-entity (*avastu*), since it is impossible for a real entity (*vastu*) to be devoid of all conventional usage.

Regarding the position that "it is not [the case]," there is a contradiction with this very linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)—namely, that it is devoid of all linguistic usage consisting of affirmation and negation—because that which has not been linguistically used cannot be negated. Regarding the position that "it is linguistically used," there is likewise a contradiction upon examining the nature of the object itself; for it is impossible for something to be both outside the scope of all linguistic usage and yet be linguistically used. Furthermore, if a non-entity (*avastu*) can be the object of the linguistic usage of negation, why could it not also be the object of the linguistic usage of affirmation? For the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is equal in both cases.

If it is argued that for the son of a barren woman, the lack of being a speaker is proven by his very lack of consciousness and so forth, whereas there is no such proof for his being a speaker—if this is said, we reply: no, because even in that case, "sonship" (sutatva) exists;
for the son of a barren woman is not non-son, since otherwise there would be a contradiction with one's own words.

This is merely a verbal expression and not the ultimate truth. If it is argued that this [self] is indeed the son, we say no; for even insentience (*acetanya*) possesses such a nature. Indeed, that which is other than sentience is called "insentient" because it is a different essential nature (*svabhāvāntara*). If it is argued that what is intended here is simply the cessation of sentience, and that such a thing is indeed possible, we say no; because in that case too, what is intended is merely the cessation of the state of being a non-son (*asutatva*).

If it is argued that non-consciousness cannot function as a reason unless it includes another capable entity as its object of determination—since mere exclusion of being a son lacks the capacity for either production or cognition by its own nature—the answer is no; for this same logic applies equally to the case of non-consciousness as well.

If it is argued that even that which has the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is a probans only if it is excluded from "that which is not that" (*atasmāt*), just as *śiṃśapā*-ness [is excluded from non-śiṃśapās], whereas the son of a barren woman is excluded not only from non-sons such as jars and the like, but also from sons such as Devadatta and others, and therefore is not a valid reason—well then, this very lack of consciousness (*acaitanya*) in the self is also of such a nature. For the son of a barren woman is not excluded from conscious beings such as Devadatta and the like, just as he is from unconscious things such as wood and the like.

If it is argued that "the property of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*) is a quality restricted to a real entity (*vastu*); how then could it be established in a non-entity (*avastu*), given the contradiction?"—from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this contradiction established?
Is it because a non-entity, as distinct from being a speaker, is invariably perceived, or rather because being a speaker, as distinct from a real entity, is not perceived?

It cannot be the former, for a non-entity is never within the range of perception by any means of valid cognition; otherwise, it would not be a non-entity. Nor can it be the latter, for the same logic applies.
For non-speakerness (*avaktṛtva*), like speakerness (*vaktṛtva*), is not the object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as something distinct from real entities.

If it is argued that there exists at least a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) of that which is distinct from them, then who can prevent a conceptual construction of that which is associated with it?

If it is argued: "But surely 'speakerhood' is the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to speech; how then could that apply to a non-entity, since the latter is characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity? [We reply: "How then could 'non-speakerhood' apply there, since that too is characterized by being an agent of something other than speech?"

If it is argued that the absence of the capacity for speech is not contradictory to the absence of all capacities, then from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that barrenness—the absence of all capacities—established? If you say "precisely because of its being a non-entity," then from what is even this established? If you say "because of the absence of all capacities," then this person, like a penniless debtor wandering about with mere words, deceives the virtuous here and there, yet does not even perceive the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

If it is argued that this is because of the absence of succession and simultaneity, we say no; for even if that absence were established, the demand for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would not cease. Furthermore, when "sonship" is being considered, since all properties such as "being a speaker" which are invariably concomitant with it would follow [as being present], what room is there for establishing the absence of succession and simultaneity? How much less, then, for establishing "non-substantiality," and how much less for establishing "not being a speaker" and so forth? Therefore, the means of valid cognition alone is the boundary for the regulation of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*); if one transgresses that, there is simply no regulation at all.

For indeed, when Devadatta and others are not perceived, no one would ask— absent sheer impudence— the question, "Is he fair-complexioned or dark? In that case as well, if one person gives an answer such as "He is not fair," while another gives "He is not dark," since the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the contradiction are equal in both instances, no objective determination whatsoever can be established.

Now, it is indeed correct that there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding what is not cognized; however, things such as "the hair of a tortoise" are certainly cognized. For these conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) do not arise without delineating some distinct object. Nor has it been stated as a truth that the locus of linguistic usage is necessarily the same as the locus of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: the cognition "the horn of a hare" must be either a misapprehension of something else (*anyathākhyāti*) or the manifestation of a non-existent thing (*asatkhyāti*).

The first [alternative] is not acceptable to you; for if that were so, there would be something superimposed and something that is the locus of superimposition, and thus the locus of superimposition would exist in one place while the object to be superimposed would exist in another—by this, the Naiyāyikas would be victorious.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because the reason is untenable.

For the sense faculty functions solely through its sovereignty over the object (*viṣaya-adhipatya*) in the production of cognition; because fallacious signs (*liṅga*) and words produce only "apparent otherwise" (*anyathākhyāti*); and because if those two, having set aside their own referents, were to produce "apparent non-existence" (*asatkhyāti*), there would follow the undesirable consequence that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "tortoise-hair" could arise even from words like "hare's horn," since there would be no restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*).
For that [restriction] must be either the convention (*saṅketa*) or the inherent nature of the word itself.

First of all, [the theory that words denote isolated word-meanings] is refuted precisely because the object of convention is not perceived. If that [isolated meaning] were perceived from that very [convention], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). If perception occurs solely by the power of the word’s convention, then since the word does not abandon its own primary meaning, the word-meanings themselves—though actually unconnected—appear as if connected; thus, the theory of "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*) persists. On the other hand, if the word abandons its own primary meaning, there would again be a lack of restriction, because it would convey a meaning not established by convention. If, however, restriction were due to the inherent nature of the word, then it would follow that even one who has not mastered the language would have such conceptual constructions arise, just like one who is proficient.

If it is argued that this is due to a specific latent impression (*vāsanā*), then is the latent impression alone the cause of a cognition that represents what is non-existent, or is the latent impression also [the object]?
It cannot be the first case, because it would follow that cognitions such as "the horn of a hare" would be eternal.

If it is argued that [the cognition arises] sometimes from awakening and sometimes otherwise, we say no. For awakening too must be either another auxiliary cause or the ripening of a series of successive enhancements (*atiśaya*).

In the first case, since it would be nothing other than the latent impression (*vāsanā*), the proposed position is untenable. In the second case as well, if it depends on the proximity of an external object, then it is the same as before.

If, however, it depends solely on one's own continuum, then the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyavāda*) is contradicted, because even cognitions of blue and so forth would arise solely from the ripening of latent impressions.
Even if one takes the position that it is due to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), some other cause must also be stated; and when that is examined, it does not escape the logic previously established.

Furthermore, there is no comprehension of a relationship between words such as "hare's horn" and non-existent objects; for, since the cognitions of others are not directly perceived, their objects likewise remain unperceived.

Nor is there any distinction in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) from which one might infer a specific object and thereby grasp a convention regarding it. Furthermore, the understanding of that [object] does not arise merely from the words of the person who established the convention; for all words concerning such objects would fail to communicate their meaning, as they would have an unperceived object and thus no previously grasped convention (*samaya*) would exist.

It should not be argued that when one utters the word "hare's horn," some intention (*abhiprāya*) has occurred, and therefore its referent is the object of this [intention] and the convention (*samaya*) is easily grasped; for the grasping of a convention does not take such a form. If it were so, then upon hearing the command "Bind the cow," even for one who has not previously understood the word-meaning, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of grasping a convention based merely on the perception of the speaker's intention.

Nor is it correct to say that its denotable object is a mere conceptual construct (*kalpanāmātra*) devoid of any other specific [external] particulars; for if that were the case, it would follow that even things such as a jar, a tortoise, or hair would possess that status [of being the denotable object].

Nor is it tenable that all practitioners, by virtue of their own respective latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), partake in the cognition of a relationship between words and non-existent objects; for, being ignorant of one another's communications, this would entail the consequence that [the word] is not for the sake of others. Indeed, it is impossible to cause another to engage in linguistic usage without first having them grasp the convention (*samaya*) established by oneself; nor is it possible to have them grasp it without instruction regarding linguistic usage.

Nor is there, regarding the referent of the term "hare's horn," a linguistic usage such as "one should not kill a cow"; nor is there an instruction such as "this is that horse"; nor is there an extension of a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇātideśa*) such as "as is a cow, so is a gavaya"; nor is there here a grammatical coreferentiality with a well-known word, as in "the bee drinks honey in the interior of a blossomed lotus."

Therefore, these [appearances], which are comparable to the horns of a hare and so forth, do not consist of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), because there is no cause for such a state and because it would follow that they lack practical efficacy (*vyāvahārikatva*), like a mute person’s dream. Consequently, they must indeed consist of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*). Even by following this view, one cannot establish that a non-entity (*avastu*) falls within the scope of practical linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) merely through its negation. Or, let it be that they consist of the manifestation of the non-existent; even so, a distinction from that [misapprehension] is not supported by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).

For instance, what is this so-called "exclusion" (*vyatireka*)? It must be either the absence of that from which something is excluded in a given locus, or the fact of having that absence as its very nature. In this regard, the absence of succession and simultaneity in a rabbit's horn is certainly not within the scope of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because, just as with a mountain ridge devoid of trees, a rabbit's horn devoid of succession and simultaneity does not fall within the range of any means of valid cognition.

Nor is it established by valid cognition that the horn of a hare consists in the absence of succession and simultaneity; for, like the absence of a jar, the horn of a hare is not perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that the absence of a jar is likewise not within the scope of valid cognition, we say no; for its existence is established by valid cognition precisely because it is distinct from the jar, even though it lacks a positive nature (*asvabhāva*) of its own. Or, if it were not so established, there would be no practical engagement (*avyavahāra*) with it either.

First of all, it is established by valid cognition that the jar has as its nature the absence of its own non-existence, because it is never perceived in the form of that [non-existence]. If it is argued that by this much alone the non-existence of the jar is also established as having the nature of the absence of the jar, we say no; for we do not admit that the existence of the jar has as its nature the absence of its own non-existence. Nor would another thing be established simply because the nature of one thing falls within the scope of valid cognition, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that the jar and its absence are precisely of such a nature that the determination of one is the exclusion of the other, we say no. For if the absence of the jar were not accepted as being established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) just like the jar itself, there would be no room for the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*).

Indeed, the recourse to the doctrine of intrinsic nature is possible only when a thing is established by valid cognition; it is not the case that the establishment of a thing occurs solely through the recourse to the doctrine of intrinsic nature—this is the very drum of victory for you [the Naiyāyikas] in various contexts.

In that case, is it not established by valid cognition that the pot has the nature of being devoid of intrinsic nature? From your perspective, this is indeed so; for as long as the pot has entered the path of valid cognition with whatever such nature it possesses, if there were also some ultimate non-existence of it, then [its lack of intrinsic nature] would exist ultimately.

And this is not accepted by you; therefore, just as with a jar, since its absence is also established through valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) characterized by their mutual exclusion is established. However, if it were not established through valid cognition, then for those two as well, such a state would not exist; this same principle applies even to cases such as a hare’s horn. [Objection:
But surely, let the fulfillment of conceptualized criteria alone be a constituent of inference. [Response: That is not so, because such fulfillment is easily found everywhere.

Now, it may be argued that the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) are of two kinds, distinguished as real entities (*vastu*) and non-entities (*avastu*). In this regard, the distribution of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is purely conceptual (*kālpanika*) when applied to those [instances] brought forward by imagination; however, when applied to those brought forward by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they are indeed valid (*prāmāṇika*). Thus is the distinction. Therefore, although here the exclusion of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth from imaginary fireless things is established as conceptual, nevertheless, its exclusion from real [fireless things] such as lakes must be sought as being validly established (*prāmāṇikī*); and since that is not established, how can that [property] function as a logical reason?

Thus, when a word that is authoritative is made the subject (*pakṣa*), the existence of the reason (*hetu*) must likewise be stated as being authoritative. Now, this [reason of] "being visible" does not exist [in such a word]; how then can it be a reason? In the same way, for "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—which is a property restricted to a real entity (*vastu*) alone—a real positive concomitance (*anvaya*) must be stated, and a real negative exclusion (*vyatireka*) from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) [i.e., non-realities].

And it has been prattled that "those two [presence and absence] do not exist for him; so how can he be a reason? This is not the case, for it cannot be said that while imagination proceeds toward success in the absence of a restrictive factor, it lags behind regarding failure. And thus, by mere imagination, even smoke—which is devoid of fire—would possess smoke [as its property] because of its occurrence in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa); consequently, smoke would not lead to the cognition of fire.

If it is argued that when there is actual perfection of form, what is the use of this imagined defect? Then, when there is actual lack of perfection, what is the use of that imagined [perfection]? The two cases are the same. If it is argued that the distinction lies in contradiction versus non-contradiction, from where does this [distinction] arise? If it is argued that it is because in one case there is both a real and an unreal entity, while in the other there is only an unreal entity, then is even an imagined smoke a real entity such that it could contradict the hair of a tortoise? Since the absence of smoke (*nirdhūmatva*) is also in some cases a real entity, there would likewise be a contradiction with that as well.
Therefore, just as an imagined misfortune does not constitute a fault, so too an imagined prosperity does not constitute a virtue; thus is the refutation of the negative concomitance (vyatireka).

7)] Let it be granted, then, that momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established because destruction is necessarily concomitant with existence and thus lacks a cause; yet this is not so, because the conceptual alternatives are untenable.
For that [destruction] must be either identity with the thing itself, or being indefinable (*nirupākhyātva*), or being its effect, or being its pervader, or simply being non-existence (*abhāvatva*).
Not the former, because it is impossible for the negated object and the negation to be one and the same; or, if such identity were possible, the manifold variety of the universe would be impossible.

If it is argued that its non-existence is simply its incapacity for causal efficiency at another time, and that this is nothing other than its possessing a nature that is either capable or incapable at that other time—then surely this is precisely the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). Thus, what gratification do you find in proving something unestablished by means of what is itself unestablished?

Furthermore, if its non-existence is that which persists through other places and other times, then surely this has been stated without words: namely, that this very thing persists through other places and other times.
Alternatively, if non-existence were not necessarily linked to other times and places just as it is to one's own time and place, then existence would follow [as a consequence].

If it is argued that this is because of incapacity— since the definition of existence is capacity— then is incapacity with respect to an effect in another time what constitutes non-existence at its own time, or is incapacity with respect to its own effect in another time what constitutes non-existence?

In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of its non-existence even at its own time, because it would still possess that same nature [of incapacity] even then. If you argue, "This [incapacity] applies only with respect to an effect belonging to another time," is this some kind of incantation? For one who is incapable of performing a certain action is not conventionally designated as "non-existent" with respect to that action.
Indeed, smoke is not non-existent in the world with respect to a donkey; for what reason? Because the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of that which is incapable does not cease to exist.
But regarding the second [alternative]: if incapacity has another time as its locus, how can it be of the nature of that [present entity]?
If it has that [present] as its locus, then there follows the consequence of its non-existence at that very time; whereas in another time, the opposite would follow.
Therefore,
affirmation is the essence of this entity, while negation is something other than it;
yet even upon hearing that this [negation] too is its essence, what discerning person would not feel shame?
6)] Let it be then that there is no cessation distinct from the nature of the entity; this is the remainder of the statement "it is non-existent," meaning it possesses a designation (*sopākhyā*).
But surely this too is merely an outburst of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), and that has already been swallowed like a ball of molasses at the elbow.
Or, let it be granted that cessation is incapable [of being produced]; nevertheless, what follows from its being causeless?

If it is asked, "What kind of birth can there be for a void thing? [the answer is: it is just like the restriction of time and place [that we observe]. If it is asked, "What kind of restriction of time and place could that have? then, in that case, the cessation of a jar would either never occur at all, or it would occur everywhere and at all times.

If it is argued that "let it be only the first," then this is either a negation of the nature of the existence of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) itself by means of the negation of the entity (*bhāva*), or it is a definition of the nature of cessation (*nivṛtti*) through the negation of the entity. In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the entity itself is eternal; in the second case, however, it would be the cessation itself that is eternal.

2)] Let it be then that "inevitability" (*dhruvabhāvitva*) is simply the state of being its effect; no, for even in the position that "it too is an effect," there is a contradiction, since it is unestablished that it is the effect of that very thing.

If it is argued that whatever effect belongs to something immediately upon its arising is itself its destruction, then the point of the proof is this: whatever effect belongs to a particular causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is independent of anything other than that complex. Who indeed would not accept this? However, for what reason should one conventionally employ the expression "the effect itself is destruction"? Is it because the effect possesses the absence of that [cause], or because the effect is of the nature of that absence?

It cannot be the former, because that would lead to the same consequence regarding auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), and furthermore, because the essential nature of "absence" (*viraha*) cannot be defined.

The second alternative is not tenable; for that [non-existence] would have to arise either because of the rule of non-perception of the cause as capable [of producing its effect] at the time of the effect's production, or out of conformity with conventional usage, or out of consideration for subverting arguments against a distinct destruction.
[345] It is not the first, for the shuttle and other such implements are indeed perceived at the time of the cloth.
If it is argued that "they are not those [same things]," what is the proof for this?

If it is asked, "What is the proof even for their non-difference? let there be no such doubt; for even while they remain in a state of uncertainty, the support of the object is destroyed by the force of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
It is not the second case either, for when it is said, "the cloth has been produced," no one uses the expression, "the threads have perished."

If it is argued that because the cloth is not distinct [from its parts], there is no practical usage [of the term "cloth"] when only the threads are produced due to the non-apprehension of difference, then in that case, even the force of practical usage [as a basis for existence] would not exist.
If it is argued that at least the force of practical usage exists in the case of a heterogeneous series (*visabhāga-santati*), this is not so.
For if the mere collection of threads were the production of the cloth, how could the cloth—whether as their support or as identical with them—exist prior [to that collection]?

If you argue that it is indeed something else, we reply: no difference based on genus (*jāti*) is perceived; nor has a difference based on individuality (*vyakti*) yet been established. For this very reason, if its establishment were to depend on that [collection], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Nevertheless, if it were so, what kind of fault would there be? None at all; there would simply be a lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and a failure to conform to worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), because even when that [destruction] is not established [by those means], it is established by depending on another cause.
Furthermore, the destruction of the threads must either be of the nature of the general absence of threads or its opposite.
In the first case, how could there be another thread? For generally speaking, blue does not have a nature that is contradictory to non-blue, such that it would be another non-blue.
In the second case, how could it be contradictory to that? For blue, even in its general form, is not contradictory to another blue.
If you say that this contradiction exists only at the level of specific particulars, then is destruction, in its general form, indeed of a nature that is neither [blue nor non-blue]?
If one says "om," then, having accepted either [of the two alternatives], the conventional usage of destruction is untenable.

If it is argued that because the universal (*sāmānya*) is unreal, what can contradiction (*virodha*) do there? [We reply: Any hope for a distinction based on the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) has now dissolved, since that [distinction] depends upon that [universal].

Now, just as in the view that absence is a distinct entity, there is no contradiction whatsoever—since a cloth possesses the absence of another cloth and belongs to the same class [as that cloth], or since an absence is opposed to a cloth yet coexists with another cloth—so too it will be in the view that the effect is an absence.

This is not so. For identity, relation, and belonging to the same genus with the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) are not admitted, because it would follow that there could be no counter-correlative at all, due to their being at different times and because of the relation to contradictory properties in general. But what fault is there in a relation with something other than the counter-correlative? Indeed, difference, belonging to a different genus, and being at the same time are not incompatible with relation; for while identity is incompatible with being related, you do not even admit that these [other factors] constitute incompatibility. Nor is there any sublation [of such a relation], because such a sublation does not exist.

Now, does the pot exist in the absence of the pot, or not? If the former, then since the pot exists in that which possesses it, the shards would also possess it; thus, the absence of the pot would apply to them as well. If the latter—that it does not exist—there follows the consequence of an infinite regress, because the designation of "non-existence" there would require yet another absence, and so on. Furthermore, if the practice of non-existence were applied there without another absence, the same would follow for other positive entities. This is not so, because another positive entity, being of its own kind, is not contradictory to what is of a similar kind, whereas it is impossible for that which is of a contradictory kind to be of the same kind. Moreover, if such a designation were made based merely on difference, it would follow [absurdly] even for that which possesses the entity.
However, because non-existence (*abhāva*) possesses a contradictory nature (*viruddhasvabhāvatā*), there is an absence of both the experience and the inference of another non-existence.
9)] If it is argued that there is a fault in the production of a distinct non-existence because of its identity with the pot, we say no.
If indeed pot-ness itself is intended by "the state of being a pot," then that is already accepted [by us].
For we do not admit that when a non-existence arises, the pot attains the state of non-pot.
If you mean its existence at that time, then the non-existence has not arisen; for that non-existence is simply the nature of the pot's non-abiding at another time.
If it is argued that "let there be, then, the lack of a material cause (*nirupādānatva*) as the subverting factor, because origination is pervaded by having a material cause," we say no.

This is because such a claim is subverted by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends [the nature of] phenomena, and because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is restricted to existent things (*bhāva*).
By this, the lack of an effect (*nirupādeyatva*) is also explained.
"And because it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) even if qualities and so forth were established.
If it is argued, "In that case, let 'pervasion' (*vyāpakatva*) be 'inevitability' (*dhruvabhāvitva*)," we say no.

Because there is neither identity with that nor the production of that, even according to our own position, the apprehension of pervasion does not occur through a rule of concomitance, since it would be contradictory due to the disparity in timing.

Nor does it occur through a rule of immediate succession after birth, because that is unestablished; or, if it were established, the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) would follow from that very fact. If it is argued, "Let there be pervasiveness by virtue of mere future existence," let it be so; however, this does not establish independence from other causes, for it is rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by the case of a jar today which exists merely as a series of potsherds tomorrow.

By this, the objection that there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to dependence on a cause of destruction—since a deficiency in the causal conditions might be possible—is refuted; for destruction shares the same logical status as the series of potsherds. Let it be, then, the final position: namely, that destruction is not produced because it is a non-entity (*abhāva*), like prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); or, even if produced, it ceases because it has been produced, like a jar.
This is not so;

for it is not a valid proof that "prior non-existence arises because it is a non-existence or because it is perishable, like destruction or like a jar," or that "what has not arisen does not cease because it has not arisen, like space or like a hare's horn.

If it is asked, "What is the refutation of these [arguments]? [the answer is: because their pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not severed from existence, they lack probative force (*aprayojakatva*); there is sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) which grasps prior and posterior non-existence; and there is counter-reasoning (*pratikūlatarka*) characterized by the undesirable consequence that the effect would re-emerge both before and after [its destruction].
If it is asked, "What is the fault in its re-emergence? [the answer is: it would follow that the cognition of the temporal separation [of the effect] would lack both [prior and posterior] natures.

If that [cognition] were not in accordance with reality (*ayathārtha*), then—just as at the time of seeing two moons there is no temporal separation of the moon's location—the absence of temporal separation for the possessor of that [effect] would lead to the consequence of non-contradiction, since the entity would exist simultaneously with its prior and posterior non-existences.
But if [the distinction] exists according to its true nature (*yathārthatva*), then its emergence is untenable.
By this, the emergence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), as well as the emergence of prior non-existence at that very time, are refuted;
for both types of non-existence, like existence, possess a nature that is opposed to both [existence and its opposite].

[ĀtmaViv (B: 267. 13–268. 2 = C: 318. 1–319. 8)] But how is the establishment of stability [of the self] further [demonstrated]? From recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and because momentariness is untenable.

If it is argued that recognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it belongs to a class of fallacious cognitions due to the non-difference of its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇābheda*), we say no.
Because there is a rule of non-deviation due to the distinction between intermediate characteristics.
If it is asked, "What is that [characteristic]?"—it is the state of having as its object something not conjoined with contradictory properties, and that is established here.
If it is argued that even such a thing might sometimes deviate, we say no.

If the cognition of unity—which is not overwhelmed by the association of contradictory properties—were to be fallacious, it would follow that unity must be abandoned everywhere. And in that case, even multiplicity would not exist; thus, you would become a complete nihilist.

Therefore, the occurrence of difference necessarily entails the association of contradictory properties, or conversely, the absence of such association necessarily entails the exclusion of difference. This is the established rule for the conventional usage of difference and non-difference.

If it is argued: "Even though we carefully observe unflinching lamps and lotus buds, we do not perceive any association of contradictory properties; nevertheless, setting aside recognition, you establish difference therein"—by the force of what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is this done?

If it is argued that because the destruction of the substratum is known to be the cause of the destruction of fire, and because such [destruction] is perceived here at every moment due to the progressive diminution of the wick and oil—whereby the destruction of the preceding and the production of the succeeding is established by logic—[we reply: surely this is merely a conjunction of contradictory properties (*pratyanīkadharma-saṃsarga*), since it is impossible for both "destroyedness" and "non-destroyedness," or for "destruction of the substratum" and "non-destruction of the substratum," to coexist in a single flame.
Thus, regarding this person who does not give even for the cutting off of a hundred heads, yet gives twenty-five—what can we say here?

If it is argued that even in this case there will be a difficult-to-comprehend association of contradictions, then: is it the case that in the instance "this is that very crystal," a contradiction is suspected among the associations established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that there is an association of those things whose cognitions are contradictory; or rather, that certain associations of contradictions in their unperceived natures exist as either contradictory or associated?

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it has already been refuted. Nor is the second, because it is sublated by the non-perception of those things that are incapable [of being perceived]. Furthermore, even for those things that are incapable [of perception], [the claim of their existence] is set aside by observing the absence of causes and the absence of the pervaded and the pervader. Nor is the third, because it leads to over-extension (*atiprasañjaka*), resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of unity everywhere.
By this, the proof of stability is established through inference, having drawn out the definition-part from recognition itself.

For instance: the entity under dispute does not differ even when there is a difference in time, because it is not associated with contradictory properties despite that difference; whatever is not associated with contradictory properties even when there is a difference in X does not differ even when there is a difference in X, just as a single atom remains one despite the difference in its corresponding atoms; and this entity under dispute is likewise; therefore, it does not differ even when there is a difference in time.

Regarding this pervasion (*vyāpti*), no one disputes; as for the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), it has already been established. Furthermore, the impossibility of momentariness follows from the fact that the conventional usage of a continuous series cannot be explained otherwise. For words, logical marks, and conceptual constructions, if they do not bring about the apprehension of a common form, they are incapable of even bending a blade of grass; this is beyond dispute when one examines whether external objects are stable or unstable.
[ĀtmaViv (B: 278. 1–8 = C: 330. 14–332. 3)] Furthermore, there are three positions: that [the object] is either false (*alīka*), or a mental form (*ākāra*), or an external entity (*bāhya-vastu*).

Among these, the first position is not tenable; for that [object] cannot be established as such on the basis of experience alone, because experience does not register its falsity. Alternatively, if it were so [established], it would contradict purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*); for even after experiencing it, one who seeks causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) does not act [thinking] "this is indeed false."

If it is argued that this fault does not apply because there is a manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*), this is simply not the case, because what manifests is precisely a positive form (*vidhirūpa*).
For here, in this location of the mountain, what manifests through word and inferential mark (*liṅga*) is not "it is not non-fire," but rather "fire exists."

Even if there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form "I cognize an absence" (*nivṛtti*), nevertheless, the very mention of the referent of the word "absence" is what constitutes the mention of the absence. For there is no such thing as a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratīti*) that does not include its qualifier. Therefore, just as for others a conceptual cognition is a "cognition of a universal" because the common form flashes forth even in the absence of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "I cognize a universal," so too for us, the cognition of absence is that which is projected by the cognition of the excluded object. If you say this, then alas!

If the establishment of the cognition of a universal is based on its being of a positive nature when there is the manifestation of a common form, then what has happened to the establishment of the cognition of exclusion (*nivṛtti*) in a mind where the form of non-existence does not manifest?

For the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not "this is not a non-cow," but rather "it is a cow"; thus, even in the absence of a mental form (*ākāra*) consisting of the thought "I perceive the exclusion of others," if there were a manifestation of the form of exclusion (*nivṛttyākāra*), who could deny the cognition of that exclusion? Otherwise, if it does not so appear, yet one acts as if it did, then let it be that a cognition of a horse exists within a mind having the form of a cow. Furthermore, even if there were a manifestation of mere exclusion, activity would not be possible; for one seeking a jar does not act on the grounds that "the non-jar does not exist," but rather that "the jar exists."

If it is argued that this fault does not apply because there is the cognition "only the non-existence of a jar," we say no; for as long as the negation of the jar's existence is not rejected, the very rule [of exclusion] remains unestablished.
But if that [negation] is rejected, what other injunction could there be? For the rejection of a negation is itself an injunction.
If it is argued that "if the cessation [of the action] does not manifest, one who is instructed to 'bind the cow' might as well bind a horse," we say: no.
This might indeed be so if the horse were also a cow; however, a cow is a cow and a horse is a horse.

Otherwise, even when there is cessation (*nivṛtti*), from what would you have confidence? (387) If it is due to another cessation, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). (388) If there were a confusion of the intrinsic natures (*svarūpa-saṅkara*) of the thing to be excluded, the cessation, and their substratum, there would be a confusion of activity (*pravṛtti-saṅkara*). (389) If the restriction is established by the very difference of intrinsic nature, why should it not be the same even when only a positive entity (*vidhi*) appears? (390) If it is argued that the difference of intrinsic nature itself is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because a positive entity has as its nature the exclusion of others, we say no.

Because that [negation] would be absent in the case of a false object, it would follow that its own nature is established as non-false; furthermore, a specific particular (svalakṣaṇa) cannot ascend into conceptual construction.
Moreover, one who is instructed, "Bind the cow," proceeds toward a cow and not toward a horse, because the latter is not perceived.
But when he perceives a horse, then even though he is inclined to act toward it, he will desist precisely by perceiving the absence of the cow—so what is there that is untenable?

It might be argued as follows: "Indeed, it is not possible for anything to exist while disregarding experience; therefore, who could deny the manifestation of a positive injunction (*vidhi*)? Even its negation, which is subordinate to that [positive injunction], certainly manifests, because otherwise the status of the injunction as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) would be untenable. For there is no such thing as being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) unless it distinguishes the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) from others; nor is the distinguishing from others anything other than the communication of exclusion (*vyavacchitti*). Therefore, just as from words such as *indīvara* (blue lotus) or *puṇḍarīka* (white lotus)..."

If it is argued that in all cases there is a cognition whose primary feature is a positive injunction (*vidhi*) such as "blue" or "white" which has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), while the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyavaccheda*) merely appears as its internal content; let it be so for now. However, we have no insistence at this point that a positive injunction must be manifesting. Otherwise, since the excluded and the excluder would not be cognized, there could be no exclusion at all—just as in the case of a blue lotus and the like, if the quality of blueness were not cognized.
Furthermore, a cognition that does not touch the object to be negated cannot touch the negation itself, because the determination of the latter is dependent upon the determination of the former.

Nor can one negation be the very object of another negation, as this would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). However, in the case of an affirmation (*vidhi*), which is determined independently of anything else, this fault does not arise.

Then, having shifted the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) onto the conventional designation (*saṅketa*), what was refuted by Jñānaśrī—that very point—becomes like a blind man being led elsewhere by a ball, merely deluding the common folk through its relocation to another position.
If it is argued, "Let the unreal (*alīka*) be manifested," [we reply: No.
Because of contradiction:
"something" has the sense of an affirmation (*vidhi*), whereas "nothing" has the sense of the unreal (*alīka*).

For if the unreal were defined merely by its exclusion from what does not possess that form, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would be unreal.

But if there is a transformation of mere form (*rūpamātra*), how can there be such a thing as affirmation (*vidhi*)? If it is argued that this very same fault applies because the affirmative aspect is superimposed (*āropita*), we say: no.

Since there is no contact with conceptual construction regarding the affirmation of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and since the affirmation of a universal (*sāmānya*) is not admitted, by process of elimination, contradiction remains precisely in the case of the affirmation of the unreal (*alīka*).
If it is argued that this is merely a conventional usage of affirmation due to the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*):

This might be possible if even the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were to manifest by abandoning its positive nature, and if even the unreal (*alīka*) were to appear by discarding its negative form.
But it is not so;
for since both are partless, they do not manifest by assuming another mode, and because a form that does not manifest cannot exist.

For this very reason, the axe is laid at the root of the imagined relationship between part and whole. Furthermore, that which is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a common form (*sādhāraṇa-rūpa*), and it cannot be unreal (*alīka*).
For its conformity to space and time is not intrinsic, because it is insubstantial; nor is it conceptual, because that [conceptual construction] is momentary;
nor is it superimposed, because it is not established elsewhere either.

If it is argued that unity alone is apprehended due to the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*), we say: no. This is because there is an absence of real difference; or, if difference were present, it would contradict its being merely conceptual (*kālpānika*). Furthermore, that which is ultimately non-existent cannot result in ultimate non-difference, and the non-apprehension of a superimposed thing is untenable. Moreover, there would be no occasion for the superimposition of non-difference, as this would entail the ultimate existence of what is merely superimposedly non-existent. Finally, that which is free from the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and thus its non-apprehension would apply even throughout the three worlds.
Because it is easily accessible.
If it is argued: "In other cases, when a difference in the ultimate sense is perceived, how could non-difference be superimposed? [The reply is:

If that is so, then that which is not superimposed upon something in its manifestation must necessarily be superimposed upon that very thing when it is not manifest, and not merely upon that which bears the same name, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For this very reason, the non-apprehension of a difference— whether it be existent or non-existent— that resides in a different locus, is not conducive to the superimposition of identity.
Nor is the establishment of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) possible through reasoning, because such reasoning does not exist.

If it is argued that there are two logical principles: first, that whatever is common to both existence and non-existence must consist in the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), as for example "incorporeality" (*amūrtatva*); and second, that whatever is the cause for the conventional usage of similarity among things that are absolutely distinct must be of the nature of the exclusion of others—[we reply:
no, because this is a case of "misrepresentation due to the lapse of time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*).
For the "consisting in" (*niṣṭhā*) of something already manifest cannot be established by logic; rather, the very body of what is manifest has already been examined, so this effort is fruitless.
And when even what is certainly non-false is merely an appearance of experience regarding the logical principle (*nyāya*), then what need is there to mention the case of the false?
For it has been stated that in the case of the false, there is nothing whatsoever— even if unperceived— that could be established by the logical principle.

Furthermore, this commonality between existence and non-existence cannot first of all consist in being both forms, because of their mutual contradiction; nor can it consist in being a property of both, because that is not accepted.
For it is not accepted that "cowness" is a property of non-existence as well.
It does not possess that property because it is inconclusive;
for even a particular (vyakti) possesses the properties of both existence and non-existence, and thus is not of a single nature consisting solely of negation.
Nor can there be similarity between those two, because it is impossible.
If it were so by the mere exclusion of that [other], there would be no distinction from the probandum itself.
Nor can there be co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "existent" and "non-existent," because of contradiction and because it could be established otherwise;
for that which exists cannot be the object of the cognition "it does not exist."

If it is argued that [the object] must exist by resorting to another mode, then in that case, what contradiction would there be in establishing its affirmation (*vidhi*) by relying on that very distinction of modes, such that the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) could be established?

If it is asked, "When it has the nature of affirmation, what further thing is there to be added?", then it is the same for its having the nature of negation (*niṣedha*): "What further thing is there to be added?
Therefore, if it is argued that this is precisely why there is commonality (*sādhāraṇya*), even so, it remains impossible to determine whether it consists of both or whether it excludes both.

Therefore, whether it be the attainment of another limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) by means of "existence" and "non-existence," or the restriction of the limiting adjunct already attained, those two possess purposefulness.
This same principle applies equally even in the case of a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

Since all particularities are pacified [absent] in the position of the unreal (*alīka*), where could there be the prescription of another attribute (*upādhi*) or its restriction? Thus, this is a specific defect [of that view].

Consequently, the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) is established as denoting only the individual qualified by the universal "cowness" (*gotva*); however, because these individuals are scattered across different places and times, they are not capable of fulfilling the request of one who seeks a functional purpose (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, the cognizer desires particulars. And that desire of his is warded off—whether by restrictive or prescriptive statements such as "the black-spotted cow is in the pen," "the pot-uddered one," "the one with the large bell," or "Nandinī"—so there is no defect whatsoever in the process of verbal cognition (*vācya*).

If it is argued that since there is only the cognition of the mere individual as qualified by "cowness" (gotva), the employment of words such as "exists" (asti) is therefore futile, we reply: that word is used precisely for the sake of that limited cognition.
However, its utility lies in the cognition of multiple attributes, because those were not previously cognized; this has already been stated.

However, as for the one who considers himself clever and maintains the following position: "Whatever cognition has a manifestation common to both the existence and non-existence of a thing does not have that thing as its object—for example, the cognition of a cow does not have a horse as its object," and so forth;

if this very commonality of the cow-cognition to both the existence and non-existence of the horse constitutes its having the horse as its object, then the same would apply to the external cow itself. In that case, the reason is indistinguishable from the probandum.
If there is an expectation for specific qualities such as existence (*asti*) and so forth, then there is the fault of being too narrow (*asādhāraṇya*).
For the conceptualized cow (*govikalpa*) cited as an example does not expect specific qualities such as the existence of a horse.
But in the case of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), there is indeed a contradiction.

For that which does not have something as its object cannot indeed have a requirement for the restriction of its specific features; otherwise, it would follow that even the cognition of a cow would require such a restriction of specific features. If it is argued that there is no presentation of its existence or non-existence, then if that [existence or non-existence] is simply its own nature (*svarūpa*), the fault is one of unestablished proof (*asiddhi*).

For it has never been established for me, nor even now for you, that the conceptual construction of a cow does not manifest the actual nature of the cow. Furthermore, if you claim it manifests another attribute (*upādhi*), then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Indeed, there is no rule that whatever does not manifest another attribute of something must necessarily not manifest that thing either.
[ĀtmaViv (B: 323. 1–13 = C: 381. 8–384. 5)] But surely there is indeed a restriction;

for instance, that which does not bring about the cognition of a property inherent in something else does not bring about the cognition of its own nature, just as the conceptual construction and the word for "cow" do not bring about the cognition of a horse.

And likewise, even in the case of those two cows, with respect to blueness and so forth, there is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). For even when there is cognition of a property (*dharma*), there would have to be a restriction based on a difference in assistance—namely, that some properties are cognized while others are not—and this difference in assistance would arise from a difference in capacity (*śakti*). But such is not the case here, because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, since there is no difference in capacity, there is no difference in assistance; thus, there are only two possible courses: either the cognition of everything together with its adjuncts (*upādhi*) or the non-cognition of them. In this way, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established.
This is poorly argued.

For, given the difference between the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*), the occurrence of cognition and non-cognition when they do not arise simultaneously is established precisely because they are to be cognized by distinct causal complexes (*pratiniyatasāmagrī*).

Furthermore, this being cognized by a distinct causal complex is based on the diversity of intrinsic natures; that [diversity] is dependent upon its own causes; those [causes] are established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*); and that [concomitance] is to be inferred from the effect.

As for the argument beginning with "because of the non-difference of the capacity" (*śakteḥ abhedāt*), that would be tenable only if the cognition of the distinction between limiting adjuncts (*upādhibheda*) were dependent solely upon the substratum (*dharmimātra*), or dependent solely upon the cognition of that [substratum], or dependent upon the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the cognition of that much alone; but this is not the case. Furthermore, if the cognition of the distinction between limiting adjuncts were dependent solely upon the substratum, then even when the limiting adjuncts are not being cognized, there would necessarily be a cognition of their distinction, just as there is a cognition of the difference between the blue and yellow colors of a cloth even when those specific colors are not being perceived. Alternatively, if the cognition of the distinction between limiting adjuncts were dependent solely upon the cognition of the substratum, then even when the limiting adjuncts are not being cognized, there would necessarily be a cognition of their distinction, just as there is a cognition of the difference between the blue and yellow colors of a cloth even when those specific colors are not being perceived. Or, if the cognition of the distinction between limiting adjuncts were dependent upon the causal complex for the cognition of that much alone, then even when the limiting adjuncts are not being cognized, there would necessarily be a cognition of their distinction, just as there is a cognition of the difference between the blue and yellow colors of a cloth even when those specific colors are not being perceived. But none of these is the case. Therefore, the cognition of the distinction between limiting adjuncts must depend upon the cognition of the limiting adjuncts themselves. Consequently, since the cognition of the limiting adjuncts is absent, the cognition of the distinction between them is also absent. Thus, the objection regarding the non-difference of the capacity is refuted. By this, the following objection is refuted: "If properties (*dharma*) are not cognized through words or logical marks (*liṅga*) even when the substratum (*dharmin*) is cognized due to its distinctness, then let them likewise not be cognized through the sense organs as well.
For we accept that which was raised as a consequence at a time when the causal complex for perceiving those respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is absent.

Furthermore, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possess diverse potencies—since a logical mark has the power to bring to mind a well-known invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), a word functions within the boundaries of linguistic convention (*samaya*), whereas a sense organ depends even upon the objective power (*artha-śakti*) of the object.
However, an object is not established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) merely because it is related; for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Rather, it is only logical that when a substratum (*dharmin*) is perceived by a particular means of knowledge, that [substratum] is not perceived by that same means if a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) is not perceived, or if all qualifying attributes are unperceived. And in that case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); this is the summary.
It might be argued as follows: if the sign (*liṅga*) and the word (*śabda*) have exactly the same object as the sense-faculty, then a difference in their appearance would be untenable.

For having a single object is observed to be pervaded by a non-difference in appearance, as in the case of what is seen by the left and right eyes; yet this is not so here. For while in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) appear with clearly defined forms, restricted by place, time, and state, they do not appear in that way in the verbal or inferential conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

For in that case, some form appearing as if excluded from heterogeneous things, as if its aspects were mutually intermingled, as if indistinct, and not previously familiar through direct perception, becomes the object of experience; yet a difference in appearance cannot be established by a mere difference in means, for the means of comprehension are not capable of altering the form of the comprehension itself, nor is it possible to establish the logical connection [of the reason] on the grounds that a single entity possesses two forms.

The formal argument for this is as follows: That appearance which is contrary to the appearance of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding some object does not have the same object as that [perception], just as the appearance of a cloth is not the same object as the apprehension of a jar; and likewise, at the time of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there is an appearance contrary to the appearance of direct perception regarding a cow.
This too is flawed.
The argument is inconclusive because of two appearances—one variegated and one non-variegated—which are mutually contradictory yet both have the same blue object as their domain;
for that which appears as blue in a variegated perception is not the very same blue that subsequently appears alone, nor even at that same time, to another person.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction between those two [cognitions] in the form (*ākāra*) by which they have a single object, and that there is no single object in the form by which there is contradiction—[and] that there is contradiction in the form of another property (*dharmāntara*), while there is a single object in the form of the mere blue—it follows that here too, there is contradiction in the form of another property, while there is a single object in the form of the mere individual (*piṇḍa*) possessing the nature of a cow (*gotva*). Therefore, if one intends to negate only that much [the latter case], the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*);
if one intends the former [the universal], it is a proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

For we do not admit that at the time of conceptual cognition arising from words or logical marks (*śabdalaiṅgika-vikalpa*), all specific properties (*dharmaviśeṣa*)—such as the restriction of place, time, and so forth—attain the status of being objects [of that cognition].
2)] But how is it that the distinction between clear and unclear manifestation occurs only with respect to the substratum (*dharmin*) itself?
Not in any way whatsoever.

For, in whatever manner phenomena appear, in that very manner there arises the conventional usage of "insight" (*pratibhāna*); and in whatever manner there is non-comprehension of phenomena, in that very manner there arises the conventional usage of "dimness" of insight—even among people regarding direct perception at a distance or nearby—but not when there is total non-comprehension.
If it is argued that even the cognition of "far" and so forth constitutes a counter-example (pakṣa), let it be so; however, even by that much,

there is no avoidance of the sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) regarding the proof of a distinction between property and property-bearer, nor is there an avoidance of the "inconclusive due to doubt" (*sandigdhānaikāntika*) even when such a distinction is doubted, because the difference in appearance remains possible even by that much.
And if it were not so, there would be no ground for confidence in your cognitions of "extreme distance" and the like.
If you argue that this is because the object is actually obtained [in those cases], [we reply as follows:]
But surely, even apprehension occurs only by not subverting what was previously apprehended.
For a *śiṃśapā* tree is not apprehended by setting aside its being a substance, its being earthy, its being a tree, and so forth.

If it is argued that [the object] is that in which the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) occurs, then since this applies to all [cognitions], what is the certainty as to whose purposeful action it is? If you say nothing at all; rather, because there is an absence of mixed purposeful actions, there is only one real entity (*vastu*) therein, and since there can be no difference in appearance regarding a single [entity], we maintain that the cognition there has only a single objective support (*sālambana*), even so, in the absence of certainty as to which one it is, that same lack of confidence remains. Furthermore, even unmixed purposeful action does not arise from the individual entity alone, since everything is possible from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

For this very reason, there is no such thing as [causal efficacy] by way of a continuum (*santāna*). Indeed, there is no such thing as causal efficacy that is restricted to a single continuum. If it is argued that something is established as such only with respect to a particular causal efficacy within the scope of perception and non-perception, then even those things perceived from a great distance would have to be so established; for the fact that all of them are the efficient causes for their respective causal efficacies falls within the scope of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
It might be argued:
"The difference in appearance is not the cause of difference by way of having different properties (*dharma*), but rather by way of being indirect (*parokṣa*) or direct (*aparokṣa*).

For that [difference] cannot be established even by resorting to a difference in properties, because even in those [properties], cognition arises as either indirect or direct; and if one were to pursue further properties in those cases as well, it would lead to an infinite regress. If this is said:
No, for those two do not have the form of an object.
For the properties of cognition are of two kinds: the delimitation by an object and the distinction of genus.

In that regard, the distinction or the exclusion of non-distinction regarding an object occurs through the distinction of the delimitation of its objects, and not by means of a second [cognition], because that is established solely by the distinction of its causes, as in the case of perception, inference, and scripture.

And just as sensory cognition—belonging to the class of direct perception—is produced from a specific cause even when the objects differ, so too, why should it be denied that sensory and inferential cognition—belonging to the classes of both perceptual and non-perceptual—occurs from a specific cause even when the objects differ?
