Alternatively, in the case of exclusion (*vāraṇa*), the difference in causes would be irrelevant to the difference in effects, and thus that [difference] would result in being accidental (*ākasmika*).

If it is asked, "What is the definitive cause here for this difference in genus (*jāti-bheda*) rather than a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi-bheda*)?", the answer is simply experience (*anubhava*).

For at the time of determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), the states of being indirect (*pārokṣya*), direct (*apārokṣya*), memory (*smṛtitva*), and immediate experience (*anubhūtitva*) do not manifest; for what manifests is [the forms] "that possesses fire," "this possesses fire," and "he possesses fire."
However, at the time of the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), there is the manifestation of that [object], because of the mental articulation: "I infer this," "I see this," or "I remember that.
How then is there the conventional usage of "the object is remote" (*parokṣa*) or "it is perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*)? It is just as one says, for example, "inferred," "seen," or "remembered."

10–17)] As for the argument beginning with "even those things that are absolutely dissimilar," etc., that too is inconclusive due to doubt (*sandigdhānaikāntika*), because the conventional usage of similarity can be accounted for even by a positive property (*vidhi*) of that same nature.

For this conventional usage is neither causeless, nor does it have multiple causes, nor does it have as its single cause the non-relation of multiple things; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, this [cognition] remains as having multiple associations with a single cause; and if such a thing is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpa*), what contradiction could there be that would prevent pervasion (*vyāpti*)? On the contrary, it was previously shown that the contradiction lies precisely in its being of a negative nature (*niṣedharūpatā*). Enough, then, with these elaborate digressions! Nor does the conceptualization of *apoha* serve to account for practical activity (*pravṛtti*) and other worldly transactions; for if one were to act toward one object based on the appearance of another, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that this is not a fault because of "determination" (*adhyavasāya*), then what is this determination? Is it the appearance of the unreal as having the nature of a real entity, or as being identical in essence to the real entity, or the non-apprehension of their difference, or that which arises from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of real entities?
Not the first [alternative], because that [particular] does not appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Not the second, because it would follow that verbal expression and conceptual construction could not function with respect to a unique object (*asādhāraṇa-viṣaya*), since that [unique object] is not conventional (*asāmayika*). Therefore, there is an absolute contradiction between the conceptual construction and the real entity, just like the case of the eye and the sense of taste; for if they shared a common object, the real entity would not appear [in the cognition], because it is unique.

Not the third [alternative], because the rule of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the cognitive activity would be untenable, since the non-apprehension of difference is easily available everywhere.
If it is argued that "the difference from those [other things] has been apprehended," is this when those other things are being apprehended or when they are not?
Not the first, because even those particular characters (*svalakṣaṇa*) are beyond the scope of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because a difference whose limit is unknown does not manifest; or, if it were to manifest, the difference from even the intended specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is to be determined would be grasped, since there is no distinction [between them].

If it is argued that "the non-grasping of a difference from what has been grasped, but the grasping of it from what has not been grasped," then if the difference is defined by its properties (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the opposite would be the case.
If it is defined by its own nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), then due to the lack of distinction, it would be grasped from everything except where there is a grasping of identity (*tādātmya*).

If it is argued that since it lacks an intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpatvāt*), how could there be a distinction characterized by an intrinsic nature for it? [We reply: Then such a distinction would also exist for that which is not apprehended, as there is no difference [between the two cases]. If it is argued that although it lacks an intrinsic nature, it appears as if it possessed one and as if it were distinct, then is it not the case that it appears as if possessing an intrinsic nature in relation to the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), or does it flash forth as if it were the very nature of the object of determination? In the first case, there would either be no cognition at all, because there is no distinction [from non-cognition], or there would be a cognition of something devoid of intrinsic nature; in both instances, the application of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible.
The second [alternative], however, has already been refuted.

Nor is the fourth [possible], because it would entail the consequence that an experience of yellow— arising from the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of an experience of blue— would cause one to act toward a blue object.
If it is argued that experience is not the motivator, but rather conceptual construction (vikalpa), and since that [conceptual construction] has that very [object] as its domain;
[we reply: by "since" is meant either directly or through a causal chain.
In the first case, there follows the undesirable consequence that verbal and inferential cognitions would not be motivators.
But in the second case, that same over-extension remains.
If it is argued that there is a restriction because the operation of experience is prioritized, [we reply: no.
What is the meaning of "confirmation"?

It cannot be the state of having experience as its sole object, because conceptual thought does not touch that [experience]. Nor can it be the superimposition of the nature of experience upon itself, because conceptual thought is by definition free from construction (*kalpanāpodha*) and non-erroneous with respect to itself; and because with respect to its object, it has an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression. Furthermore, if there were no such determination, its status as conceptual thought would be contradicted; and when a specific [object] is perceived, a superimposition is impossible.
Nor can there be the superimposition of validity upon that [conceptual content], because if its object were indeterminate, the necessity of purposeful action would be untenable;
and if its object were ultimately real, it would follow that it is a conceptual construction involving synthesis.
Furthermore, there is no engagement with that which has an unreal object;
for it is denied that the unreal can manifest as if it were not unreal.

Nor is it the case that the failure to grasp the difference from one's own self [the cognition] itself constitutes the operation of that [cognition], because the nature [of the cognition] is known by itself and the difference from the object has already been established.
Nor is it immediacy (*apārokṣya*), because that too is common to all cognitions with respect to themselves,
whereas it is absent in the case of the object in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Even if such a state were possible, it would be untenable because it would fail to account for the restricted engagement [of cognition] with respect to other objects. Nor is there conformity to the object, because that too is absent.
For what indeed could be the identity of form between that which is ultimately real and that which is false?
If the word *rūpa* denotes the substratum (*dharmin*) and the word *samāna* is a synonym for "one," then what coherence is there with the subject at hand?
Or if *rūpa* denotes a property (*dharma*), and *samāna* means "one" or "of the same kind," even so, what coherence is there with the subject at hand?
If it is argued that this is "exclusion from what is not that" (*atadvyāvṛtti*), we say no;
for since that [exclusion] resides in both the unreal and the real, there is an absence of both unity and homogeneity.
If it is argued that this conventional usage of "similarity" (*sārūpya*) is merely based on conceit and not ultimate, we say no.
Because it is precisely *abhimāna* that is being considered;
for there is no such thing as another *abhimāna* that transcends the modes already considered.
By its very nature, a certain conceptual construction operates with respect to a particular object even when that object does not appear.
What can be done about this?
And this specific nature of it has come about solely from its own causes.

If it is asked, "In that case, who is to be questioned?"—then what? Does conceptualization (vikalpa) operate upon that [object] while being entirely unrelated, since there is no other form of relation; or is it related by way of its own nature (svabhāva); or is conventional usage (vyavahṛti) itself the relation? It cannot be the first, because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
In the second case, however, the answer would be by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet that itself is the manifestation.
For when engaging in practical activity (*vyavahāra*), there is no other relation of object and subject between cognition and the cognized apart from the proximity of intrinsic nature;

this is because it will be stated later that even for those who maintain the theory of the manifestation of an object as being existent, non-existent, or inexpressible (*sadasadanirvacanīyārthakhyāti*), the proximity of intrinsic nature is unavoidable.

In the third case, however, it is evident that there is self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), because one follows after a cause only with respect to the restriction of its own linguistic usage (*svavyavahāraniyama*).
If it is argued that this restriction is like the production of the non-existent from a causal power (*kāraṇaśakti*), [we reply: no.
True.

This must be considered: even by the power of the cause, it must be restricted to a specific genus; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of acting toward water as well, based on the conceptualization of fire.

If it is argued that a conceptualization of a form capable of burning and so forth causes one to act toward a real fire— such that either a universal (*jāti*) or an adjunct (*upādhi*) serves as the regulator—
then one would not act toward a mass of jewel-rays on that basis,
because the capacity to cause action toward that which belongs to such a class exists only with respect to fire.
If it is argued that this is because that very object manifests in that form,
let it manifest;

however, its fitness for engagement is not necessarily tied to that manifestation, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of non-engagement with a particular fire (*vahni-svalakṣaṇa*) due to a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of "fire."
Either accept that there is also a manifestation of that [non-existent object] therein, or else avoid activity toward what is not fire based on the conceptual construction of fire.
By this, the view that similarity of form (*ākārasārūpya*) is the cause of restriction is refuted.
For activity is observed even in the absence of similarity with the object to be sought, and mere similarity with what is not to be sought leads to over-extension. Furthermore,
in the externalist theory (*bāhyavāda*), the intended similarity between cognition and its object is impossible due to the disparity in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).
Alternatively, if there were equality between insentience (*jāḍya*) and sentience (*caitanya*), it would follow that one of them must be superfluous.

Nor can a distinction in effects be established based on internal differences even when there is equality, because [the effects] arise without being governed by a corresponding totality of causes (*sāmagrī*).

Furthermore, the equality of the causal totality cannot be inferred from the effect, because in external cases, the cause that follows upon smoke and so forth is perceptible, whereas in the case of the cognition of smoke, a deviation from that [cause] is observed.
Nor is it logical that the very same cause should be visible in one instance and invisible in another.

Furthermore, if blueness and so forth were a specific genus (*jāti*) belonging to cognition, how could it transcend that [cognition] to touch the object of knowledge? And if it belonged to the object of knowledge, how could cognition qualify it? This has been largely considered in the context of the introduction to the problem of the confusion of genera (*jātisaṅkara*).
Therefore, since there is no other alternative, one must—however grudgingly, like putting a sandal on the neck—accept that it is only that which has manifested (*sphurita*) that instigates activity.

If it is argued: "In that case, let it instigate activity toward its own manifested form alone; for once the seeker has engaged with that, he obtains an object similar to it, just as one who engages with the luster of a gem obtains the gem itself," we say: No.

Because there is no engagement with that which lacks the capacity for the desired purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Nor is it possible to superimpose the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) onto an external object, since the latter is not touched by the former.

Nor can one superimpose externality onto the form itself, because when its own nature (*svarūpa*) is manifesting, there is no opportunity for the superimposition of what is not its own nature (*asvarūpa*).
Furthermore, the example that one seeking a gem proceeds toward light only because of the cognition of a gem, and not because of a cognition of that [light] itself, is also fallacious.

Moreover, in the theory of the manifestation of forms (*ākāravāda*), there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of an object that does not manifest; for the occasional nature of forms is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of the forms of hair and so forth perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia.

Since even the correspondence with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*), when it manifests, has as its body nothing more than a mere form, and since an external object is unestablished; and because,

just like the forms of objects that lack a support (*nirālambana*), the form of causal efficiency might also— due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— be entirely without a support, there is no subverting argument against the counter-position, and thus the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) remains unestablished.
Therefore, the establishment of the external and the claim that cognition possesses a form are merely the whimsy of the ignorant.
Let it be, then, that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is indeed external is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Even though, by its own nature, it is not associated with conventions and is thus not capable of being connected with verbal expression, nevertheless, having attained a common form through its proximity to the exclusion of what is not of that nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*), it indeed becomes so.
For just as one cow is excluded from non-cows, so too are others; if this is argued, then what is this so-called "non-cow"?
Is it that the selflessness (*anātman*) belongs to a single specific cow-characteristic (*gosvalakṣaṇa*), or rather that it is the absence of properties belonging to that [cow]?

In the first case, the word "cow" and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would not apply even to another cow, because there would be no difference from horses and so forth in terms of their being non-self.

Furthermore, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): because the exclusion of non-cows—such as buffaloes and elephants—would result in the linguistic usage of "cow" being applied even to a horse.
If you argue that it is excluded from the cow as well, then does the intended cow not also exclude itself?
If it is argued that although the horse is excluded, this [cow] itself is also a cow—
then if its "cowness" consists merely in the exclusion of the non-cow, that is the same in the case of the horse as well.
If it is something else, let that be stated.
In the second case, however, that which is excluded from what is devoid of the property residing therein would be precisely that which possesses it;
and regarding that, there is no dispute.

If it is argued that the common form (*sādhāraṇaṃ rūpam*) may simply be the individual objects (*piṇḍa*) themselves, whose forms are mutually intermingled, and that there is no need for an exclusion of what is not that form (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*), we say: No,
because such an intermingling does not exist.
For that [universal] is not real, because individual objects are characterized by contradictory properties.
Nor is it merely a product of conceit, because a brindled cow (*śabaleya*) and others appear as distinct entities.
If it is argued that there is a conceit of identity regarding their properties, we say no.
Because no property other than those belonging to *dharma* itself is admitted; or,
if such were admitted, the dispute would be rendered futile.

It might be argued as follows: let it be that distinct particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone possess the capacity to generate conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) with a uniform form; and in relation to those [cognitions], some are designated as "cows" while others are designated as "non-cows.
In this regard, that capacity is not subject to further questioning, because it is determined by its own causes.

If it is argued that otherwise one would have to postulate another universal even for universals themselves in order to account for the corresponding linguistic usage, and likewise, that one must postulate a further ground for the subsistence of "cowness" (*gotva*) within individual cows in order to account for its restriction to them alone—and thus, in this way, there would be a downward infinite regress on both fronts—[we reply: If such is the case, why is a single linguistic usage not established by means of something entirely distinct from those [individuals], without depending on any other cause? Why is a distinct linguistic usage not likewise accomplished by means of some single non-distinct entity? For the recourse to the nature of capacities (*śakti-svabhāva*) is equal in both instances.

Now, this being the case, the conventional usage of "one" would not occur anywhere at all, or it would be without a basis; both of these are undesirable. (This is equal to the following: the conventional usage of "many" is also undesirable. Therefore, just as there is a conventional usage of "one" by means of a single [entity], so too there is a conventional usage of "many" by means of many; such is the restriction of functional capacity (*sāmarthya-niyama*).
3)] What, then, is the basis for the conventional usage of "one" with respect to multiple universals?
It is the same as that which serves as the basis for the conventional usage of "many" with respect to the single moon.
If it is argued that this [latter] is erroneous, then this [former] is also indeed erroneous,
because the subverting evidence is equal in both cases. If it is argued that everything must be erroneous, then why should the conventional usage of difference not also be so?

If it is argued that this is because of the stability of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsthiti*), then why do you not also see that there are similarities and dissimilarities in the causal efficiencies that establish the distinction or non-distinction between individuals? These too might be erroneous, and if so, the same applies to the distinction between causal efficiencies as well. If you say, "Let it be so," then abandon your obsession with external objects.
If it is argued that this very [intention] is the disposition (*āśaya*), we shall address that later.

Alternatively, let us assume there is no cognition of the similarity or dissimilarity of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Even so, how could there be a persistence of error (*bhrāntyanugama*) without disregarding a single underlying cause? For even that effect would, in the absence of a similarity of causal complexes (*sāmagrīsājātya*), result in being accidental (*ājaksmika*). Otherwise, even the recourse to a succession of such [causes] would be nothing but a mockery.

Since the conventional usage of non-difference is established by those various distinct individuals themselves—provided they are of such a nature—there is no point in the effort of pursuing that [universal]. Therefore, even for the conventional usage of superimposition (*āropa*), it is simply impossible if one disregards a universal that is not superimposed.

If it is argued: "In that case, let the establishment of *apoha* [as the universal] proceed on the grounds of a sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding the universal and so forth," we reply: Where is there a sublation when the conventional usage cannot be established otherwise?

Otherwise, even a *svabhāvahetu*—which, by bringing forward a powerful subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), rests upon the impossibility of being established otherwise (*ananyathāsiddhi*)—would be destroyed by the mere suspicion of a subverting argument. Therefore, setting aside the obsession with subverting arguments, let the practice of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) be established as possible in another way;
yet this is not possible, because there is no other alternative.
Furthermore, there is no subverting proof either;
for that [proof] would have to exist either by way of its own nature or by way of cognition.
[The proof] would consist either in non-perception even of the intrinsic nature [of the object], or in the attribution of contradictory properties.
It is not the first, because it is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
For one begins to contemplate the body of a common form (*sādhāraṇākāra*) only while it is manifesting, not when it is unmanifest.

You might argue: "We deny the manifestation of the common form in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but not in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because that is established by those whose vision is clouded by a mass of darkness consisting of the grasping of similar conventions, and not by us; for the treasury of mental constructions (*kalpanākoṣa*), due to its immediate proliferation, does not establish reality. This is not so, because [the cognition] arises even in the absence of the association with words (*śabdānusandhāna*).

8)] Even so, if it is argued that this occurs solely due to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that [word], then does the conceptual determination of a single form arise by the force of the latent impression of grasping the convention for a common word even in the absence of a single object of that convention, or when such an object exists?

It cannot be the first case; for, just as in the case of various individuals possessing dewlaps and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a corresponding conceptual determination occurring even in the case of words such as *svarga*, *locana*, *bāṇa*, *ambu*, and *kuliśa*—despite the absence of a single referent—merely by virtue of the latent impression of grasping the convention for the word "cow" (*go*).

If it is argued that this object is indeed desired [by him], [we reply: he does not perceive a common form among individual cows possessing dewlaps and so forth, yet he perceives one among the ten things denoted by the word "cow. What can be said here? Surely his eye is nothing but his own whim!
If it is argued that this could be said by the other [party] as well, [we reply: it may be said, but it is impossible to subvert the linguistic usage rooted therein.
5–8)] But surely, even by this much, conceptual construction may be established; however, how can direct experience be?
Precisely because conceptual construction is established as having a real object.

If it is asked, "How does that have a real basis (*savastukatā*)?"—[we reply: "Because of the destruction of other causes such as the latencies of sound (*śabdavāsanā*)," so remain silent. If it is asked, "Why is it not perceived in the interval?"—[we reply: "Because of the absence of the causes for perception."
If it is asked, "Why is the whole not perceived in the bowl, just as a jujube fruit is perceived there?"— it is not so,
because they do not occupy different locations.
However, it is indeed perceived through its distinction, because when a lump is experienced as not being in contact with other lumps, it is experienced as being in contact with that [other] one.
Nor is the second [objection] a subverting argument, because the whole shares the same status regarding proof and refutation.

If it is argued that the connection with the body being born is untenable because [the universal] does not migrate, because it is non-existent there, and because it is not produced there—if this is your view: how, then, was it known by you that it is non-existent there?

If you say, "Because if it were existent there, it would follow that even the space (*ākāśa*) and so forth located there would possess the nature of a cow," we reply: this is not the case, for even later on it does not connect with the space and so forth located there;
and as for the body with which it *does* connect, it is never absent from that very place.
How, then, can there be a contradiction?

Even if one were to employ the term "there" figuratively by taking the physical body— which is like a useless goitre— as a mere indicator, then since that usage is established solely through the body's approaching, receding, arising, and perishing, the claim that "it does not go" and so forth is merely empty boasting on the part of an archer who has missed his mark.

For instance, the absence of approaching and departing with respect to the individual object (*piṇḍa*), and the existence and non-existence with respect to the location characterized by that [object]— how could these be consistent? Furthermore,
if it is argued that its non-existence is easily established when the individual object has not yet arisen, on the grounds that "it does not exist because [the object] is absent"— this is not so.
Since the existence or non-existence of an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) does not depend on a second entity, whereas connection or non-connection do depend on a second entity,
what is the meaning of the statement "it does not exist when that [second entity] is absent"?
If it is argued that [the effect] is not connected because it is non-existent,
that is indeed so.
If it is asked how it could be connected later on:
Because that non-connection exists, it is necessitated by the non-existence of that [effect];

thus, the objection—"How can the lump, which did not exist previously, come into being later?"—comes to an end. And since that [objection] falls into the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), it is a case of "vomiting what one has not even swallowed."
Even so, if it is asked how there can be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) when the universal and its possessor are absolutely distinct, we reply:
what is this?
For grammatical coreferentiality is a relation with a common substratum; and we do not perceive any contradiction between that [relation] and distinction.
If it is argued that this would lead to the same consequence for cows and horses as well, [we reply]:
surely that is the locus of a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*), not a locus of contradiction.

And if even among the sons of Maitra there were someone who was dark-skinned, then the same consequence would apply to those who are currently being observed; where, indeed, would such a thing be difficult to find?
If it is argued that a distinction must nevertheless be stated, we reply:
there exists an intrinsic distinction such that only some things are related to some things, and not everything with everything.
If it is asked: "Why should the rule of following (*anugamana-niyama*) not also arise from the very nature of things?

[The answer is: because there is no contradiction in one thing being related to many, nor in many things being related to one; however, there is a contradiction in the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of "one" and "many" being applied to what is "many" and "one," respectively.
Nor is there a sublation by means of cognition; for the rejection of its own nature is contradicted by experience,
the rejection of its cause is discarded by its very arising,
and the rejection of its oneness is thwarted by the absence of the superimposition of contradictory properties.
Because mediacy, immediacy, and so forth are unestablished;
because it is impossible to deny the validity of that [cognition] without denying its object; because it has already been shown that such an object cannot be denied;
and because the denial of its being produced by the sense organs is sublated by the fact that it conforms to the presence and absence of those sense organs.
And because there is no deviation from its conformity once it has come to rest in the state of being a direct perception (*sākṣātkāritva*);
otherwise, it would follow that even non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) would not be produced by the sense organs.
For the cognition of a woman afflicted by desire arises even without that [external object],
and since there is no sublation (bādhaka), there is no occasion to postulate that it is conditioned by the operation of perception;
otherwise, if such an occasion existed, it would follow that one could likewise postulate its being a misconception (viparyaya).

If a direct conceptual cognition were to arise solely through the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) without depending on the sense faculty, there would be the undesirable consequence that its opposite would never arise;
for its initial production is dependent upon the absence of auxiliary factors such as prior memory. This is the general direction of the argument.

Suppose, then, that the acceptance of *apoha* is for the sake of a specific purpose. If you argue that the supreme purpose is indeed the establishment of the ineffability of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-avācyatva*), because through the shaking off of the web of conceptual constructions one attains a profound and sublime meditative absorption (*samādhi*), we reply: who would have faith in this which lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

Neither perception (*pratyakṣa*) nor inference (*anumāna*) serves as a means of valid cognition here; and as for scripture (*āgama*), you yourself have already convinced your disciple that it says nothing at all.
Furthermore, such a conscious being cannot even be made to understand this, because the contradiction with one's own words is so blatant.
To explain: [ĀtTaViv (B: 423. 1–7 = C: 509. 10–510. 2)] Nor can a conscious being be made to accept this, because the contradiction with one's own words is so prominent.
For instance:
Is there, with respect to any object whatsoever, any conventional operation of negation or affirmation established by the mind through words— either in some cases or not?
If it certainly exists, then how is it that there are not so many refutations?
If it does not exist at all, then the proof [of your position] is contradicted by your own words.
Thus, this verse is merely directed at you because of your shifting of the subject matter.

Nor is silence your only recourse here, as it is for us; for such silence is appropriate only for one who remains indifferent when there is a contradiction in every respect regarding speech. But here, in this positive injunction, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Furthermore, you are not indifferent, because you have engaged in this for a specific purpose.
Therefore, enough with this finger-lamp; let us proceed to the method for destroying the darkness.

Since the engagement of those seeking heaven and liberation would not be established if there were a contradiction regarding the scripture's contact with the reality of things, it is precisely our own investigation that is supremely excellent in its purpose.

Therefore, regarding the inquiry as to what is denoted by words—whether it be from the perspective of appearance (*pratibhāsa*), or from the perspective of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), or in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*)—the following has been answered in succession: that the form excluded from others (*anyāpoḍhākāra*) residing in conceptual construction, the particular characteristic excluded from others (*anyāpoḍhasvalakṣaṇa*), and "nothing at all" have each been refuted. Among these, in the first case, there is a contradiction with convention (*samayaviparyāsa*), because the form of conceptual construction is not the object of linguistic convention.

In the second case, however, there is a contradiction regarding activity, because there would be no regulating factor for that which has not yet been seen. In the third case, there is a self-contradiction; for by this [statement], one is stating the reality of this very same point, or else, if one does not state it, it would not be a response in reality—this is the conclusion. Thus, it is established that momentariness does not constitute a sublation of the self.
Thus ends the discourse on momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda). 519.
[The Refutation of the Theory of External Objects:
If it is argued that while the Proponent of Cognition (Vijñānavādin) is awake, external objects themselves do not exist; how then could there be a self?

Being thus questioned, let him explain this: do you intend to express that the two parts—the apprehended and the apprehender—are non-different while being ultimately real; or rather, that they belong to the same genus; or else, that the apprehended portion is unreal?

In that regard, whatever reason (*hetu*) is adduced for the first thesis to be proven—whether it be the necessity of simultaneous perception, the state of being an object of apprehension, or the state of being manifest—it is clearly fallacious.
For indeed,
a cognition is experienced as apprehending a multitude of mutually contradictory forms, such as blue, white, and so forth; this is like raising a weapon for its own destruction.
For if it were to delineate mutually opposing properties, how could that single existent be of the nature of both?
And if it were not to delineate them, how could it be said to have that form?
For self-awareness lacks any form that is not delineated.

Fear arises regarding the external object because it is superimposed with such contradictory properties; for even if that were the case, if there were no difference [between subject and object], there would follow the consequence of a confusion (*saṅkara*) among purposeful action, consciousness, and volitional activity, as well as the consequence of the impossibility of discernment (*vivecanānupapatti*). However, this is not the case for cognition (*vijñāna*), for its existence does not depend upon purposeful action, but rather depends solely upon appearance. Furthermore, there is no volitional activity directed toward purposeful action therein, because there is no purposeful action distinct from the naturally flowing stream of cognition, nor is there anyone who desires such purposeful action.
If it is argued that the absence of discrimination (*vivecanābhāva*) is the ultimate consummation because its nature is self-cognized (*svasaṃviditarūpatva*), then what of it?

Does consciousness, having reached a state like the hermitage of one whose tranquility has matured, result in the abandonment of eternal enmity—such as between a snake and a mongoose—regarding blue, white, and so forth; or does it result in the abandonment of their mutual hostility, which is like the abandonment of the fruits of long-standing enmities by those who have become quiet?

First of all, the first [alternative] is not tenable; for if there were no contradiction between affirmation and negation—which are inseparable from one another’s negation and affirmation—then the consequence would follow that contradiction is utterly abolished in the world.

Nor can it be said that this is acceptable as a conclusion, because even in such a case there is no cessation of the aforementioned nature [of contradiction], since contradiction consists in nothing more than that.
And since the establishment of that [non-difference] is itself the establishment of difference, the second [alternative] is also not tenable.
As for the distinction shown for the sake of maintaining consistency regarding external objects, let that belong to those [externalists] alone.

For if one has confidence that the attribution of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) establishes difference, what is the point of adducing the restriction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāpratiniyama*)?

If not, then even so, what is the use of it? For even that [restriction] would only exist when there is a difference established by the attribution of contradictory properties to the two causal efficiencies.

Furthermore, just as there would be no restriction regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the external world—this being the "punishment"—likewise, there would be no restriction regarding the manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) in cognition either; this is indeed the very "punishment.

If it is asked, "Where is the restriction that prevents a confusion of manifestations? Might they not manifest simultaneously? we reply: No, we do not mean that non-confusion consists in non-perception at the same time; rather, we mean the non-perception of blue as yellow, or of yellow as blue.
That alone is the root of all contradictions;
otherwise, even the perception and non-perception [of the object] would remain unestablished.

Even that which is said to be unperceived is indeed perceived; for the very statement that "that which is perceived, such as a horse and so forth, is not perceived" is itself a cessation [of the claim of non-perception].
If you argue that it is not perceived in its own nature, then does yellow ever appear as blue even when they are perceived together, such that there would be no contradiction?
Therefore, both contradictions are equal and equally capable of being resolved through the abandonment of [the notion of] difference.
If the maturity of only one [of the two forms] were to occur— according to the maxim of the beautiful mendicant girl— by this,
the absence of discrimination is also refuted, because discrimination consists precisely in the cognition of the two forms without their being confounded.
Moreover, if all things are momentary, how can there be a discernment of external objects even from the perspective of a single person?
Even from the perspective of multiple persons, it remains doubtful.

If it is argued that there is no doubt because one person informs another, [we reply: it is precisely through non-difference [that the distinction is made]. The goal is the discernment (*vivecana*) of reality; and if that were so, what would be the use of presenting that [information] as well?
For even in the case of cognition, which belongs to the same class as external objects, there must indeed be discernment.

[The opponent argues: "This superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), being sublated by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), does not establish difference; this is like a stick for driving camels, since it is by self-awareness itself that this [superimposition] is established. [The author replies: Then let the manifestation (*prakāśamānatā*) establish multiplicity, and the superimposition of contradictory properties also establish unity. Even so, what follows for the nature of the manifestation of forms such as blue, which are devoid of both unity and multiplicity? This is merely a distraction from the field by fools.

For indeed, unity is simply the state of having a determinate form, while plurality is the state of having an indeterminate form; and upon the cessation of those two, there remains nothing but the formless, since it would neither have the form of blue nor the forms of blue, yellow, and so forth.
This might be argued.

If it is argued that the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is the cause of difference in the ultimate sense, whereas this [superimposition] is merely conceptual (*kālpānika*), then in that case, the formless purity of consciousness would be established all the more effortlessly, like a crystal; and the multitude of forms would manifest as something other than the Self (*anātman*). Thus, in either case, the arguments such as "simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambha*) are *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (vitiated by the lapse of time). Furthermore, let alone the consideration of the superimposition of contradictory properties.

This distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender, or the distinction between the blue object and so forth that appears—does it exist as real or as unreal? If it were real, that same fault [of the loss of unity] would follow.

If it were unreal, then this [distinction] would not be the nature of consciousness; thus, even in the case of what is not-self, there is an incapacity [to prove identity] due to the rule of simultaneous perception, and therefore the argument is inconclusive.
If it is argued that difference does not manifest at all, then let there be, for now, either a contradiction with the cognition common to all people or a contradiction with one's own words.
In that case, the reasons (hetus) are unestablished;
for when difference does not manifest, we do not perceive either the meaning of "together" (sahārtha) or its pervasion (tadvyāpyatā).

If that [difference] does not even appear, how can there be a distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the other members of the argument? For whom are you attempting to teach, and for what purpose? If neither positive nor negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is perceived, what power does the reason (*hetu*) possess, and from where does the disagreement arise, and of what nature is it?
Thus he begins this investigation, yet he does not even accept difference as being merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*); surely even a madman has been surpassed by him!

If it is argued that only a difference established in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a factor for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), and not one established in direct experience (*anubhava*), then even that [difference] does not escape the alternatives of whether it appears as true or false.
If it is argued that what is non-existent and not appearing at all is nevertheless determined (*adhyavasīyate*), this term "determined" requires further clarification.

If it is argued that the purpose of determination (*adhyavasāya*) is the production of a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding that object, then: if that convention is itself of the nature of non-cognition, how could it be produced by that [determination]?
If it is of the nature of cognition, how can it have that as its object without a regulating factor (*niyāmaka*)?

If you say, "By the power of the causal complex of its own causes," then this person—while there is no other regulating factor for the distinction between a cognition in the form of a convention and a false [external] object—relies on the power of the cause to posit the relationship of object and subject (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*), yet does not do so for the experience and the experienced. This is like someone who, having lost his appetite for milk, develops a craving for fermented sorrel (*sauvīra*).

If it is argued that even difference (*bheda*) is merely a form of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*) and not external, then if it is indeed non-existent, how can it be a form of conceptual construction?
If it has that form, reflect upon this: how can it be non-existent?
If it is argued, "Let it then be that [consciousness] exists as a real entity," [we reply]: if consciousness perceives non-duality, how can there be the manifestation of difference?
If it perceives two forms, how can a single thing possess a dual nature?
If you say it has a variegated form (*citrākāra*), then for you who observe it, this is already swallowed by the dilemma of whether the variegated is one or many.
If there is multiplicity, how can there be identity with a single cognition?
And if the cognition itself is multiple according to its various forms, how can there be the perception of a variegated form, since each [form] would be cognized only as its own self?
If, on the other hand, it is a unity, how can there be the perception of diversity?

If it is argued that the determination of multiplicity is produced solely by the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from various things such as non-blue and so forth, then: if there is no identity (*atādātmya*) between the thing and those exclusions, how can there be a mention of the exclusions?
If there is identity (*tādātmya*), how can there be multiplicity?
Even if there is unity, how can there be a determination of difference produced by that?

If it is argued that this "multiplicity" is merely the manifestation (*ullekha*) of this consciousness and not a separate reality, then one must state whether it is its own nature (*svarūpa*) or not its own nature.
In the first case, who other than a fool would say that a single thing has a multiple nature?
As for the second [alternative], however, it is indeed accepted by us; yet it must be accepted by you as well.
If you say, "This is an error," then even in that [error], either its own nature or what is not its own nature would manifest, since there is no other possibility.
It might be argued:

"Just as that [object] does not, in reality, become that very thing even though it appears as such, so too this [subject] does not become that very thing even though it appears as non-that; therefore, even when its own nature appears as non-that, there is no impairment whatsoever of the definition of the apprehended object. If, however, even this appearance as non-that were itself the very nature of this [subject], then perhaps this argument would be useful for the present context.

If it is asked how there can be manifestation of that which is not its own nature (*asvarūpa*), we shall indeed explain it in that way; nevertheless, let one also direct one's attention to this: how can "non-thatness" (*atattā*) be its own nature? Furthermore, what fault is there in the manifestation of that which is not its own nature?

If it is argued that this relationship between the distinct object of cognition (*vedya*) and the cognizer (*vedaka*) is not based on a causal operation, because such a restricted operation is absent; nor is it based on their genus, because that would lead to the untenable consequence that there could be no fixed determination such that "one thing is to be known by another"; for indeed, such a procedure does not exist among naturally established categories like "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth—then surely this same fault remains in the case of non-difference as well.

For instance, the expression "the cognition of itself" is not a conventional usage based on an activity (*vyāpāra*), because such an activity is absent in respect to its own self; nor is it based on a genus (*jāti*), because that would entail the consequence of commonality. Indeed, no restriction is observed such that by virtue of its genus alone a cow cognizes itself but not another; furthermore, cognition does not cognize another in the same way it cognizes itself, for that would result in the absurdity of everyone being omniscient.

If it is argued that it belongs to no one, but is merely a cognition (*vedana-mātra*), even so, just as it is non-inert with respect to itself, it would have to be non-inert with respect to another; and just as it is blind with respect to another, it would follow that it is also blind with respect to itself, because its nature is such by its very kind (*jāti*).

If it is further argued that, although it is of such a kind, it was produced from its own causes in some specific way so that it possesses this particular form, you should not speak so loudly, for others too might hear it thus.
If it is argued: "Let there be no non-difference, or let it not; however, we deny difference by means of its being manifest," we say no.
For in a real entity, the very cessation of difference is the nature of non-difference.

Suppose, then, that the variegated [cognition] is indeed devoid of both difference and non-difference, because manifestation is impossible if there is non-difference, and because variegation is untenable if there is non-difference. This is not so; for just as the simultaneous affirmation of two mutually contradictory properties is impossible in one place, so too is the negation of both.
Nor should it be said, "Let that [negation of both] also exist," for by entering into the doctrine of *syād-vāda*, you would likewise fall into the position of a Digambara.

[ĀtTaViv 477.14–19] Suppose, then, that the painting is simply empty of the four peaks, because it is of a wondrous nature; for if it is argued that its existence despite the absence of both unity and plurality constitutes its "wondrous" meaning—since the word *citra* (painting/wondrous) signifies a marvel—then why should it not rather be the pinnacle of the four peaks? For the reason given—that it possesses a wondrous nature—is the same. Furthermore, just as the non-establishment of each individual alternative results in the negation of that alternative, so too would it result in the affirmation of its opposite.

Moreover, regarding the actual absence of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) here, this has been stated by way of another expression: that these four alternatives appear as being truly selfless, or rather, do not appear at all.

Among these, their non-appearance is not a [valid] response. But as for their appearing, it is a marvel that they possess the nature of an object (*grāhya*), even though they lack the defining characteristics of an object.
And thus, rather than a non-dualism of the variegated, let there be a dualism of the variegated, in accordance with its manifestation.
This might be so.

If you argue: "Let there be a destruction of the characteristic of being an object (*grāhyalakṣaṇa*) both externally and internally; however, the fact that blue and other things are manifest (*prakāśamānatva*) cannot be denied, and that alone is what we accept," then this is like guarding a cow after it has already been sold.
For what is this "manifestness" which is not destroyed even when the characteristic of being an object is entirely destroyed?
It is not a relation with light, as it was stated that such a restriction would be untenable.

Therefore, one who wishes to preserve the manifestness of blue and other objects must either exert effort toward the definition of the apprehended (*grāhya-lakṣaṇa*) or abandon that manifestness itself.
Otherwise, you are like one who laughs at the person who removes gold from a garment and ties it into a knot, while you yourself take up the gold and tie it into a knot on the hem of the sky.
Thus, this is unestablished (*asiddha*) in every respect and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in every respect.
By this, the second position is refuted.
For the deficiency of the object's defining characteristic (*grāhyalakṣaṇa*) is not removed by its being of the same class (*sajātīyatva*), since the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains as it was.

If it is argued that in the case of insentience (*jaḍatva*), the manifestation of light is impossible, we say no, because the situation is symmetrical. For just as for one who maintains that cognition is not self-cognized (*asvasamvedana*), cognition—even though manifest—remains insentient within itself when considered from the perspective of another; likewise, for one who maintains self-cognition (*svasamvedana*), cognition—even though manifest within itself—remains insentient when considered from the perspective of another. If it is claimed that cognition is non-insentient even with respect to another cognition in some way, then why should it not be so with respect to external objects? Thus, the reason is of doubtful occurrence in the counter-example (*sandigdhavipakṣavṛttitva*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the external world the characteristic of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyalakṣaṇa*) is entirely destroyed, whereas here, by the rule of having a common material cause (*upādāna*), there is established the mutual awareness of various forms even though they are ultimately distinct?
[Reply: No.

For if there is a rule regarding their mutual manifestation, one must speak either of a material cause or, in general, of the capacity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), since otherwise such an effect would not arise; and thus, this [same argument] is easily applicable even to the arising of a cognition whose nature is restricted to an external object, so the previous fault remains.
[ĀtTaViv 489.

5–9] “Let the third alternative then be the case, since the definition of an object of apprehension (*grāhyalakṣaṇa*) is in every way untenable; for in its absence, it is impossible to even rely upon the causal efficacy of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*). If you argue that reflection on causes has its occasion only when an entity is established through investigation, and not when it remains undiscriminated—then does the manifestation of these [entities] cease because their definition as objects of apprehension cannot be stated, or does their existence (*sattva*) cease?

Not the first [alternative], for it is not possible to deny an object of definition (*lakṣya*)—even one clearly perceived—merely by means of a lack of knowledge regarding its definition; for such lack of knowledge can be accounted for even by its being difficult to comprehend, and because the negation of those [definitions] is untenable in the absence of their appearance.

Not the second [alternative], for in that case, the non-occurrence of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) would exclude existence; if the characteristic were applicable to non-existence, then since it is inapplicable in both ways, why this attachment to non-existence?
If you say, "Because that very thing is the characteristic," then why should existence itself not be so?
If you say, "Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)," that is the same [for both].

If it is argued that [the object] is the domain of conventional usage dependent upon feeling (*vedanā*), let this be granted for now; however, from where does the restriction [that it belongs] "to that very [feeling]" arise?
If it is argued that such an arising of feeling occurs from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then this is possible only when [the object] exists, but not when it is non-existent—this is the distinction.

For just as when there is knowledge, there arises desire; from that, effort; from that, activity; and by that, the attainment of the object is accomplished—such is not the case with the unreal (*alīka*), because it is impossible to attain it, or else, if it were possible to attain, it would not be unreal.
If it is argued that this very conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is also unreal, then all the more so there is an absence of a definition, since even the means to it (*taddvāra*) is absent.

If it is argued, "Let it be that the universe is simply incapable of withstanding analysis in every respect," then does this mean there is now a collapse of reality (*tattvopaplava*), or a void at the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhāśūnyatā*)?

It cannot be the first, because there is no evidence for the stability of an inquiry that has reached such a stage; or, if such stability did exist, how could there be a collapse of reality, since this very inquiry itself would not have collapsed, and by the same logic, other things would likewise attain that state, rendering [the claim of collapse] fruitless.
For its fruit is neither excessive engagement, because one remains unsatisfied by tasting the sky, nor is it the removal of heat by embracing a mass of illusory flames;
nor is it excessive withdrawal, because even in mere insensibility, suffering that has already descended does not cease.
Nor is suffering itself something that need not be abandoned simply because it cannot withstand analysis, for one who is in such a state lacks the capacity for analysis.
Nor is there a fixed status according to worldly convention, for even prior to investigation, that status is established effortlessly for common people and others alike.
Nor is there cessation from the mere next world, since that is equal to this world.
If it is argued that "this [world] is indeed seen," then if the term "seen" (dṛśi) refers to cognition, the other world is likewise so.
If it is said that [the scripture] is a statement of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), then it follows that inference and the like would have no scope here at all.

If it is argued that even that [inference] is indeed direct perception, then the otherworldly [result] is likewise nothing but direct perception; even so, what is the use of inquiry? For even without it, that [perception] is easily obtained. If it is argued that this [inquiry] nourishes that very [perception], we reply that it is because they share the same defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). If it is argued that there is no engagement with that [otherworldly result] simply due to a lack of interest, then, since there is no difference [between the two cases], one should likewise nourish [the perception] here as well.

[ĀtmaViv 499.10–17] Having heard news of the Son of the Wind (Hanumān), a young monkey, leaping a certain distance in emulation of his prowess, fell into the great ocean and said: "This shoreless Akūpāra is false; the *Rāmāyaṇa* is a lie. What is the use of this?
Just as in the state of a commoner, it is entirely fruitless even to know or to declare merely this much: "What kind of world is this?"
Nor is this [claim] to be trusted even if it were fruitless, for it can be accounted for simply by the absence of proficiency in such reflective discernment (*parāmarśa*).
For it is not the case that because a person blind from birth is unable to know or describe blue, therefore that [color] is unknowable or indescribable for the world at large.
[ĀtTaViv 501.9–17]

If it is argued that emptiness alone is the supreme nirvāṇa, we say no; for if that [emptiness] is unestablished, how can the entire universe be said to have it as its remainder, since mere words are easily available everywhere?
If it is established by another, then that other must also be admitted, and the characteristic of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyalakṣaṇa*) becomes unavoidable.
And if that "other" is merely conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), there would be no distinction between the universe and emptiness; how then could even that [emptiness] remain?
If the other is of an unconditioned nature, then if it is established by another, there is an infinite regress.
If it is not established by itself, how could it establish emptiness?
If it is established by itself, then you have arrived at our path.

For instance: because it is established by itself, its nature is that of self-experience; and because it is emptiness (*śūnyatva*), it is not limited by time, and is thus eternal. For this very reason, it is not limited by space, and is thus all-pervading (*vyāpaka*). For this very reason, it is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*) and untouched by investigation, since investigation proceeds by taking recourse to the relationship between attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*). For this very reason, there is an absence of particulars (*viśeṣa*), and thus it is non-dual (*advaita*), because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not ultimately real. Furthermore, being "without a counter-correlative" (*niṣpratiyogika*), it is positive in nature (*vidhirūpa*); however, this is with respect to the unexamined phenomenal world.

The conventional expression is "empty. Nevertheless, what connection can there be between pure experience—which is empty of conceptual proliferation (prapañca)—and that proliferation? If it is asked, "Is it not the case that this [experience] does not manifest? [the answer is: in reality, there is no connection whatsoever; however, from the perspective of conventional truth (saṃvṛtti), there is a subject-object relationship, just like the relationship of container and contained between the sky and a city of Gandharvas. And this [relationship] is exactly as it will be established by the Naiyāyikas; the distinction in this system is simply that this [subject-object relation] is grounded in the object of cognition (vedya).
For it is ignorance itself that manifests in such and such ways that it is experienced and designated as such and such.

And due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) brought about by its respective *māyā*, even pure experience (*anubhūti*) enters the path of conventional discourse as if it were divided, just as the sky appears divided by the millions of hollows in the pots and pans seen in a dream.
Let this suffice for now; why should a seller of ginger worry about the ship?
Therefore, it is unavoidable that even the non-self (anātman) flashes forth when experience is established;
for once that [non-self] is established, there must necessarily be some characteristic belonging to it as well.

And that [relation], when there is no contradiction with the external object, resides either in the cognition alone or in both; when there is a contradiction with the external object, it resides in the cognition alone; but when that [cognition] is eternal, it resides in the object alone.
For instance, the defining characteristic (*lakṣya*) here is the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*).
And that is a specific nature consisting merely in the fact that the manifesting consciousness (*prakāśa*), being existent, belongs to that [object].
And precisely because it is its very nature, it does not depend on any further assistance; and precisely because it belongs to that [nature] alone, it does not belong to anything else.

Even when the question arises, "What is the fruit of this?", there is the external engagement in conventional usage regarding its object, and internally, there is the determination of the cognition by means of it.
Even when questioned as to why it is of such a nature, the answer is simply the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), just as in the case of cause and effect.
Otherwise, if another auxiliary factor were required for that [power] as well, there would be an infinite regress; if no such factor is required, who can prevent its being common to all?
Therefore, one must discern that "that very thing is produced," and "by this [cause], this very thing is made an object."

One must investigate what is meant by "being made an object" (*viṣayīkriyate*) and what is meant by "being produced" (*kriyate*). It should be discerned that "producing" (*karaṇa*) is simply the generation of an effect, and "being made an object" is simply arising as belonging to that [cause].

Furthermore, one should reflect that just as here [in the case of cognition] there is no assistance (*upakāra*) distinct from the nature of consciousness itself, so too here [in the case of causality] there is no effect distinct from the nature of the cause.
[ĀtTaViv 519.7–12]

Therefore, it is a great rashness to claim that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must also be disregarded; for if that were the case, the dilemmas "it would necessarily exist" or "it would necessarily not exist" would arise, and consequently, one or the other of light and darkness would result in being immutable (*kauṭasthya*).

If you argue, "Let it be conventional (*sāṃvrta*)," then let the subject-object relation (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*) also be so. There are only two possible courses: if there is a powerful sublation (*bādha*) between the object and its effect, then it is conventional; if not, then it is not. [ĀtTaViv 522.1–8]
The truth of the matter here is this:
first of all, the definition does not reside in both [existence and non-existence], because there is a manifestation even of that which is stable, whether it be existent or non-existent.

Nor can it reside in an external object that is ultimately real while cognition is eternal, because that would exclude the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) and thereby destroy the Sāṅkhya system.
Indeed, there is no occasion even for investigation without the prior disappearance and subsequent manifestation [of an object];

nor can it be established as residing in momentary cognition by way of being an unreal apprehended object, because that which is void lacks specific qualities, because cognition is devoid of form (nirākāra), and because it is impossible to superimpose [such an object] since it is unestablished elsewhere as well.

If it is argued that even non-existent particulars appear, we say no; for "non-existent" means either belonging to another time or another place, or being of no nature at all, or having the nature of a mere exclusion (vyāvṛtti).
In the first case, there would be the consequence of their existence in other times and places.
In the second case, however, they would lack the status of being particulars.

In the third case, if blue—which is unreal—is of the nature of the exclusion of non-blue (*anīla-vyāvṛtti*), it follows that non-blue things would be ultimately real; if those [non-blue things] were unreal, then blue, whose essence is their exclusion, would result in being non-unreal.
Even so, if it were unreal, there would be no distinction [between them].
If it is argued that there is indeed no distinction in terms of that form, then by what means is there a distinction?
If it is said to be by way of blue, yellow, and so forth, then is that something additional to it? In that case, it would have to be non-false (analīka).
If it is not additional, then from where could it come by means of that [other] either?

If it is argued that particularities manifest due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), let them manifest; who would object to the cause? However, if those [particularities], such as blue and so forth, were of the nature of nothingness (*akiñcidrūpa*), how could they be particularities? We reply: if they are of the nature of nothingness in one form, then in that very form they are indeed of the nature of something (*kiñcidrūpa*).

If you argue that "unreality" (alīkatva) is merely the inability to withstand analysis, even so, this is merely a change of terminology; for the inability to withstand analysis is contradictory to having any form whatsoever. Or, if there is no contradiction, then even blue and other such objects—which do not withstand your own analysis—would indeed possess some form, leading to the undesirable consequence that your own analysis is itself a "bad analysis" (durvicāra), since it does not even touch upon the mere shadow of blue and the rest. Either enter the belly of the doctrine of "indescribable manifestation" (anirvacanīyakhyāti), or abandon the mire of your own intellect and remain within the path of logic by accepting the ultimate reality of blue and the rest.
Therefore,
there is no functioning of cognitions apart from the distinction of the objects grasped.
If this powerful means of knowledge is sublated, then victory belongs to the doctrine of sensation;
if not, then this very world is such as it is—blameless and real—and what room is there for the Tathāgata? (1)

In this regard, let that very "investigation" (vicāra) be examined— what it is and of what nature— which serves as the basis for proclaiming the world to be false, or indescribable, or incapable of withstanding investigation.

If you argue that it is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) accompanied by reasoning (*satarka*) as established in verbal form, then if that too cannot withstand investigation, what is the use of such a pseudo-investigation that is merely a fabrication?

For instance, a certain fool, having seen an elephant at the king’s gate, speculated: “Is this darkness eating up the roots? Or is it a cloud raining and thundering over cranes? Or perhaps this is a kinsman, according to the words of the supreme teacher: ‘He who stands at the king’s gate or in the cremation ground is a kinsman. Or else, is this the shadow of that which is seen upon the ground? And he was refuted: “In that case, the first [option] is not possible, because the flapping of a pair of winnowing baskets is inconsistent with it. Nor is the second, because it lacks the four pillars.”
Not the third, because he lacks the whirling of a club;
nor the fourth, because he lacks the disgorging of a hundred human heads.
Therefore, this is nothing at all.
Does the true nature of the elephant cease to exist merely because of this? Or rather, it would be better to have a second fool as a proponent who says, "This is that very thing.

If you argue that it withstands such investigation, then it has already dissolved of its own accord through arguments such as "the false" (alīka) and so forth; there is no need even to wait for a further response.

If it is argued that [the truth] is established by worldly consensus (*lokasiddha*), then its "purity of context" (*parikaraśuddhi*) must likewise be accepted as such; otherwise, if one were to transgress even worldly consensus, inquiry would result in nothing more than arbitrary verbalism. In the world, a sentence is a factor for the comprehension of meaning when it possesses expectancy, semantic competency, and proximity; when its parts are syntactically connected; when its meaning is not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); when it is free from defects such as contradicting one's own words, one's own actions, or one's own knowledge; and when it does not imply a reason that subverts its own intended meaning—just as in the case of the statement, "This mountain over there possesses fire."

The other [types of cognition] are devoid of the [essential] constituent (anaṅga), such as: "This is white in front," "The mountain possesses fire," "The mountain has fire because Devadatta ate there," "The white one, Ḍittha, is running," "A rabbit has horns," "My mother is barren," "I am mute," "I do not know this," and "Having entered my ear, an elephant roars; let a remedy be told.

And for that purpose, there are proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). Among these, proof is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) endowed with the five features conducive to pervasion (*vyāpti*) and subsistence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), such as "because of possessing specific smoke.
The other is a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*), such as "because of being a reservoir of water.
And the auxiliary to that is reasoning (*tarka*).
That too, relying on the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), takes the form of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*).

And the undesirable is of two kinds: the abandonment of what is authoritative (*prāmāṇika*) and the acceptance of what is unauthoritative (*aprāmāṇika*). For example: "If water were not to quench the suffering of thirst, it would not be drunk; and if that very [fire] were to burn another intensely, then it would also burn me, who am nearby.
Any other, however, is a fallacy of reasoning (*tarkābhāsa*).

For example, if water were to destroy the suffering of thirst, it would not possess form, just like space; and if that very [suffering] were to disappear within it, it would have made me fragrant as well.

Furthermore, a refutation is established as being one that does not imply the reasoning that rejects itself, which is invariably connected with the non-establishment of the point to be refuted, and which is proven.
For instance, when "possessing fire" is the property to be proven, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is not a valid reason because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Otherwise, however, in the case of a fallacy (*tadābhāsa*), it is as follows: "This smoke does not establish fire, because it is seized by the suspicion of an unperceived *upādhi* in every respect, and because it is a knowable object (*prameyatva*), and because it is contradictory (*viruddhatva*).

Other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as well are limbs of inquiry precisely through the shadow of inference, since they proceed by placing *tarka* and non-otherwise-establishment (*ananyathāsiddhi*) at their forefront; therefore, in those cases too, this very same method is to be followed.

Such being the case regarding worldly convention, if you investigate by means of formal proof (*sādhana*), your very thesis (*pratijñā*) cannot even maintain its status as a valid member of the argument. For instance,

in such statements as "nothing exists," "nothing is true," "nothing is an agent," "nothing withstands investigation," "nothing has an objective basis," "there is no seeing," or "there is no established tenet" (*siddhānta*), the self-contradiction of one's own meaning is first and foremost unavoidable.

For then the thesis itself would not exist—it would be neither true, nor functional, nor withstands analysis; likewise, its cognition would not have an object, its fruit would not be vision, and its referent would not be an established tenet—such would be the consequence.
If it is argued that this is indeed accepted, we say no; for the contradiction is not removed by mere assertion.
For if the meaning of the proposition—"nothing exists" and so forth—were to touch upon the proposition itself, how could this meaning be understood?
If it is not [established], how can it be non-contradictory? And if it is non-contradictory, how then does the meaning of the thesis become established?
Thus it comes to this: like a female serpent struck by its own venom, she bites herself.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because of the qualification "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*), then there must be either an investigation into that [reality] or a transgression of worldly convention.
The first [option] has already been refuted; since it takes the form of a mere proposition, it is thwarted by its own offspring—the arguments—just as a crab is destroyed by its own eggs.
In the second case, however, there is that same contradiction, like the crossing of one's own shadow:

for if the transgression of worldly boundaries is not the established nature of the inquiry, then if it is the established nature of that inquiry, there can be no such transgression; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction regarding whether the object of negation is established or not:
for if the object of negation is established, its negation is not absolute;
and if it is not established, then even less so.

If it is argued that [it is] established by worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*), then it is indeed already established, for nothing whatsoever is established from anything else. If it is argued that this convention is not subject to sublation (*abādhya*), we say no; for if it were not so in one case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its being likewise in all other cases. If it is argued that it is sublated everywhere, then [we ask]: is it by a convention whose establishment depends on that [sublation], or by one independent of it, or rather by non-convention itself?
First, how could that which depends on it for its own establishment subvert that very thing? For in the world, there is no subversion of the perception grasping heat by an inference of non-heat.
Second, the [second] case is impossible, for a negating means of valid cognition cannot exist independently of the establishment of the object to be negated.
In the third case, however, the opposite consequence follows: having begun with the state of being subverted by inquiry, one seals it with the absence of inquiry.
Nor has even this been established; for that [non-existence] must be either a perception established without effort, or a mere lack of affirmation.
In the first case, there is contradiction and lack of proof;
in the second, there is a transgression of common worldly understanding, as well as the undesirable consequence that your own non-desire would be sublated by the non-desire of another.
By this, the reasons [for the existence of a self] are refuted;

for they are: because of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*), because of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), because of non-existence (*asattva*), because of the impossibility of conceptual construction (*vikalpānupapatti*), because of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*), because of the impossibility of action (*karmānupapatti*), and because of mutual contradiction (*mitho vyāghāta*), and so forth.
For all of these indeed invoke a reasoning that rejects causal efficiency (*svārthakriyā*), and they depend upon the establishment of the object to be negated.

The first and second reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because they deviate with respect to their own result; the third and fourth are unestablished (*asiddha*); the fifth is inconclusive for the same reason as before; the sixth is both unestablished and inconclusive due to contradiction (*vyāghāta*); and the seventh is both unestablished and inconclusive. Thus, all of them are "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
By this, the examples as well are to be dismissed.

For they are like a rope-snake, like the cognition thereof, like a hare’s horn, like a face in a mirror, like a dream-cognition, like the cutting [of wood] when the object to be cut is non-existent, like the act of cutting, like fire and water which mutually dry up and extinguish one another, and so forth.

By that very same [process] by which the non-existence of the snake there, the falsity of the cognition thereof, the non-productivity of a rabbit’s horn, the inability of the mirror-face to withstand analysis, the objectless nature of dream-cognition, and the impossibility of cutting in the absence of something to be cut were determined, by that very same [process] the existence of the rope there, the truth of the cognition of it as not being a snake, the productivity of the rabbit [horn] in other cases such as cows, the ability of the mirror to withstand analysis, the object-supported nature of non-dream cognition, and the establishment of cutting as residing in the thing to be cut— along with the cognition and the action— are likewise established.
Alternatively, if that [concomitance] is not established, then all these are merely fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) due to being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Let the last one be devoid of the means of proof (*sādhanavikala*).
