The contradiction between established tenets (*siddhānta*) is characterized by their mutual exclusion, whereas that between water and fire is characterized by their nature as destroyer and destroyed; moreover, inference does not proceed on the basis of mere similarity of words—this is the general direction [of the argument].
If it is argued that the investigation should therefore proceed by way of refutation, we shall examine what that [refutation] might be like:

"This [self] is not gross, because that would entail the consequence of its being devoid of contradictory attributes; nor is it subtle, because that would entail the consequence of its appearing as such; nor is it independent of others, because that would entail the consequence of its being eternal; nor is it all-pervasive, because that would entail the consequence of its being inactive; nor is it non-pervasive, because that would entail the consequence of its being unamenable to control," and so forth—if this is the argument, we say no.

Because these are fallacious reasonings (*tarkābhāsa*), characterized by mutual non-contradiction, lack of a root, looseness, leading to an undesired consequence, and failing to reach a definitive conclusion;

for just as in the case where one says, "This mountain is not without fire, because that would entail its being smokeless," and "Nor is it possessed of fire, because that would entail its being perceived as such"— of these two, one is a fallacy, since it is impossible for both to be non-fallacious when they mutually negate each other's objects— so it is here as well.
For there is no injunction of grossness and so forth other than the negation of grossness and so forth, nor is there an injunction of non-grossness and so forth other than that negation.
Moreover, these [arguments] have weak foundations, because the logical connection (pratibandha) is unestablished.

Alternatively, if the pervader, the pervaded, and their locus are established, the dispute is resolved. Furthermore, in the first case, there would be the consequence of proving what is already accepted, because the non-association of contradictory properties is accepted in the case of a gross object determined through experience.
And we shall explain it accordingly:
furthermore, the second [reason] is favorable.
Because the negation of non-coarseness (*asthūlatā*) is supported by the perception of coarseness (*sthūlatā*), and because the conventional usage of that form is pervaded by such an appearance;

and likewise for the third [negation]. Because the negation of independence (*anapekṣatva*) is supported by the perception of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*), and because the rule of independence is pervaded by being eternal (*sadātanatva*).

The fourth [reason], however, has an unestablished pervasion (*aprasiddhavyāpaka*), because since existence and non-existence are contradictory, a negation cannot be established in the same locus as an affirmation.
The fifth, however, is indeed favorable;

for the rejection of unity in an object intended to be manifold is supported by the perception of multiplicity, and because the conventional usage of such a nature is pervaded by its appearing in that way.
But the sixth [alternative] is indeed accepted by us.
Now, is difference (bheda) the essential nature (svarūpa), or mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva), or a distinct property (dharmāntara)?

Not the first, because the co-usage of "the jar" and "different" would be untenable. Not the latter, because it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) in cognition; for the absence of difference is defined by the definition of its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and that very definition is the definition of difference itself. Not the final one, because it would entail an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it is asked, "How then can that [distinction] be established?"—is it that the cognition of difference simply does not exist; or, even if it exists, is it eternal; or, even if non-eternal, is it causeless; or, even if caused, is it without an object; or, even if having an object, is its object sublated?
Among these, the first is unsurpassed because it is free from all contradiction;
the second is to be disregarded because it conforms to the state of deep sleep;
and the third is also to be abandoned because of its contradiction.
The fourth [alternative], however, must be rejected precisely because it involves the delineation of a distinction.
As for the fifth, it is considered: is the object of that [cognition] one of these [five] as its self, or something other than them?
In that regard, if it were indeed something else, how could it be sublated by these incongruities involving a different locus?
For in this way, by the very act of denying the thief, it would clearly become an admission of the Maṇḍana position.

Alternatively, if it is some other self, even there, if its true nature is merely another property (*dharmāntara*), then out of fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), one should abandon the entire further series; so how can that [self] be abandoned?

For an infinite regress does not negate an object that is appearing; rather, it merely causes the series to cease, as when one scent is followed by another scent. Now, if the truth is that the cognition of difference relies solely upon mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), even in that case, where is there self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*)? For by that [admission], there would simply be no cognition of difference at all. Yet such a cognition exists; therefore, it must imply some other cause, but it does not cease of its own accord simply because it is not a cause for itself.
If it is argued that [the self arises] by the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), what follows from this?

For the mere fact of being "ignorance" does not itself eliminate the fault of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). If that were the case, even jars and other such things would arise by themselves, independent of potters and so forth.

Alternatively, if it is held that because it is afflicted by the fault of self-dependence, the self is not its own cause, and therefore its birth must come from some other source—which is difficult to specify—it is called "ignorance"; then the dispute is merely over a name. This is the meaning of the investigation.

Nor is even that difficult to define; for it has been established that the perception of the locus when the counter-positive is not perceived as such, and the recollection of the counter-positive when its own nature as the locus is not remembered, are the causes for the apprehension of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).

[ĀtTaViv 568.11–17] Now, if the truth is that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself is the object of the manifestation of difference, then even so, let the simultaneous usage [of the terms "locus" and "counter-positive"] be abandoned as untenable; but what wrong has difference committed?
If it is argued that even this [difference] is perceived, it would be merely contingent (*naimittika*), not inherent in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).
For in such instances as "Bring the jar" or "Look at the cloth," a discerning person does not employ even a word for difference.
However, in a commentary, there is no fault even in using them together for the sake of awakening the ignorant, just as one might say "jar" and "pot."
Nevertheless, what is the ultimate truth? All three [aspects] are true according to their respective natures.

For it is established by experience that there is the non-cognition of a cloth as having the nature of a jar, its cognition as not having the nature of a jar, and the cognition of its distinction from it; among these, the first alone constitutes negation (*abhāva*), because there is no other property belonging to a further negation.

Among the three categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), there are three [types of difference], since all three are possible: "This is a cloth, not a jar," and "This is a thread"; "This is fragrance, not color," and "It is sweet-smelling"; "This is motion, not upward throwing," and "It is horizontal. Furthermore, the definition of difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*) is the cognition [of one thing] when its identity [with another] is not cognized; that of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is the uncontradicted negative cognition occurring in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*); and that of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is opposition (*virodha*), which is the non-coexistence in a single substratum—this is the general direction [of the analysis].

The seventh [reason] is also indeed favorable, because the rejection of pervasiveness in the case of a jar and so forth is supported by the observation of non-pervasiveness, and because pervasiveness is necessarily concomitant with the absence of motion.
Let it be that [the property] is indeed intended in some cases;
for precisely because it is non-prescribable in some instances, it is therefore designated as "non-pervasive" (avyāpaka) when it is prescribable in some instances.
If it is argued that it must be so in all cases, we say no.
Because pervasion is unestablished and because there is a contradiction.
For there is no necessary connection (pratibandha) such that "whatever is non-pervasive is not to be predicated everywhere.

You intend the meaning of "non-pervasive" to be "existing in some place," while the meaning of "not to be predicated" is "not existing everywhere"; thus, there would also be a contradiction between these two.
If it is argued that "how can that which has the nature of an object be negated?", we say no;
for while having the nature of a negation is indeed contradictory to that which is to be enjoined (the positive correlate), it is not contradictory to being the counter-positive of a negation.

If it is asked: "How can there be a negation of that which exists? For if it exists, what is the fault?"—if you say, "It would entail the consequence of no contradiction between these two," we reply: even such a consequence does not constitute a fault when there is a distinction in their modes.
But if they were non-distinct, who would accept both affirmation and negation such that a lack of contradiction would follow for them?
By this, non-contradiction should also be understood in terms of differences in time and so forth.
Let it then be that the superimposition of contradictory attributes (viruddhadharmādhyāsa), such as being grasped or not grasped, consists of five kinds, including the destruction of gross objects.
No; because it is unestablished. [ĀtTaViv 587.3–10]
For instance:

it is neither an empirical experience nor an accepted tenet that whatever is perceived by something, in a certain place, and at a certain time, is not simultaneously perceived by that same thing in that same place at that same time.

If it is argued that there is the perception of one part accompanied by the whole while there is the non-perception of another part accompanied by the whole, then the meaning of the statement is simply that when the whole is being perceived, some parts are perceived and some are not—according to the logical principle that "affirmation and negation, when accompanied by qualifiers, apply to the qualifier. Thus, the consequence (prasaṅga) regarding the perception and non-perception of parts is merely transferred to the whole; enough of this.
By this, the cases of being covered and not being covered are also explained.
It remains to be asked: why should there not be a perception of such grossness even when a few parts are obscured, as in the case of the state of being unobstructed?
That too is incorrect;

for that specific universal of dimension, which is distinct from the object itself and perceivable by a restricted causal complex, is not perceived even when the object is perceived, in the absence of those [unobstructed] parts.
By this, the conjunction of motion and non-motion is refuted;
for when motion is produced in a specific part due to a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), at that moment the whole (*avayavin*) remains motionless.
If it is argued that, in that case, the destruction of the substance would follow from the destruction of the conjunction due to the disjunction of the two parts— the moving and the non-moving—
then what of it?
If you say this implies an abandonment of your own tenet (*apasiddhānta*), we say no.

If it is argued that even so, because [the opponent] accepts [this] in some cases, the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would apply everywhere; even then, what harm is there for the whole (avayavin)?
And yet, this is not the case.
This is because it is not accepted that there is a rule whereby action produces a disjunction that is the opposite of the conjunction initiating a substance;
rather, due to a specific cause, such a particularity is observed only in certain actions.

By this, the following [position] is refuted: that when the hand moves, its constituent atom must also move; from that, there is a disjunction of the moving atom of the arm; then, according to the principle that "whatever is conjoined with or disjoined from something is also [disjoined from] the substance which is its effect," there is a disjunction between the arm and the hand; from that, the destruction of conjunction; and from that, the destruction of the body.

For it is not the case that the motion of the atoms of the hand necessarily initiates a disjunction of the atoms of the arm. If it is argued that "if it does not initiate that [disjunction], then the definition of action (karma) is violated," we say no.
This is established even by the production of spatial divisions [of the whole] from space and so forth, just like the action of that which is being pushed.

Why this distinction? If, even when a part vibrates, the whole remains motionless, then alas, it would neither conjoin with nor disjoin from the spatial loci such as space that are conjoined with and disjoined from the parts. If you say this, we reply: no, for that [conjunction and disjunction of the whole] is accomplished precisely through the conjunction and disjunction of its parts.
And this should be understood correctly by consulting the Vaiśeṣika system.

If it is argued that the whole (avayavin) would then be perceived as motionless even when it rests upon moving parts, this is not undesirable, because of the common experience that when the hand trembles, the body does not tremble.

Alternatively, it should also be understood that whatever is perceived as dependent upon something else is conceived as moving whenever that [substratum] moves—even if it is itself immobile—just like a face in a mirror or the moon in water. Enough with this dispute over common experience; for if you argue that in this way [the whole] would be perceived as moving everywhere, we reply: when a part moves, it is exactly so everywhere, so nothing is untenable. But how could it be perceived in that way if it were immobile?

If it is argued that, nevertheless, because that which rests upon a moving or unmoving substrate is perceived as moving or unmoving, there might arise a cognition of duality—just like the moon in moving water—the answer is: this might indeed occur if there were a separation of the substrates.
For there is no such thing as the delusion of two moons in a single body of water when its parts are not divided;
rather, that very same [moon] is perceived as moving when the [water] moves, and as unmoving when it is unmoving.
If it is argued that even in the case of the waves, there is a "thousandfold" [simultaneity], this is indeed so, because they are not perceived as being separated from one another.
If it is then argued that there would consequently follow the establishment of distinct existence (*yutasiddhi*) for the moving and the non-moving, we say no.

Because the probans itself is not established as being necessarily connected [to the probandum]. Nor is the opponent's own admission a refuge even when there is pervasion (*vyāpti*) in a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).
And such an admission by the opponent does not exist in this case either.
If it is argued that "this [identity] is indeed seen in cases such as cloth and water," we say no;
for in the case of cloth and its threads, the opposite is also observed.
If you say, "This is false," then how can that [other case] be true?
If it is argued that there is no sublation [of the pervasion], then another sublation must be stated here.
If it is argued that "the very fact of being mobile and immobile" is that sublation, we say no;
for one could equally state the converse: "Why is this not a sublation even in the case of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*)? Thus, the argument fails.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction between being attached and not being attached, we say no;
for that is due to delusion.
If it is argued that there may be a contradiction regarding the conjunction and non-conjunction of substances possessing color based on those [atoms], we say no;
for this has already been refuted against the proponent of the atomic theory (*paramāṇuvādin*).
If one asks, "What then is the situation regarding the other [theory]?", the answer is simply that very same [refutation], because there is likewise no contradiction.

Even if contradiction is admitted on the basis of a difference in mode, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established, because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and its absence would themselves remain unestablished;

or, even if they were established, one would not abandon the coexistence of natures that are not contradictory despite the difference in modes. Nor, in this way, should conjunction alone be rejected on the grounds of its dissimilarity to other categories, for it would follow that those very categories must likewise be rejected on account of their dissimilarity to it.

Nor is this alone correct; for it is by means of a real dissimilarity (vaidharmya) possessed of a restrictive rule that the other is negated, since the reality of the [negating] property is itself established by a dissimilarity that is not unreal, and because the establishment of a negation is inseparable from the cognition of the object to be negated.
If it is argued that the establishment of a negation occurs through an imagined object of negation, such as a rabbit’s horn, we say no.

Because it has been refuted; because, if conjunction were established as merely conceptual by mere words, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); and because the analogy of a hare’s horn is unestablished due to the absence of non-perception of the capable (*yogyānupalambha*). If it is argued that its establishment follows from this very sublation (*bādhaka*), then there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
If it is claimed that the function of sublation occurs merely through the possibility of explaining the cognition of conjunction otherwise—just like the recognition of sound—that is not so.

If an experience were established as being otherwise due to error—without providing a corresponding limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) such as a mass of smoke—then an inference contrary to it would proceed; for there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an inference of "non-hotness" proceeding with respect to fire.
Furthermore, recognition has no other corresponding limiting adjunct, just as the cognition of conjunction has none.

If one were to overstep this principle of necessity, how could the possibility of the "otherwise-establishment" (*anyathāsiddhi*) of even the probans-cognition intended by you—which is itself erroneous—be prevented? And if that is not prevented, how could an inference proceed when its root is thus weakened?

Just as in the case of other direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*), since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) also exists in terms of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—such as sound or the production of qualities through heating—the validity of that perception is established; thus, there is no room for the suspicion of its being erroneous.
Let it be, then, that there is a contradiction consisting in the fact that [the whole] occupies that space while [the parts] do not occupy that space.
No,
because there is no defining characteristic of contradiction. For when there is an injunction of contact with that location, there is not necessarily a prohibition of contact with another location.
There may indeed be the states of being in that location and not being in that location; however, by whom is their conjunction admitted?

If it is argued that perception itself, as the determiner of a single association, brings forth this contradiction by way of excluding its absence in order to achieve the result of excluding other [associations], this might indeed be so if perception were to arise necessarily rejecting the association with another for that which is associated with one; but this is not the case. Since perception is engaged in the simultaneous association of one thing with many without distinction, it would either reject all associations, or none at all, or even its own self—under any circumstance.
One should not illuminate a contradiction, because even in the case of a single atom, one ultimately accepts its conjunction with multiple atoms.

By this, the dilemma regarding subsistence (*vṛttivikalpa*) is refuted, since the subsistence of a whole (*avayavin*) through its atoms shares the same logical status as the subsistence of the atoms themselves.
[ĀtTaViv 611.
1–7] Let it be, then, that there is a contradiction between blue and non-blue and so forth within a variegated [object].
For it is not a single form, because that would contradict its variegated nature; nor is it multiple, because that would contradict its inherence in a single composite whole.
Nor is it manifold and all-pervasive, because that contradicts the fact that it is not perceived as such;

nor is it non-pervasive, because that contradicts its being of a different nature from its own constituent parts located elsewhere, otherwise there would be a contradiction regarding the established distinction between what is contradictory and what is not.
Nor is the whole merely formless, because that contradicts its visibility; if this is argued, we say no.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction in accepting oneness by intending either "variegatedness" (*citratva*) to mean multiplicity (*nānātva*), or the inherence (*samavāya*) of multiple mutually contradictory universals (*jāti*), then this objection holds; however, such is not our position. Indeed, variegatedness is not multiplicity, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a cognition of "variegated" even in the case of many white things. Nor is variegatedness the inherence of multiple contradictory universals in a single substrate, since that has already been refuted by the very fact of their mutual contradiction.

Moreover, variegatedness (*citratva*) is indeed a specific universal (*jāti*), just like blueness and so forth. Because it is manifested by a collection of heterogeneous colors residing in the parts, it is not perceived even when there is the perception of a whole (*avayavin*) accompanied by parts of a single color. For this very reason, there is never a cognition of variegation even in a variegated triad of atoms (*tryaṇuka*). If it is asked: "Even so, let there be no cognition of variegation on a non-variegated side; but from what does the cognition of whiteness arise?"—the answer is: because the cognition of the whole is likewise [based] upon the distribution of the colors of its parts.

For this very reason, where the form of the parts (*avayava*) is not perceptible, this [perception of color] is also absent in the case of a *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust); rather, it is only by superimposing the visible form of external light that a yellowish *trasareṇu* is perceived.
This might be so.

If it is argued that "variegatedness" (*citratva*) is a specific genus (*jāti*), then how can the cognition of variegatedness arise with respect to a mere collection of forms belonging to contradictory genera? To this we reply: indeed, no one ever has a cognition of variegation in the sense of a mottled object with respect to cloths that are simply blue, white, and red; rather, who can prevent the cognition based on their mutual difference (*vaidharmya*)? For the word "variegated" (*citra*), like the word "dice" (*akṣa*), possesses multiple meanings.

If it is argued that a variegated cognition (*karburapratyaya*) arises even when blue, yellow, and other colors are mutually mixed without having produced a new substance (*anārabdhadravya*), this is true; for such a cognition is possible because of the misconception (*abhimāna*) that another substance has been produced, just like the cognition of an excess of bulk (*sthailyātiśaya*).
[ĀtTaViv 617.5–11] In that case, let there be the total dissolution of everything due to the cessation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
To explain: when an atom is joined with many other atoms, does it join each one by means of a single part or in its entirety? There is no other possibility.
It cannot be the first case, because an atom lacks parts; for if it did possess parts, its status as an atom would be contradicted.

Not the second [alternative], because it would entail the consequence that there is no contact with another atom; for it is impossible for that which has its existence fully completed in one place to also exist in another. Not so.
Because it shares the same security and vulnerability as cognition (*buddhi*).
For instance, cognition too, whether apprehending an existent or a non-existent object, or whether assuming a form in its entirety or only in part, [is subject to the same conditions].

Not the first, because it would entail the disappearance of the objective forms such as yellow and so forth; for it is impossible that the very same object, or its form, could be entirely exhausted in being blue while simultaneously having an essence mixed with yellow and other colors.
Not the second, because that [object] does not exist.

If it is argued that the absence of mental modes (*anākāratva*) and the absence of objects (*aviṣayatva*) are indeed accepted for cognition, then does that which appears not exist, or rather, is there nothing at all that appears?
Not the first, because even if blue, yellow, and so forth were non-existent, the dilemma regarding the operation of cognition would remain as it was;
for the entire cognition cannot consist solely of the representation of blue, as this would entail the consequence that yellow and the rest are not represented.
Nor is it a part of that, because it has already been stated that such a thing does not exist.
Nor is the second alternative possible, because the dilemma regarding its occurrence would be equally untenable in the case of external objects as well.
It might be argued as follows:

"The meaning of the word *kṛtsna* (entirety) is a complete aggregate (*samudāya*), whereas the referent of the term 'part' (*ekadeśa*) is merely some portion of that aggregate. Since cognition (*buddhi*) does not possess the nature of an aggregate—because it is of a single form—how can there arise the conceptual alternatives of 'entirety' or 'part'? If you ask how it can then have that as its object or take on its form, and if you reply that it is because no other mode is possible, we say: 'By way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpeṇa*). If this is your claim, then the peak of the temple of logic has clearly been struck down by one who, out of mere malice toward us, has gone too far."
By this, the state of being located in that place or not in that place is refuted.
For it is as follows:

If perception, while delimiting the blue aspect of cognition, were to exclude the yellow aspect—which is invariably concomitant with it—by means of excluding its absence, then how could a single cognition possess both the blue and yellow aspects? Such an objection would indeed apply equally [to our position] if there were an invariable concomitance between the blue aspect and the absence of the yellow aspect; but how could that be so, given that cognition possessing the blue and yellow aspects is determined as being of a single nature?
If it is argued that because [the object] is restricted to each individual form, the cognition of a variegated [object] would also be impossible, this applies equally to atoms, wholes, and so forth.
For even in those cases, it is not as if there could never be a cognition of a thing composed of many atoms; thus, the process of understanding the object is identical.
As for the mere difference in verbal expression, what use is it?

By the very establishment of conjunction through the sixfold contact, such arguments as "due to the distinction of directions and locations," "due to shadow and obstruction," and so forth, are refuted.
By the very establishment or non-establishment of the atom (*paramāṇu*), properties such as corporeality (*mūrttatva*) are rendered untenable;
however, qualities such as being pierced by space (*ākāśavyatibheda*) are simply impossible.

In all these cases, during the stage of the formal argument (*hetu-daśā*), there is a contradiction between the two members of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the fallacy of "misplaced timing" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*).

During the stage of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-daśā*), there is the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and the unestablished nature of the pervasion (*vyāptyasiddhi*), because the example is unestablished; furthermore, this is due to the presence of a counter-reasoning characterized by infinite regress (*anavasthā*) which undermines that [reductio], and because of the consequence that the atom would be non-cognizable (*ameyatva*).

Nor is there dissolution of the atom, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its non-existence, and because the reasons that would entail its having parts lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therefore, this atom is something else entirely— a "red seed" (*raktabīja*)— whose parts emerge even after piercing through the belly of Yukticāmuṇḍā.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that reductio ad absurdum arguments (*prasaṅga*) will have imagined bases and imagined logical connections;
for by means of a conventional usage imagined according to one's own whim, there would follow the consequence of the total collapse of all conventional usages involving affirmation and negation.

For it has been stated more than once that, when one takes account of worldly convention (*lokavyavasthā*), the subsequent negator cannot come into existence because it would contradict that convention;
otherwise, all of this would apply equally even to the case of cognition (*buddhi*).
For that [atom] too would follow as having parts because of its simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms] and so forth.
If it is argued that these [conjunctions] are not established in it, we say no,
because they are established by inference.

For instance, it can be argued that cognition is corporeal and conjoined with the six [senses] simultaneously, because it exists or because it is an object of linguistic usage, like an object of cognition (*bodhya*).

If it is objected that this [argument] has no force because the contrary [view—that cognition is incorporeal] is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*), we reply: you should apply the same reasoning elsewhere as well; this is the general direction.
But another, wishing to become fearless by closing his eyes, says: "In that case, let there be the annihilation of even the intellect (*buddhi*).
But what can be said in this regard, where there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of reasons and so forth?
If it is argued that it may be merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), this would only be so if convention itself were ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
Otherwise, however, just as it is not real, it is likewise not even conventional.
If it is argued that convention is also conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*), then if this too is non-existent, nothing further has been stated.
But if one accepts that what exists ultimately for another conventional perspective is indeed real, then that very cognition cannot be discarded.

If it is argued that it is "conventionally real" because it both exists and possesses sublation (*bādhaka*), then if it truly exists, how can there be sublation? And if there is sublation, how can that which is touched by it be real?

If it is argued that "it is indeed observed to be so," then in that case, it is precisely the existence [of a property] residing in the same substrate as the sublater (*bādhaka*) that must be abandoned. If it is asked, "Why is not the existence [of a property] residing in the same substrate as the sublater itself abandoned?"—we say no;
for it would follow that the sublater itself must also be abandoned.
In that case, both [alternatives] are indeed unavoidable.
This is so;
however, mutual contradiction must be abandoned.

For it is impossible to establish either the co-inherence of two contradictory things in a single object, or the contradiction between two such things, except by relying on one's own conventional doctrine (*svasamaya*); yet at the time of critical inquiry, there is no room for the introduction of one's own conventional doctrine. Furthermore, one must provide an explanation in exactly the manner that removes misconceptions. Thus, this results in the absurdity of extinguishing one lamp with another lamp only to produce darkness.

By this, the claim that "everything is annihilated because the relationship between cause and effect is untenable" is refuted. This is because the effort to refute that [annihilationism] is untenable, whether it be successful or fruitless; for the refutation of the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) is already accepted, and the refutation of the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, if one attempts to establish [annihilationism], it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) if the production is from what is non-existent, and if it is existent, the effort is fruitless.
It might be argued:

"Let these refutations not apply to the composite whole (*avayavin*); however, there would still be non-perception (*anupalambha*), for nothing other than a collection of atoms is perceived. This objection is obstructed by a lack of distinction, because the experience of a single gross object is established for all people.
If it is argued that "it is merely a conceptual construction," we say no;
because it appears with clarity.
If it is argued that its clarity is adventitious (*aupādhika*), that is not so, because even the adventitious condition (*upādhi*) cannot exist without such an experience.

Otherwise, since the clarity of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding blue and so forth could likewise be established in that same way, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is because the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of perception applies only to an object that has been grasped and ascertained; and when ascertainment is sublated, perception itself is also sublated.
Nor are the atoms themselves gross, for that would contradict their true nature.

Nor is their collection so, because you do not admit the existence of a state of being collected; or, if you do admit it, what wrong has the "whole" (avayavin) done? Furthermore, the atoms in their collective state cannot possibly appear as such, since they are individually not gross.
Nor is grossness (*sthaulya*) merely the state of pervading various directions and locations, for that is impossible in each individual atom (*paramāṇu*).
Nor is it correct to say that grossness is simply that which inheres in a plurality of things within a single object, because there is a fixed cognition that "this one thing is gross."
Nor is this [notion of a whole] established by means of a unity superimposed upon the parts alone, because that is impossible;
for no one anywhere superimposes a unity upon the atoms of the hands, feet, chin, nose, and so forth. Nor is there no cognition of grossness when those [atoms] appear as distinct.

Furthermore, when reality itself is manifesting, it is impossible for there to be a superimposition of its opposite, unreality. Moreover, in this way, even ten million atoms, if superimposed with the nature of a single atom, would appear only as a mere atom, and not as something gross.
Nor is it correct to claim that this is the greatness of [the object's] pervading various directions and locations, because of the contradiction.

For if atoms situated in various directions were to appear as the locus (*deśa*), they would not be superimposed as a single entity nor as a locus; and in that case, whose pervasion of various directions and locations would there be, since the locus itself (*deśin*) would not be manifest?

Alternatively, if they were to be superimposed in such a manner, they would not appear as multiple or as a locus; and in that case, whose pervasion of various directions and locations would there be, since the locus itself would not be manifest?
Therefore, if there were a superimposition of unity, there would be only the appearance of a mere atom.

[ĀtTaViv 643.12-15] If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status regarding aggregates of substances that have not yet begun?"— it is not, first of all, a superimposition of the nature of a substance of such magnitude based on the similarity of spatial pervasion.

And it should not be the case here either, because [the reason] is unestablished elsewhere as well. Nor does a single, gross object appear as something non-existent, since the subverting arguments have been refuted.
By this, the property of appearing (*pratibhāsadharmatva*) is also refuted; for that too cannot escape three possible courses: it must be either non-existent, mental (*bauddha*), or real (*vāstava*).

Furthermore, since atoms are individually beyond the senses, how could they become perceptible even when combined, given that a collection of things beyond the senses remains itself beyond the senses?
If you argue that perceptibility arises from a specific production [of a new whole], then why do you still stretch out your hand in sleep?

Let it be so; nevertheless, the distinction between universals (jāti) based on a difference in moments has been refuted, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of a confusion of universals (jātisaṅkara).
However, if production occurs without that difference, then from the perspective of ultimate reality (tattvadṛśā), there is no distinction whatsoever as to whether it is "that" or "of such a kind."
Or, let there be a specific distinction of genus (*jāti*); nevertheless, it must be understood that grossness (*sthūlatva*) alone is the determinant for being perceptible by the senses.
Otherwise, even a single atom, if it were ever produced in such a state without having attained grossness, would become perceptible.

However, since the relationship between cause and effect is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the fact that what is the opposite of that [grossness] is invariably imperceptible, while such [grossness] rests solely in perceptibility, is thus determined.
Nor do they arise as gross even when aggregated;

nor is plurality itself grossness, for if it were, then subtlety would simply be its opposite, which would entail the undesirable consequence that even things occupying extensive space would be perceptible.

If it is argued that "contiguity" (*nairantarya*) is also intended [to be present], we say no; for that is impossible even in the case at hand, because the atoms of form (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) are interspersed with atoms of taste (*rasa*) and so forth.

Nor can contiguity be superimposed [upon them], because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): there would be the apprehension of those coarse objects once contiguity is superimposed, and the superimposition of contiguity would occur only when their apprehension has taken place.

Therefore, since grossness (*sthūlatā*) is the necessary condition for perceptibility, if it were not the condition, it would follow that even atoms occupying an extended space (*vitata-deśa*) would be perceptible; yet, because each of those atoms lacks grossness, atoms are indeed beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Consequently, there would be no perception of anything at all, because the whole (*avayavin*) is unestablished.
If it is argued, "Let the object be something gross that lasts for only a moment," we say no.

Because the simultaneous perception of the part and the possessor of the parts is contradicted by experience, and because when objects such as jars and cloths are destroyed and threads and potsherds are produced, there would be a contradiction regarding their resistance (*sapratighatva*) due to having a common material cause;
thus, by the principle of a "conclusion established through the context" (*adhikaraṇasiddhāntanyāya*), once grossness is established, the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is refuted.
By this, the following argument is refuted: "Whatever exists is partless, like consciousness; and the pot and so forth, which are the subject of dispute, do exist.
This is because the pervasion (vyāpti) is not established, as there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka) against the contrary case.
Furthermore, there would be scope for the Cārvāka’s counter-argument that "whatever exists is composed of parts, like a jar, and consciousness exists";
or else, there would be an equal logical impasse (*samādhi*).

If it is objected: "Surely consciousness is indeed partless and self-cognizing, whereas there is still dispute even today regarding the fact that a jar possesses parts; so how can there be a transformation [of the argument], or how can the resolution be the same?"—[we reply: because dry disputation is unavoidable even regarding consciousness.
For no one experiences a cooking-pot devoid of a neck, lips, sides, belly, and so forth.
Or, let it be granted that because of its existence, the possession of resistance (*sapratighatva*) is established for the jar, while non-resistance (*apratighatva*) is established for consciousness.
Furthermore, is this an independent proof (*svatantrasādhana*) or a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*)?

It cannot be the first, because if one takes as the subject (*pakṣa*) the gross and other forms such as color (*rūpa*), or atoms (*paramāṇu*) denoted by the word "pot" and so forth, it would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, on the other hand, one accepts a single gross entity and then formulates the thesis, there is the fallacy of "missing the time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*); but if no such entity is accepted, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

If it is argued that "there would be a contradiction (*bādha*) if one accepts [the subject] as being established by valid cognition, and there would be the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) if one does not accept it in any way; yet this is not the case here," then this argument merely serves to conceal the fallacy of an unestablished locus by attributing a locus even to the proof of the fragrance of a sky-lotus—so enough of this!

If it is argued that an inference of partlessness could be made by taking as its basis pots and the like, which are established through worldly consensus just like mountains and such—otherwise, even the inference of fire on a mountain would not occur due to being undermined by conflicting views such as the theory of Brahman’s illusory transformation (*vivarta*)—we say: not so, because there is no contradiction.

For even when the illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman and so forth is established, no other types of substrata and the like are possible. To explain: in every case, it is only the dream-fire that is proven by the dream-smoke in a dream-mountain; however, since there exists a distinction between the real and the unreal even within conventional worldly practice (*sāṃvṛta-vyavahāra*), one must remain firm in that [distinction]. But here, if the gross object itself is made the subject (*pakṣa*) under the designation of "pot" and so forth, how could there not be a contradiction with the probandum (*sādhya*) which is partlessness?

If, on the other hand, [the subject] is the atom itself, how is it not a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)? If you argue that this is not so for one who holds a contrary view (*vipratipanna*), we reply: no one indeed disputes that atoms are partless. If you say the proof is for the purpose of dispelling worldly delusion, even so, if that which the world perceives as a single gross object is the subject (*pakṣa*), there is a direct contradiction; if something other than that is the subject, it is simply proving what is already established.
If it is argued that this "one" is gross and thus false, then let that alone be what is to be proven; what is the use of this "existence" (*sattva*), which is like the teats on the neck of a goat?

Furthermore, it is not possible to apply this [reason] to that very [subject], because they belong to different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*). Therefore, inference proceeds toward a subject only when there is a desire to prove a property and a dispute regarding its contradiction with that [property], according to the form under which the subject is intended; it does not proceed otherwise.

Nor is the second alternative [viable], because it does not result in a definitive conclusion (*viparyayāparyavasānāt*). For the subject of dispute is not partless; therefore, the counter-proposition—that "it is not existent"—is not established. Furthermore, one who does not desire the thesis cannot force the presence of parts upon it, nor is that [partlessness] accepted by you. If that were accepted, its non-existence could not be proven, either due to the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), contradiction, or being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*). Nor can the counter-proposition proceed by virtue of what is desired by the opponent.
What, then, is the reasoning regarding the whole (*avayavin*)?
In that case, is reasoning more authoritative than direct perception?
If so, what is this [reasoning] other than within the intellect itself?
Therefore, this [position] is without substance.

Nevertheless, that which is devoid of all superimposition of contradictory properties must be designated as one, just like consciousness (*vijñāna*). And thus, that which is the object of experience as a single gross entity under dispute is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), because the linguistic convention of "oneness" is invariably concomitant with that much alone.

For this convention of "one" cannot be without a cause, as that would lead to the absurdity of no restriction; nor can it have another cause, for then the same convention would absurdly apply even to fluidity and solidity, or cold and heat.

If it is argued that, therefore, there must be perpetual doubt regarding external objects because it is impossible to distinguish between the real and the unreal, we reply: first of all, the distinction is not untenable simply because everything is [alleged to be] in accordance with reality, for that would contradict what follows. To explain: the common worldly understanding—"I have perceived something erroneously"—and the technical definition of the Naiyāyika school—"misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*)—are either true or false. In either case, the subsequent argument cannot establish that everything is in accordance with reality.
If it is argued that this is merely verbal dispute and not actual cognition, we say no;
for such a dispute would be untenable. For investigators do not dispute over mere conventional usage, nor do they dispute by claiming that "this does not exist."

If it is argued that the dispute concerns the meaning of words, this being so, since it is impossible to negate what has not been cognized, and because a dispute aims at negating the opponent's intention, how could there be no cognition of the object to be negated for both the proponent and the opponent?
Furthermore, it is not possible for activity directed toward one thing to arise from the cognition of another, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is the proximity of that cognition the determining factor, precisely because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor is it the non-apprehension of difference accompanied by that [cognition], for if the non-apprehension were predominant, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of cessation even when one does not intend to express the difference, since the non-apprehension of non-difference—the cause of that [non-cessation]—is likewise present.

If it is argued that this [cognition] is not a cause of cessation, but rather a perception of difference (*bhedagraha*), we say no. For one would not desist from silver simply by thinking "this is not silver," because the perception of difference—which is its cause—is absent; or, if it were present, there would be the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) due to the cognition of difference in what is non-different. Therefore, just like the cause of engagement, the cause of cessation must also be accepted by you as being merely non-apprehension (*agraha*); and thus, that same defect remains exactly as it was.

Now, if difference (*bheda*) is the primary factor and non-apprehension (*agraha*) is subordinate, then one would not act toward silver upon having a cognition of "non-silver" (i.e., silver), because there is no absence of difference between the aspect of "this" (*idam-aṃśa*) and the aspect of "silver" (*rajatāṃśa*); this should be inferred by oneself.
If it is argued that, just as in the case of activity (*pravṛtti*), non-apprehension of both is likewise present in the case of cognition (*pratipatti*), we say no.
This is because the primary reality (*tattva*) is not intended [here] as the subject of discussion, since that [reality] is established solely through a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
However, the rule is that [the primary reality] does not manifest [as such].
Nor is it the case that both difference and non-difference constitute the primary reality, whereby it might be so; this is the general direction [of the argument].

Nor can it be the case that everything is non-correspondent (ayathārtha), because that would contradict subsequent statements regarding the correspondence or non-correspondence of the cognizer thereof.
Therefore, the actual state of affairs is simply the distinction that some things are valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and some are not.
And this [object] does not fall within the sphere of linguistic convention while setting aside the course of cognition; rather,
it is investigated whether its nature is determined intrinsically or extrinsically.
Even regarding the first [alternative], it must be either "by itself" or "by its own grasper.

In that regard, the first is not tenable because self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is unestablished; for luminosity (*prakāśatva*) is a unique property, and inference cannot proceed on the basis of a mere similarity of terms.
Nor is direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) itself a means of valid cognition here, because its distinctness remains doubtful.

For one whose apprehension is not itself perceived, the vision of an object is not established; if one thing were known by another, there would be an infinite regress. Furthermore, an action does not become the object of an action of its own kind, as in the case of cutting. If it is argued that this fault does not apply because it is preceded by reasoning (*tarka*), we say no. For the establishment, accomplishment, or cognition of "vision"—which is a synonym for "apprehension"—must be accounted for.
In the first case, there would be the consequence of perceiving and feeling what has not yet come into being, because that which is unperceived is not established.
Nor can there be the perception of a non-existent thing by means of a non-existent [means of perception]; thus, in self-awareness, there would be no awareness at all.

In the second case, however, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*), for that which has not been perceived does not thereby become perceived. And this being so, it does not follow that the object itself would not be perceived; for the cognition of perception is not the same as the knowledge of the object, but rather the actualization (*niṣpatti*) of perception. If it is asked, "How can there be such conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the actualization of perception when perception itself is not seen?", let it be so; for the existence of a realized entity does not cease simply because of a lack of conventional usage.
And thus, the linguistic convention regarding objects based upon that [cognition] would be impossible to avoid.

Nor does this lead to an infinite regress, because we do not admit that [the cognition of the cognition] must necessarily be cognized, just as in the case of a certainty (*niścaya*). Otherwise, even the ascertainment of an object would not be established for one whose own certainty remains unascertained; yet that [certainty] is not a certainty even with respect to itself.
This, therefore, resembles the story of the bridegroom who ate the beans.
As for the phrase "like cutting, etc.," we do not pay attention to it as a mere illustrative example.

Knowledge is not the object of another act of knowledge, because it is an action of that same class; for whatever action belongs to a certain class is not the object of that same action, just as the act of cutting is not the object of another act of cutting—this, however, is a violation of logic.

If it is to be proven that consciousness is in every respect non-objective for its own kind, the subject matter is contradicted; for the cognition of one person is known by the cognition of another person, and even one's own cognition is within the range of memory and so forth.
Furthermore, if it is to be proven that it is objective to itself, the reason is contradictory because the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Nor can it be grasped by its own grasper, because such a distinction is untenable.

For the apprehension of a means of valid cognition is not invariably restricted to what is true, since there is the conceit of being a means of valid cognition even in the case of an invalid cognition;
otherwise, there would follow the consequence of non-activity arising from erroneous cognition.

Therefore, even if validity should appear at first glance, nevertheless, since there is no cause for certainty, from where could the conviction arise that "this is indeed a valid means of knowledge"? And yet, such certainty is sought, because it is a constituent part of worldly activity concerning the next life.
If it is argued that this is ascertained without obstacle through the removal of doubt, then from what does that very removal of doubt arise?
If it is argued that [the certainty] comes from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), then that too must either have certainty as its result or not.
If it does not, then there would be no cessation of doubt, because the latter is something to be accomplished by certainty.
But if it has certainty as its result, then that which is sought [as the ultimate certainty] is not self-evident (*svataḥ*).
If it is argued that at least there must be a mere manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) by its own nature, what follows from that?
This too is not possible, because a cognition of the conditioned (*upahita*) cannot occur when the condition (*upādhi*) has not been apprehended.
Validity does not consist merely in the presentation of an object, for that is common even to fallacious cognitions.

Rather, it consists in the correspondence with a real object (bhūtārtha) on the part of a cognition that is already an experience. Nor, even when there is a correspondence with an object, is its reality (bhūtatva) grasped therein, because the specific qualification that excludes superimposition is not grasped.
And because superimposition is common to that which is not being attended to;
if it is argued that in some cases a distinction is also attended to, we say no, for nowhere is this done by the first instance.
Otherwise, in the state of non-habituation, there would be no doubt even in that case.

However, when it arises in the state of repeated practice (*abhyāsadaśā*), the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) occurs by the power of remembrance produced from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*); thus, it enters into the very body of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) and remains dependent on something else (*parataḥ*).

If it is argued that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) even in that case, we say no; for that [synthesis] does not proceed by way of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), since the certainty of that [pervasion] has already been established previously.
However, it might be by way of the result (*phala*), provided that validity must necessarily be ascertained.
If it is asked, "How can there be a cognition of another's validity by means of one whose own validity is unknown?", [the answer is: it is just like the cognition of an object.

Let it then be by way of the subject (*dharmin*) and the mark (*liṅga*); for there is no inference from those two when they themselves are not ascertained, and their ascertainment is impossible without the ascertainment of validity.
No, because of the absence of duality.

For where a duality is perceived—whether in the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) or in the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*)—by way of being real or unreal, there, due to the lack of certainty regarding reality, the mark is not ascertained because it is beset by the suspicion of being a fallacy (*ābhāsa*). But where that cognition is restricted to that [single object], there the ascertainment of the mark occurs by that much alone, since no suspicion of its being a fallacy arises.
For experience that is restricted to a single aspect is indeed a certainty (*niścaya*).
And since there is no duality within a cognition that grasps both the knowledge itself and its properties, this is the established position.
However, the Nyāya tradition maintains that even the ascertainment of its validity (*prāmāṇya*) arises from something external (*parataḥ*).
The teachers of the *Tātparya* [commentary] maintain that it is precisely because of this distinction that such [knowledge] arises from itself (*svataḥ*).
One might think: [ĀtTaViv 701.15–702.4]... [the following objection].

But how is this very point to be determined—that it is restricted to a single alternative (ekakoṭiniyata)—given that even there is no finality? No; for although the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not directly apply to the self (*ātman*), it nonetheless applies by way of a universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*) with respect to whatever condition (*upādhi*) it adopts. Indeed, the condition there is the possession of that property and the belonging to that class; and that is no different even in that case, because it is a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*). Furthermore, once a restriction has been ascertained in a general sense, there is no room for the suspicion of duality regarding a particular instance subsumed under that [restriction].

Just as the word "designator" (*vācaka*) does not directly establish its own status as a designator—due to the contradiction with its own function (*vṛtti*)—nevertheless, because it is applied by virtue of a certain general attribute (*upādhi*), the word "word" (*śabdaśabda*) is not dismissed by the doubt of whether it is a designator or not, nor does an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) follow; so it is here as well.
Furthermore, there are logical arguments (*tarka*) in this regard.

If the cognition of an object (*dharmajñāna*) were to be erroneous, it would either be without an objective support (*nirālambana*) or have a non-existent thing as its support; however, that has been refuted. If the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) were to be erroneous, then even that which has an object as its function would not exist, because for anything other than cognition, there is no inclination toward an object. If that which belongs to the same class [as valid cognition] were to be erroneous, then non-erroneousness could never be established anywhere.

If that [object] were not established, there could be no error (*vyabhicāra*), because error consists in the appearance of something as otherwise than it is; and if the reality of the object were established, then the state of being "otherwise" would be impossible, since that [reality] is the very limit of such a state.
By this, the claim that there is no distinction between the states of dreaming and waking is refuted.

Since the theories of *asatkhyāti* (the appearance of the non-existent) and *ātmakhyāti* (the appearance of the self) have been refuted, and since *anyathākhyāti* (the appearance of something otherwise) is untenable without the establishment of *tattvakhyāti* (the appearance of reality),
if that [tattvakhyāti] were not present even in the waking state, it would simply not exist at all.
If it is asked, "Even so, how is the distinction between these two states to be made?"—it is not so, because it is established by common worldly experience (*loka-siddha*).

If it is asked, "What is the definition of these two?"—the dream state is characterized by the sublation of the agent, object, instrument, place, time, and continuity, while possessing a coincidence (*kākatālīya*) that appears consistent; whereas in the waking state, there is a coincidence regarding continuity, and the sublation of only some particular object occurs.

By this same reasoning, one should also understand that dream is a particular state consisting of a sublated continuum, while waking is a continuum that sublates others and so forth, ending with the continuum being sublated; this is the general direction.
Therefore, we consider it logical that the entire universe is indeed real, though it is disregarded by those seeking liberation who are swift in their purpose because it serves little practical need.

If it is asked, "In that case, what is this excessive attachment of the Naiyāyikas toward the protection of the world?"—it is out of the fear that if they were to suddenly neglect it, there would be an opening for fallacious reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*), which would lead to the total collapse of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and thus, a discerning person who takes delight in logic (*nyāyaruci*) would not attain the ultimate truth (*tattva*).
Thus ends the critique of the doctrine denying external objects (*bāhyārthabhaṅgavāda*).
Regarding the doctrine of the destruction of the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality (*guṇaguṇibhedabhaṅgavāda*):

If it is argued that, because there is no difference between quality and the possessor of quality, there must be selflessness (*nairātmya*) since only momentary consciousness remains, we reply as follows.
There is, indeed, here a synthesis of a single object through both seeing and touching.

This [synthesis] must have as its object either (1) each individual [sense-object], or (2) the aggregate [of them], or (3) something distinct from those, or (4) an aspect not conforming to the real entity, or (5) a false object.
[ĀtTaViv 712.3–7]
The first [alternative] is not tenable, for it is not the case that whatever is form is also touch.
Nor is form graspable by the tactile faculty, because it would follow that even a blind person would have cognitions of blue and so forth.

Nor is it logical that a single entity should appear otherwise through a difference in its instruments, for that would entail a lack of essential nature (*anātmakatva*) and the impossibility of establishing the distinction between difference and non-difference.

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for that [identity] would have to be either by way of being a single location, or by way of being simultaneous in time, or by way of having a single effect, or by way of having a single cause.
[ĀtTaViv 715. 4–17]

First of all, it is impossible for there to be a single portion of the material cause, because those two have distinct and specific material causes; or, if such a possibility were granted, it would simply result in the conclusion that they are one and the same substance, and thus the dispute would be resolved.

Nor is its existence possible by way of being supported by a locus such as the ground; for when a specific color-form (*rūpaviśeṣa*) on the ground is perceived by the eye, and the pot is also perceived by the eye on that same ground, one can ascertain that the specific color-form on the ground is the support [of the pot], because the two are in a relation of upper and lower and are connected within a single cognition. But as for the tactile qualities (*sparśādayaḥ*) and so forth which have that [pot] as their locus, what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has them as its object? For tactile qualities and the like do not appear in a visual consciousness.

Nor can it be said that this is the function of the skin, for even by means of the skin, there is the cognition of the relationship between the locus and the located (ādhārādheya-bhāva) regarding the touch of the ground and the jar. Furthermore, such a relationship is not possible between two aggregates (*samudāya*), because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*): for the synthesis of the two aggregates would depend upon their having a single locus, and the synthesis of a single locus would depend upon the synthesis of the two aggregates.
Moreover, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), as the question would never cease: "By what is the ground itself constituted as an aggregate?
[ĀtTaViv 717.8–10]

For this very reason, they do not constitute a collection by virtue of occurring at the same time either, because there is no evidence for their simultaneity; or, if such simultaneity were to exist, it would follow that even a donkey and a camel would form a collection due to their being simultaneous, since the non-apprehension of difference—which is required here—is impossible in that case as well.
For this very reason, they do not constitute a collection by virtue of having a single effect either, because there is no single effect in the form of something to be produced (*upādeya*).

The claim that there is a purposeful action characterized by the fetching of a single quantity of water and so forth is also not tenable; for water as something distinct from color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities is not admitted, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that each individual [quality] is to be fetched, and the collection [of these qualities] is unestablished.
For this very reason, it cannot be [the case] by way of having a single cause either.
But if the collective usage were to occur without a basis (nimitta), there would be the fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Regarding the third [alternative], there is no dispute.

Nor is it the fourth [alternative], for that would have to be based either on the system of consciousness (*vijñānanaya*) or on non-correspondence (*visamvāda*), as in the case of a double moon and so forth.
But regarding the first [position], what partiality is there toward form and the other [sensory objects]?
Nor is even the second [position tenable], because of [their] attainment and the persistence of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
If it is argued that those two [properties] belong to form and so forth, we say no; they do not belong to those, but rather to that [single entity] alone—why should this not be the case?

If you argue that there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), we reply: neither the contradiction between succession and simultaneity nor the contradiction between the red and non-red is a subverting proof, because such contradictions have already been refuted, and because [the object] is occupied by momentary, atomic material substances.
If you argue that there is an absence of relation, let there indeed be no relation.
If it is asked, "How is it perceived as being like that? [we reply: "But there is no [intrinsic] connection.
If it is further asked, "How is it perceived as being like that? let your own answer be: "Because they arise in such a manner," just as [you maintain] the body is possessed of consciousness.

If it is argued, "Since all purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is accomplished by form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities] alone, what is the use of postulating a substance (*dravya*) distinct from them?", we say: No.
Since all purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is accomplished by that much alone, there would otherwise be room for the talkative assertion: "What is the use of postulating form and so forth?
If it is argued that [form and so forth exist] because they are perceived, the same [response applies].
[ĀtTaViv 721.18]
By this, the view that [the object] has an unreal nature is also refuted.
If it is argued that the proof of non-difference is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), then what is that?

If it is argued that there is a rule of simultaneous apprehension, we say no; for the rule of simultaneous apprehension is unestablished, since in cases such as the perception of a yellow conch-shell, the conch-shell is perceived even when its whiteness is not perceived.

If it is argued that this is not a conch, but rather "like a conch," just as in the case of the hair seen by one with ophthalmia (*taimirika*), then oh, what a virtuous discernment! For you establish that the hairs seen by one with ophthalmia do not exist because they lack the capacity for tactile contact with the palm of the hand and for specific causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), whereas here, even though those two are possible, [the object is not a conch] because its mere whiteness is not perceived.
If it is argued that this is due to pervasion (*vyāpakatva*), is there pervasion between the two things or between the two perceptions?
There is no disagreement regarding the first point.

Furthermore, the absence of the pervader alone does not necessarily entail the absence of the pervaded or its perception; for if it did, it would follow that smoke and the perception of smoke would also cease upon the non-perception of fire.
Or rather, why do you not imagine in that case as well that "this is not smoke, just like smoke [is absent]," on the grounds that the possession of fire is not perceived?

Therefore, it should be stated that the exclusion of the pervaded does not follow from the non-perception of the pervader, but rather from the exclusion of the pervader itself; and that [exclusion] is unestablished in this case. This same point applies to the present instance as well. However, the pervasion of perception is refuted right here, for it has been stated that even the non-perception of whiteness occurs because of the perception of the conch-shell.
It might be argued: "The yellow [color] has indeed arisen in the conch-shell. This is not so, because another person perceives only its whiteness.

Nor is the necessity of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) a valid reason for proving non-difference, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for instance, non-luminous form is invariably perceived together with luminous light, yet it is distinct from it.
If it is argued that this is not the case because there is no spatial separation (*deśāviccheda*), we say no.
[The argument fails] because of non-establishment and because of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to the body and the embodied one.

If it is argued that there is no interruption of those two because they are perceived even when that [body] is perceived, [we reply] that this is equal [to our case], since those who possess form and so forth are perceived even when form and so forth are not perceived.
If it is further argued that nevertheless there is never a reversal [of the relationship], [we reply] that this is equal [to our position].

For in your system, just as there is no perception of the embodied self when the body and so forth are not perceived, it is likewise impossible for the body to be perceived when the embodied self is not perceived. Whether there be simultaneous perception or non-separation of location, these would necessarily follow from the requirement of the totality of conditions for the completion of cognition. If you argue that they are distinct because of the necessary imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), what contradiction is there? If you ask, "What is this contradiction of properties?"—it is such things as: even when one is perceived, the other is not; even when one is named, the other is not; even when one is negated, the other is not negated, and so forth.

In cases such as "the blue lotus moves," when the distinction between exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) is rejected, the same principle as previously stated should be followed, since there is no difference in other respects except for the difference in limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
Furthermore, if the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) are non-different, how could there be clarity and lack of clarity in their perception from a distance or nearby?
Nor does another [cognition] arise in that very same way merely through a difference in person, because a single [cognition] cannot possess two forms.
Nor is this [subsequent cognition] something entirely different, because it is recognized as being identical due to its occupying the same location.
Furthermore, that recognition is not erroneous, because even for one who is in close proximity to such a thing located in a different place, it is not perceived as being so.
Nor can that perception be entirely without an objective support (*nirālamba*), because it would otherwise be impossible for it to be restricted to specific locations such as trees and so forth.

Nor is it correct to argue that this restriction arises because [the object] is merely a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), since perceptions do not conform to the delineation of those locations; or, if they do so delineate them, then that very [delineation] is the objective support condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), because the conventional usage of "objective support" is invariably tied to that much alone.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that the location (*deśa*) is the objective support (*ālambana*) and not the tree and so forth, because there is no distinction between the location and the located (*deśin*) since no difference is perceived. Nor is it correct to say that while the second part—the particulars—indeed manifest, they are simply not ascertained; for it cannot be maintained that the movements of the clusters of stars do not appear to anyone other than one whose vision has been cleansed by the ointment of yogic purity.
And because non-ascertainment is untenable:
a reason must be stated for why the self, though experienced, is not ascertained. If you say it is because the latent impression (vāsanā) has not arisen, no; [that is not a valid reason].

Having perceived a substratum (dharmin) possessing all its specific qualities, even when there is recollection of that entire object for one standing at a distance, a definitive ascertainment (niścaya) does not arise that conforms to the operation of the original experience.
Nevertheless, if one were to postulate such an experience, why could it not be the case that everyone always knows everything, yet does not ascertain it?
If it is argued that, due to the force of error, there is a determination of contrary particulars and thus no determination of the particulars actually experienced, we say no;
for if a determination were contrary to experience, it would follow that there could be no confidence in any determination whatsoever.
And what can be said of a case where even the contrary is not determined, such as the conjunctions and disjunctions of posterior parts with prior ones?
Thus concludes the discourse on the refutation of the distinction between qualities and the possessor of qualities.
[Non-apprehension:
"In that case, let there be selflessness (*nairātmya*), because of non-apprehension. If this is argued, it is not so.
And because of the doubt arising from the non-perception of all [non-existent things], and because of the deviation [of the reason] due to its own perception;
if it is argued that this is not so because of the qualification "being perceptible," we say no,
because that [qualification] is unestablished.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the argument] is established through the opponent's own admission (*paropagama*), we say no; for it is an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*).

If the opponent were not to admit this so abruptly, this proof would surely fail; and even if one were to disregard the opponent’s perspective and accept the object of perception itself, it might still be possible—yet this cannot be done, because that [object] possesses a nature conditioned by that [perspective]. This is the summary.
The detailed argument that non-existent things are not momentary should be inferred accordingly.
Now, what is the proof for the existence of a self?
To begin with, it is indeed perceptual, because the conceptual construction "I" is established for all living beings.
Nor is this [construction] devoid of a real object or one whose object is doubtful, because it is not derived from words and is not subject to denial.
Nor is it inferential, because it arises as a self-evident cognition even for one who has not reflected upon a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Nor is this [cognition] memory, because that is impossible in the case of what has not been previously experienced.

Nor is it correct to say that this objectless conceptual construction is beginningless due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because it would then be common to all conceptual constructions such as those of blue and so forth.

If one lacks confidence here regarding the basis of latent impressions, then what confidence could there be in other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from which confidence in conceptual constructions of blue and so forth might arise?

Therefore, abandoning the doctrine that [the world] consists of nothing but latent impressions (*vāsanā*), some adventitious cause must be stated; and that [cause] is either the words of a reliable or unreliable person, or a logical mark (*liṅga*) and its fallacy, or direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and its fallacy.

In this regard, just as the conceptual construction of "blue" takes the final [moment of] conceptualization as its object because the first and middle modes are absent, so too does the conceptual construction of "I."
