In this regard, when [the conceptual construction] arises immediately following a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it possesses a real object (*savastuka*) directly; however, in the case of its appearance as that [object], its possession of a real object is at the root through a mediated succession (*pāramparyāt*).

Nor does it follow that [a cognition] is baseless (*nirmūla*) only upon the cessation of external perception, for that would entail the same consequence for mental conceptualization (*buddhi-vikalpa*) as well.
In that regard, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the basis there, and here too it is mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*); thus, there is no distinction whatsoever.

If it is argued that [the object] will be a real entity such as the body and so forth, we say no; for if it were to have as its objective support the body, the sense organs, the intellect, or their collection in their unconditioned state, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It might be argued that this [notion of "I"] could apply to one's own body and so forth; however, it must be stated what constitutes "one's own" (*svārtha*) in that context.

Selfhood (*svatva*) consists in non-difference from everything that exists. Thus, when a thing is experienced by that very [self], then because the cognizer is not distinct from the object of cognition, the notion "I" would arise.

If it is objected that objects such as jars are never non-different from a cognizer and therefore never become the locus of the "I," then, according to your view as well, the cognition "I" regarding the body and so forth would merely be of the nature of a superimposition (*āropa*), since they are distinct from the cognizer.
If it is argued that [the self] resides primarily in the intellect (*buddhi*), we say no;
for while that [intellect] is experienced as an action, there is an experience of a distinct agent, namely "I know," just as in the case of "I cut."

If it is argued that the form of the cognition also appears as the very self of the cognition itself, just like the forms of the objects to be cognized such as blue and so forth, then—since the form of the object to be cognized and the form of the cognition share an identical status—we have established our desired conclusion.
If it is argued that [the cognition] consists merely of its own material cause (*upādāna*), we say no.
For if that [material cause] were to appear, it would follow that its form would also appear; for a substrate (*ākārin*) cannot be perceived in the absence of its form (*ākāra*).

If it is argued that the cognizer is a stream of consciousness distinct from the stream of active cognitions (*pravṛtti-santāna*), and that we designate this as the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), then let it be so; let the cognizer be the substratum (*upādāna*) of the active cognitions, beginningless and endless.
Only the consideration remains as to whether he is of the nature of a continuously evolving cognition or its opposite; however, that has already been fully resolved previously.
What, then, is the reasoning here? It is the act of reconnection (*pratisandhāna*).

If it is argued that "this is real" is unestablished (*asiddha*), while "it is not real" is contradictory (*viruddha*), and that [the reason] is non-distinct (*aviśiṣṭa*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), we say no.
Because the meaning of the reason has not been understood.
For it is not mere recognition that is intended here.
What then? It is the restriction of cause and effect to a single continuum (*ekasantāna*).
If it is argued that this too is contradictory, we reply: this is not what we intend to say.
What, then, is the determination [of identity] based on the fact that preceding and succeeding cognitions have a single agent?
If it is argued that this too is established by way of the relationship between material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*), we say no.
Because that [causal relationship] would be absent if there were stability;

furthermore, even if things are momentary, the mere fact of one arising from another— even while belonging to the same genus— does not constitute the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādāna-upādeya-bhāva*),
for otherwise it would follow that the cognitions of a disciple and a teacher would likewise stand in such a relationship.
If it is argued that [the error occurs] "when there is a non-apprehension of difference," we say no; for even in the case at hand, such [non-apprehension] is absent.
If it is argued that there is at least a non-apprehension of a difference in bodies, we say no; for this fails to pervade cases where births are known to be distinct.
Furthermore, it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument] even in the case of a child whose father has not been perceived.
Furthermore, it would follow that the characteristics of the jar and its shards would not be so [related].
If it is argued that there is a restriction based on their being supported by a single substratum, we say no;

for such a real [substratum] is absent even in the doctrine of momentariness, since there are no moments that do not share the same duration. As for a conceptual [substratum], it leads to over-extension.
Because there is also the misconception that the body and the cognition occupy the same location.
By this—
The determination of the non-erroneous, the equality, and the oneness [constitutes] nature and modification;
from these two arise the characteristics of cause and effect, namely the material cause and the product.
This is refuted.

How is it determined by you that charcoal is a modification (*vikṛti*) of wood as its material cause (*prakṛti*), rather than being a modification of fire itself? If it is argued that this is because it arises precisely from wood related to fire, we say no.

Why could it not also be postulated that fire itself arises from its connection with wood? If you argue that this is because we are certain that what is earthy has earthy material causes, from where does this certainty come?

If you say it is because such a relationship is observed among homogeneous particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), then what is this so-called "homogeneity"? If it means belonging to the same genus (*sājātya*) or occupying the same location (*sādeśya*), that has already been refuted previously.

If it is argued that they belong to a single continuum (*ekasantānatva*), and if that too is merely the fact of arising from that [same cause], then it would follow that the same relationship holds for the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and its effect (*naimittika*).
If it is argued that it is the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādāna-upādeya-bhāva*), how could that very relationship be established by that [single continuum] itself?
If it is argued that in the case of cognitions, the very linking of them (*tatpratisandhāna*) constitutes the definition of material cause and effect, we say no.
Because it would entail the consequence of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
If it is argued that it is "the fitness for that" (*tadyogyatā*), then it must be considered: what exactly is that?
If you argue that it is a "particular capacity," that [capacity] certainly cannot be restricted to each moment.

For just as that [cause] must produce that [effect] by means of that [capacity], so too must it produce it by means of such [a capacity]; this is indeed a necessary rule. Otherwise, one could not even determine that "it was produced by that [cause]," because a moment is difficult to discern.
And thus the world would arise as devoid of causal effort (*nirīha*), and such a nature of the effect would become accidental; consequently, no regularity would be observed.
Nor could there be a specific capacity restricted to each individual continuum, because there is no basis for such distinction.
If it is argued that there is indeed a difference in kind (*vaijātya*), we say no;

for this is refuted by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Indeed, we do not perceive even in the slightest degree any distinction based on genus between the cognition of "blue" in a disciple and that in a teacher.
If it is argued that this is not a fault because [the distinction] is imperceptible, we say no.
Because it is impossible for a genus inherent in a perceptible object to be imperceptible;
or, if such were possible, it would follow that [the genus] could also apply to smoke and the like.

Consequently, just as there is a lower-order existence (*sattva*), there would be a lower-order smoke that is the effect of fire; thus, because of being tainted by this doubt, the universal of smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*) would not lead to the cognition of fire.
If it is argued that this is so because the first [moment] itself exists in such a state, we say no; for even in that case, the doubt remains as it was.

Therefore, when a difference in the nature of the cause is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even if the effect is similar in appearance, a distinction between sub-species (*avāntarajātibheda*) is postulated; for a difference in the cause is the determinant (*prayojaka*) of a difference in the result, since if it were not a determinant, that difference would result in being accidental (*ākasmikatva*).
We consider it logical that even when there is similarity in the cause, the difference in the effect ultimately results from a difference in the auxiliary causes (*sahakārivaicitrya*).
Otherwise, in the case at hand, even the existence of the next world (*paraloka*) would not be established.

It might be argued that even knowledge which has an insentient material cause (*upādāna*) could belong to a distinct intermediate class, and that even an insentient thing belonging to a distinct intermediate class could serve as the material cause of knowledge; for it is possible to raise the doubt that some specific causal factor (*nimitta*) will exist despite the non-difference in their perceived genus (*jāti*).
To this, if it is replied: "Let there then be a restriction based on a difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*," then that very [cause] is declared to be the single agent (*kartṛ*).

If it is asked, "How is there such a distinction, given that there is only one agent and not such a succession of auxiliary causes? [The answer is: No, because the state of having that as its agent excludes [the effect] from those produced by different agents, whereas such a succession of auxiliaries does not; this is the distinction. If it is argued that even so, this might occur due to some other factor, we reply: no, for that very distinction is what is being considered.

And that [distinction] does not exceed the scope of being its own nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*), belonging to its class (*tajjātīyatva*), being its auxiliary (*tatsahakāritva*), or having such a succession of auxiliaries (*tādṛksahakāritva*). Thus, it is nothing more than these.
Among these, the first is impossible; the second leads to over-extension;
and in the fourth, there is a lack of a determining factor.
Therefore, only the third alternative remains, as there is no other possibility.
Alternatively, even if this limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) were possible, it would not [be valid].
In that case, such [recognition] would lack a basis, for it is as follows:

an omniscient being either recognizes [the sequence] by way of being the single agent of multiple cognitions produced from his own [consciousness], or he does not. In the first case, precisely because of that recognition, the oneness of the recognizer is established, as well as his difference from the cognitions; for the instability of cognitions is perceived by everyone, and momentariness cannot be apprehended even by an omniscient one in relation to a recognizer. If, on the other hand, he does not recognize [the sequence], then recognition is not based merely upon the relationship of cause and effect.

For it is impossible that something which does not follow [a certain property] even when its successor follows that property should be based on that [succession] alone. If you argue: "One synthesizes [the experiences], but that synthesis is not real; therefore, the identity of a single agent is not established by that much alone," then is it the case that even for an omniscient being, a fabricated error is not harmful?
No.
One must explain how, even though there is no difference in their basis, one [cognition] is adventitious while the other is spontaneous.
If it is argued that this is due to the perception and non-perception of difference, we say no;
for the difference among the active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is perceived even by those who are not omniscient.
If it is argued that only the objects appear as distinct and not the cognitions, we say no;
for their distinction is also ascertained,
since the repetition of cognitions is observed even when the distinction between objects is not manifest.

If, even when there is a perception of difference, the non-apprehension of that difference were possible through mere cognition alone, then wood would be recognized as non-different from a tree by virtue of its being earthen, and charcoal from wood, and ash from that [charcoal].
But this is not the case. [ĀtTaViv 779.6–780.6]
It might be argued that the reconnection [of the stream of consciousness] occurs because one fails to grasp the difference between the various store-consciousnesses (*ālayavijñāna*).
This is not so;

for that "I" which serves as the locus would have to be either something entirely distinct from the continuum of active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), or it would have to consist of various occasional notions of "I" occurring within that very continuum.
The first [alternative] is not tenable.

For we do not experience ourselves as independent from the continuum through a mutual "I-am-I" impulse; or even if such were the case, because there is no relationship of mutual material cause and effect (*upādāna-upādeya-bhāva*), there would be no bond of recollective synthesis regarding objects experienced by one another. Even if that bond existed, it would follow that Caitra and Maitra could likewise share a memory; or if both were the material causes for both, then a single entity would have multiple substrates—so what wrong has been done by the whole (*avayavin*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so forth?

Nor is it logical that the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which is appropriated by the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), should not appropriate anything at all; for if that were the case, it could not even function as a causal condition (*nimitta*), since being a causal condition is pervaded by the state of being an appropriator (*upādānatva*).

Otherwise, if one were to accept merely the status of a causal condition, then upon the cessation of a single [evolving consciousness], there would be the total annihilation of the entire continuum, because there would be no distinction [between them].
If one says "om," then because the final moments would lack the capacity to produce anything, they would necessarily be non-existent.

And by the same logic, the preceding moments would also be so; thus, by this sequence, the entire world would result in being incapable of producing anything. In that case, the causal relationship—which is the basis for the recognition [of identity]—would be successfully established. Therefore, one must admit some other cause altogether; and if that were so, neither recognition nor the commencement of a previously non-existent, infinite continuum would be possible.
And thus:
incapacity due to lack of material cause; infinity due to taking up another [cause];
lack of mutual connection; and, in the case of confusion, dependence on many [causes].
Thus is the summary.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
For that [non-apprehension of difference] too must be either non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or non-apprehension of the object (*viṣaya*).
In the first case, [the notion of "I"] would arise either from the mere cognition "it was previously" or from the active cognitions themselves.
It cannot be the first, because the mention of the three times— “I knew as ‘I’,” “I know as ‘I’,” and “I shall know as ‘I’”— is untenable without a determination of their difference.

If it is somehow possible for them to arise, it is appropriate that there be a reconnection (*pratisandhi*) only with their own objects, and not even with the objects of the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*); furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no non-apprehension of difference even from those [objects].
Nor is there [reconnection] by way of the object (*viṣaya*), for that object must be either a mental aspect (*ākāra*), a distinct entity (*vastvantara*), or something unreal (*alīka*).
Not the first, because it has been refuted;
not the second,
because it is not accepted by [the opponent] himself.
Even one who might accept this would still desire a distinction based on the superimposition of contradictory properties, and the cessation of the latter upon the cessation of the former.
But the third alternative is not possible.
This is because it has already been established that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "I" possesses a real objective basis (*savastukatā*).
Even if it were without a real basis (*avastukatva*), the possibility of not grasping the distinctions relevant to the present context would not arise;

for it has been stated that the non-grasping of any of the six kinds of distinctions—namely, those based on existence, non-existence, superimposed existence, superimposed non-existence, lack of common locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*), and the inexpressible—is impossible there, as it serves as the means for the superimposition of non-difference (*abheda*).

Alternatively, in this context, experience (*anubhava*) might produce a memory that occurs at a later time, or it might produce a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). That [impression], too, must be either supersensible (*atīndriya*) or established by perception (*pratyakṣasiddha*). If it is supersensible, it must either persist for that duration of time or be continuous (*santanyamāna*). If it is established by perception, it must consist of a stream of subsequent cognitions, or be something other than that, or a specific quality thereof. Even if it is a specific quality, it must be either merely the fact of originating from experience, or a distinctness (*vaijātya*) within the continuum of the experiencer. Among these, the first [alternative] is not tenable.
Because there is no distinction between that which has not arisen and that which has been destroyed without a successor;
nor is there any other visible [entity],
because such a thing is sublated by non-perception.
Nor is mere origination from experience the distinguishing factor.

For a seed produces a sprout only when brought into contact with the soil by the hand of a laborer, and not when it falls by chance; likewise, there would be no distinction as to whether the continuum originating from the experience of blue and so forth is brought about by the experience of yellow and so forth, or by the experience of blue and so forth itself.
And thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of memory occurring even for what was never experienced, and conversely, even for what was experienced.
If it is argued that this is like the continuity of the rice-nature in a seed produced from rice, we say:
no.
Because its lack of necessity is evident from the observation of irregularity, like a pigeon whose cry is reversed by being white and black while drinking the juice of the milk-jambu fruit.

However, there may be a distinction based on a difference in nature (*vaijātya*): for example, the *āmalakī* tree, by means of the irrigation of milk, abandons its acidity and persists in sweetness, thereby manifesting sweetness even in the fruit at a later time; or the cotton seed, by the irrigation of lac-dye, abandons its whiteness and persists in redness, thereby manifesting redness in its flowers. But this is not the case here, because even in the presence of an adjunct such as a *japā* flower, [the crystal] does not assume that color, but rather maintains its own whiteness alone.

Just as in the case of a crystal, consciousness—having set aside its coloring by objects—persists merely in its nature as pure awareness (*cidrūpa*). Thus, all cognitions possess all forms; however, one form may be vivid while others are not. For those who have faith in their own philosophical system, there is no fear even of the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), for it is not possible that the very same thing is both vivid and not vivid. Nor do we perceive any meaning in the lack of vividness for that which is of the nature of self-cognition.
Even in the view that cognition is formless (*nirākārapakṣa*), cognition is indeed clear to the extent that an object is its domain; and where it is not clear, that is not its domain.
Otherwise, there would be no distinction between what is an object and what is not.
It was already demonstrated previously that this [explanation] is appropriate only if the object possesses parts.
Therefore, the *saṃskāra* (latent impression) remains as the only candidate for being beyond the reach of the senses.

Furthermore, it cannot be something that continues in a stream, because if it were so, it would follow that a result could not arise during a continuous process such as recollection and the like; nor can it be located elsewhere than the impression, because that would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of a result occurring in a different place. If one were to argue for a restriction based on a causal succession where each member serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the next, then it would still follow that recollection could occur even within a different stream of impressions.

Therefore, since there is no other possible way, one must accept—even if it is initially unpalatable—that memory is produced in its own material cause (*upādāna*) alone. Thus, because memory is connected with a later time, the stability of both the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) and its material cause is established without effort and is unavoidable.
By this, the mental impression consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) is also explained.
And thus, the following [position] is also refuted: that whichever impression (*saṃskāra*) is deposited in a certain continuum is capable of producing its fruit only there and not elsewhere.

This is because, under the view of a distinct (additional) impression, the reason (*hetu*) would be misplaced (*vyadhikaraṇa*); because the definition of the specific [impression] would be unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*); and because the mere flow of subsequent effects, being undifferentiated, would be contradictory (*viruddha*).

Furthermore, even a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that is beyond the reach of the senses is not possible in the Buddhist system. For if it were a cognition, its being imperceptible would be untenable; if it were not a cognition, it could not logically have cognition as its material cause. If it were a separate mental continuum, then since cognition itself would be imperceptible, it would follow that everything contained within it—such as memory and so forth—would likewise be imperceptible. Thus, this aforementioned synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) is pervaded by having a cause, because if it were causeless, no such regularity could be established.

And since that [effect] does not exist when there is multiplicity of agents, it is excluded from the counter-example (vipakṣa) by the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi). Thus, as it turns away from the counter-example, it comes to rest in the presence of a single agent who possesses the necessary causal conditions; this is the establishment of the logical connection (pratibandha).
This being the case, positive concomitance (anvaya) is also to be seen in the movement of the brow-creepers of a logician and so forth.
For those very brow-creepers, or those same atoms, when they are being joined together, do not remain in a state where they lack a conscious cause.
In this context, however, the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) must be qualified by the condition that its object is devoid of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmavirahiviṣayatva*);
otherwise, there would be an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacy due to such instances as: "The very same child who was seen by you is now seen by me as a youth.
Nor is this qualification unestablished, because the body alone is sentient.
Do not say so; [it is not sentient] due to its being a body, its being material, its being composed of the elements, its possessing form and other qualities, and so forth.

Furthermore, consciousness does not reside in the aggregate of the elements, because since that aggregate changes daily, it would follow that one could not remember what was experienced on previous days.
Nor does it reside in each individual element,
because when limbs such as the hands and feet are separated, it would be impossible to remember what was experienced by them.

Furthermore, if the body were sentient, it would follow that an infant would not act for the first time; for effort is impossible without desire and aversion, and desire is impossible without the recognition of something as a means to a desired end.

In this life, it is impossible to reconnect with a connection (*pratibandha*) that was not experienced and is not remembered; nor is it possible for one person to remember what was experienced by another who has been reduced to ashes in a previous birth. Furthermore, since the causal relationship between the sequence beginning with experience and ending with purposeful action (*pravṛtti*) is ascertained in this very life, and because in the absence of that [relationship] the absence of those effects is easily established, [the self must exist].
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For this very reason, the sense organs do not possess consciousness; and also because a single object is grasped through both seeing and touching.

And the mind is not like that, because it is inferred solely as an instrument (*karaṇa*); thus, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established, and the existence of a self belonging to another world is proven.
Furthermore, this [self] is beginningless, because no birth is observed for one who is free from passion.
And it is infinite because it is beginningless;
it is a substance because it is an inherent cause;
and it is all-pervasive because, while being an eternal substance, it is incorporeal.
And it is formless because it is devoid of action;
and it is devoid of action because, while being eternal, it is perceptible to people such as ourselves, and because it is the substratum of perceptible qualities.
And here there are these arguments:
if there were a beginning, then since an initial commencement would be impossible, it would follow that there is no activity whatsoever;
if there were an end, it would follow that the existence of that which is beginningless is impossible.
If it were not a substance, it would follow that it possesses no qualities;
if it were not all-pervasive, it would follow that actions such as burning or blowing could not occur in fire, wind, and so forth.
Nor can their production result from conjunction with what is conjoined, because there is no medium that directly possesses action.
Furthermore, if that which is not so constituted were its cause, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If [the Self] were corporeal (*mūrttatva*), it would follow that an eternal entity could not be the substratum for properties perceptible to beings such as ourselves, and it would also follow that it would possess the capacity to initiate action like those possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*). If it were active (*sakriyatva*), it would follow that it must be corporeal. This is a summary of the meaning of the treatise.

"This [soul] is indeed atomic, because it is the substratum of the conjunction that is the non-inherent cause of cognition, like the mind. Regarding this, some claim that the arguments "smaller even than the atom" and so forth constitute a sublation (*bādha*) and a counter-argument (*pratirodha*).
That is incorrect.
Since the soul is all-pervasive, the minute size of the mind is not established; for the sequence of actions is accounted for solely by the sequence of its conjunctions [with the soul].
As for the scripture, it was cited after omitting the first quarter-verse which states that [the soul] is even greater than the great; therefore, enough of this.
It might be argued as follows:

"Even if this [self] is established in such a manner, it must still be abandoned; for one who perceives a self becomes attached to what benefits it and feels aversion toward what harms it, and attachment and aversion are the root of *saṃsāra*. One who does not perceive that [self], however, would not even regard something as beneficial or harmful to it, and thus would neither be attached nor feel aversion, and consequently would not transmigrate. Therefore, just as one seeking freedom from poison practices the science of antidotes, so too the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should cultivate the realization of selflessness (*nairātmya*)."
No;
for one who perceives no self would have their desire for liberation contradicted. Indeed, without conceiving of a self, no one would wish to abandon suffering or to attain happiness.

This is because one would persist in the application [of effort] as long as the intention—"I must become a partaker of the fruits of heaven"—remains; for if that intention does not persist, the application ceases and the fruit is not accomplished. Furthermore, this view of selflessness would reinforce nihilism.

Furthermore, that [desire], being steeped in a powerful thirst for sense objects, would produce endless misfortune; if this were not so, how could such reckless boasts as "one should live happily for as long as one lives" even exist? As for the saying, "One should feel affection for a benefactor and hatred for a wrongdoer"—this is indeed so.

For he who considers liberation to be a benefit will be attached to its cause; by adopting that [cause] and avoiding its opposite through either aversion or a lack of conviction, he alone shall attain his desired goal, and not otherwise.
But as for that which is enjoyment, even that is likewise [suffering]; thus, what is actually favorable has been grasped as unfavorable by the dull-witted.
That one should be attached to one thing and yet feel aversion toward another is not seen even in the science of cattle-physicians.

If it is argued that, nevertheless, because it is a cause of suffering, it should be abandoned just like the sense organs and so forth—[we reply: only that which is a cause of suffering in such a manner is to be abandoned, and that [self] is thus [only] when possessed of limiting adjuncts (*sopādhi*).
If it is argued that it should be abandoned even when devoid of limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), we say no.
Because it is impossible and because it serves no purpose;
for its abandonment is not destruction, since it is eternal,
nor is it dissociation, since it is all-pervading.
Nor is there a lack of comprehension, for as effort is applied toward that object, so too does comprehension arise.
If it is argued that this is due to indifference (*upekṣā*), then indifference has indeed been maintained for all this time; yet even so, the abandonment of that [suffering] is not established.

Moreover, this is purposeless: for the relinquishing of that which possesses conditions (*sopādhi*) is for the sake of abandoning suffering, but what is the point of relinquishing that which is without conditions (*nirupādhi*)?
If it is argued that this is again due to the suspicion of a limiting condition (*upādhi*),
we say no; for there is an absence of any such seed [for such a suspicion].
But why, then, is it to be accepted? Because, such being the case, the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is established through the process of cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*).
What is its acceptance? It is discernment (*viveka*).
From what? From the non-self (*anātman*), such as the body and so forth.

What, then, is the proof for this? It is both reason (*nyāya*) and scripture (*āmnāya*). For indeed, in one who regards the body—which is strictly non-self—as the self, there arises, based upon that body, a craving directed toward the three worlds as being favorable to it; likewise, there arises hatred toward objects unfavorable to it.

And this [state] is not possible for one who perceives the Self alone, because for one who is free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*), there is an absence of desire for children or wealth; because such things cannot benefit him; because [bodily states] like cutting, moistening, burning, and drying are impossible [for the pure Self]; and because he lacks authority regarding injunctions and prohibitions.
For the engagement in those [injunctions and prohibitions] occurs through the influence of birth, caste, age, wealth, refinement, and so forth.

Therefore, the grasping at a self in what is not-self is the cause of saṃsāra; and false knowledge ceases through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). This [true knowledge] arises through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and so forth. When the cause ceases, the effect is no longer produced, and the accumulated store of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) that has already arisen is exhausted through experience. This is a summary of the essential meaning of the system.
[ĀtmaViv 823.14–824.4] "The summary of the essence of the sacred tradition (āmnāya) begins with the words, 'Indeed, he who dwells bodiless,' and so forth.

If it is argued that its authority is undermined by the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology occurring in the repeated teachings on the distinctions and reality of the doctrine of the world's falsity (prapañca-mithyātva-siddhānta-bheda-tattva),"
No;
for there is a specific intention.

Indeed, the intention of the scriptural passages concerning the falsity of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is that the Self, which is free from phenomenal proliferation, is what must be known by those seeking liberation.
For the non-dual scriptures (*advaita-śruti*), the knowledge of the one Self is the means to liberation;
for the scriptures that teach repetition (*paunaḥpunya-śruti*), this [knowledge] is difficult to master;
for the scriptures on the mindless state (*nirmanaska-śruti*), it is the renunciation of external mental constructs.
The Śruti passages concerning bliss have the Self alone as their object of attainment;
the Śruti passages concerning primordial nature (prakṛti) and so forth, as well as the systems of Sāṅkhya and others based upon them, have their purport in practice, like the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*.
Otherwise, [one might ask]: "If Āśmarathya is an expert in the Vedas, what proof is there that Kapila is not?"
"If both of them are knowers of the Veda, then what is the cause of the difference in their explanations? Thus it is said.
If it is asked, "But from what does its validity derive?", [the answer is] "Because it was spoken by a reliable person (āpta).
If it is argued, "That is unestablished," [we reply as follows].
No;
for the existence of a creator of the universe is established through inference:
that which is the subject of dispute possesses a creator, because it is an effect.
If it is argued that this reason is contradicted by a specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*), we say:
no.

For contradiction cannot be apprehended as long as the contradictory particulars are not apprehended; or, if they are apprehended, the contradiction is sublated by the rule of their simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*).
If it is asked, "How can that which is not apprehended in any way whatsoever be an object of intention?"—we reply:
No.
Because it is established through inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).

If it is asked, "How then is it established from that [inference] as well?"—the answer is: a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which makes known what was previously unknown; however, it is not possible to determine a contradiction with something unknown. This is the distinction.

If it is asked, "What kind of power does inference have to produce such a cognition?"—it is the threefold relation, distinguished by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), impossibility (*anupapatti*), and necessity (*niyama*).

In this regard, the distinction is that the positive concomitant (*anvayin*) is established by means of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and necessity (*niyama*), while the negative concomitant (*vyatirekin*) is established by means of impossibility (*anupapatti*) and necessity (*niyama*).
If it is argued, "Let there then be a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatva*) because of the reason 'not being produced from a body' (*śarīrājanyatvāt*)," [the response follows].
No;
because the distinction [of the reason] is unestablished due to the qualifier being ineffective, and thus the two arguments are not of equal strength.
If it is argued that the qualifier becomes effective once the lack of establishment has been refuted, [we reply:]...
No;
for while one might avoid the first [fallacy of] unestablishedness, a second would ensue.

Otherwise, by the argument "that which is the subject of dispute is not caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa), because it is not produced by a body," there would result a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) against the property of being produced (*janyatva*).

[ĀtTaViv 836.13–837.11] "In that case, let the impurity of reasoning (*tarkāpariśuddhi*) be the refutation: because upon the cessation of the body there is the cessation of cognition; and just as the body is of no use if cognition were eternal, so too effort is of no use if it were eternal, and thus knowledge and desire would be useless.
If this is argued, we say: No.

Because effort possesses two properties: it is indeed the effect of knowledge and has knowledge as its sole object. In this regard, agency [consists in being] the cause; thus, upon the cessation of its status as an effect, it need not depend on knowledge as its cause. However, who can prevent its dependence on knowledge for the sake of its object? Nor can it be said that its inclination toward an object exists by its very nature, for that would entail its being knowledge itself. For this is precisely the distinction between effort and knowledge: that the former is not inclined toward the object.
And it should not be argued that it may simply be without an object.
Because it would follow that [the cause] lacks causality;
and in that case, how could even that one [cause] be established?
If you say, "Let it not perish," [we reply:]...
No;
because in that case the proof is faultless,
or else, if there were a fault, that itself would constitute a sublation (*bādha*).
If it is argued that since [the Self] has everything as its object, what is the purpose of a cognition for the sake of restricting its objects?
No;
for it has been stated that it lacks an inclination toward objects by its own nature, and if such an inclination were present, it would follow that it is a cognition.
If it is argued that there will be a restriction of objects, as in the case of the effort that is the source of life,
we say no;
because they belong to different classes.

If it were of the same class [as other effects], it would follow that it too must be preceded by desire; or else, desire could not be its cause, since something of that same class could arise even without it.
Therefore, for that which belongs to the class of products, its determination as having an object occurs only through knowledge and desire.
And that [object] is what is intended to be accomplished.

But one who carries the pride of a logician says: "Surely, since deviation is observed even when there has been hundreds of instances of non-perception despite perception in similar and dissimilar cases, it is possible that even a definition characterized by the absence of observed deviation might be subject to such doubt. Therefore, another definition of the *pratibandha* (invariable concomitance) must be stated, or else a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) regarding the dissimilar case. This is the summary. Among these, the first [alternative] is not tenable, because there is no means to ascertain the absence of an unobservable limiting condition (*upādhi*), and because the restriction that "there must be only an observable limiting condition" is untenable.

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for that [causal capacity] is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and these two must either reside in a conscious being possessing a visible body, or they must reside in mere consciousness—whether visible or invisible—provided it is free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). It cannot be the first.
The first [alternative] is not tenable because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of branches and the like, and because it fails to establish the point at issue (*prakṛtāsiddhi*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;

for at the time of the absence of effects such as a jar, it is impossible to ascertain the absence of all perceivable conscious agents, just as one cannot ascertain the absence of the potter who is the efficient cause (*prayojaka*) of that jar.

For it is not necessarily the case that there is an absence [of the potter] wherever there is an absence of the visible [pot], because otherwise it would follow that such an absence [of the potter] must also exist in the case of a tree branch and so forth.

If you ask: "In that case, how can there be an inference of another mental continuum? For just as the absence of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is not established when there is an absence of the potter despite the presence of the visible and invisible, so too the absence of pure consciousness with respect to movement is not established even when there is an absence of one's own mind," we reply:
No.
Because it is a different argument.

Even when that [argument] is introduced, since the causality of the visible body alone—which exists as an inseparable part of pure consciousness common to one's own and others' continuums—is understood through perception and non-perception to be the cause of trembling within one's own body, the causality of another's mind is not thereby perceived.
Nor is it the third [alternative].
Because there is no subverting argument against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*).

For the restriction of place, time, and so forth, is possible even through a non-conscious cause that possesses a restricted capacity and occurs only occasionally due to the proximity brought about by its own causes.
This is a superficial assertion, for all three alternatives are logically possible.
To explain: there are four types of entities in the world.
[The types are] the contradictory, the externally functioning, the co-functioning, and the internally functioning; nor can a fifth type even be conceived,
because contradiction and non-contradiction, coexistence and non-coexistence, and excess and non-excess are mutually exclusive in nature.
In this regard, two [factors] should not be suspected as being limiting conditions (*upādhi*),
because it would follow that even what is not an effect would possess an agent, just like an effect;
and this is not desired.
In the case of an innate contradiction based merely on the fact that what is not an effect possesses a cause, there is no room for a specific agent as a causal factor.

Nor is it the third [alternative], because there would be no distinction between those things that share the same fortune and misfortune, and because such a doubt of deviation would not be productive [of a valid objection]. However, the fourth [alternative] might be possible.
Nor does it function as being internal to the body, for that would entail the undesirable consequence that even some things caused by a moving body might be preceded by something insentient.
This is not accepted, because it would result in the destruction of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between movement and sentience.

Nor does it function simultaneously [with the body], because if the body were not its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), then this [activity] too would not be its limiting adjunct, since the two share an identical status regarding their logical connection and disconnection.
Or else, if it were not so, the rule of their coexistence would be untenable.
Furthermore, the body cannot be the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because it does not pervade the agent.
Because the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being its effect is present;
nor is there such a state by way of being a locus (*āyatana*), because it is a limiting condition for experience (*bhoga*);
nor by way of bringing about the instruments (*upakaraṇa*), because the limiting condition is the state of not being directly governed by effort (*prayatna*).
"Because that [agency] can be attained otherwise" means that there is no occurrence of [agency] in excess [of the body],
since we do not ourselves admit an agent who is devoid of a body.

Suppose it is granted that [the probans] is inconclusive; therefore, the existence of an agent is not established merely from the fact of being an effect, because the presence of a possible adventitious condition (*upādhi*) is suspected.
Nor can the existence of the agent be established by that very adventitious condition, because that condition itself is doubtful and unestablished (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*). If this is argued, we say:
no.
In either case, because there is a fixed rule regarding the establishment of a bodiless agent,
let it be established by assuming some kind of limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),
or else let it be the state of being an effect itself; since there is no other possible recourse, this doubt alone remains, and that too is now refuted.

To begin with, the occurrence of non-eternal cognition is impossible apart from the body, because of the fixed rule of the causal relationship between the two. Therefore, [cognition] would have to be eternal; and it would also be universal in its objects, since limitation of objects is pervaded by non-eternality. This is because the restriction of objects depends upon the convergence of the capacities of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*); thus, when that [restriction], being pervaded by non-eternality, is excluded from what is eternal, it comes to rest in the non-eternal.
And when cognition has all things as its range, the same applies to the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and effort (*prayatna*), because those two share the same object as that [cognition].

And thus, since there is no room for the demoness of doubt that some effect—even one not preceded by a body—might nevertheless be preceded by an agent by virtue of some limiting condition (*upādhi*), the suspicion of such a condition must be refuted elsewhere as well along this same line of reasoning; hence, the relation [between the probans and the probandum] is established as being free from limiting conditions. Furthermore, when the existence of the probandum is established through the application of the probans, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—characterized by the absence of the probans being necessitated by the absence of the probandum—is also established; therefore, there is no need for a separate consideration for its sake.
Even in the second case, apply your ear-cup and let go of this clamor.

For instance, regarding neutral objects such as a staff and so forth—whether visible or invisible—you yourself must be asked: "Does the conscious agent cease its activity, which occurs inseparably from the operations of various causal factors, or does it not?"
If it is not so, for what reason would the causes remain indifferent?
If [the cause] has ceased, how can there be doubt regarding the absence of the unobservable?
If it is argued that "nevertheless, the absence of such a thing as possesses positive concomitance is also required," [we reply:]...
Who here would disagree? For in both cases, the status of being the "instigator of the causal factors" (*kāraka-prayoktṛ*) is equal.

If it is argued that the embodied being (*dehin*) is such [an instigator], what is the meaning of this? Does the conscious being instigate all causal factors only by means of the body’s (i.e., the body’s performance of) activity, or rather while itself instigating the body?
It cannot be the former, because since the body is also a causal factor, if it were to require another body to instigate it, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
The second [alternative] is not tenable, because it is subject to deviation in cases such as the movement of a fragment of poison.

If it is argued that [the self acts] "while supporting the body," then is this body to be supported by the self in its capacity as an agent for the sake of employing other causal factors, or merely by virtue of being acquired through its own karma? In the first case, there is no contradiction, because the body is necessarily presided over [by the self] insofar as it serves as an instrument for some action.
But who with intelligence would assert that even that which is not an agent [is] something to be presided over by him?

Even in the second case, one who is unable to preside directly might employ something by taking up what is to be directly presided over; however, there is no rule that what is unfit for direct presiding by one is likewise so for another, as this is contradicted in the case of the body itself.

In the third case, however, the body is like the fleshy protuberance on a goat's neck; it does not establish its own role in the discernment of the utilized parts, just as the presence or absence of fire from grass is irrelevant to the mere fact of smoke.

Furthermore, if there were necessarily a requirement for a body even when one is not the agent and does not employ those [instruments], then whoever possesses a potter’s body as the maker of a jar would likewise possess a camel’s body and employ the staff and other tools; for there is indeed no difference between the body of a camel and that of a potter merely by virtue of being acquired through their respective past karma.

If it is argued that for a specific effect, a specific body must be required even if it is not useful, this is a contradiction. Or, if there is no contradiction, then when a jar is to be produced, the body of a camel would also necessarily have to be required, as there is no distinction [between them].

Therefore, just as with a pair of tongs or a mass of iron, the restriction regarding the location of the agent in a body occurs solely by way of being the instrument (*kāraka*) and its prompter (*prayojaka*), and not by virtue of being a body per se.
Furthermore, the body is neither the agent nor the prompter in every action.
If that is the case, then there is no proof for a specific controller of the body.
If it is argued that such a controller is established by the very same logic applied to the controller of the causal factors of sprouts and the like;
No, because it is a different argument.

Even when that [argument] is introduced, the inference of that [Self] is not based merely on the effect or merely on the locus of the causal agent, for from those only the existence of a mere agent is established; rather, having inferred those [mental states] through signs such as joy, fear, grief, and smiles, one infers the enjoyer by means of them—thus, this [objection] amounts to nothing.
Even regarding the third impurity of envy (*īrṣyā-kaṣāya*), close your eyes and listen to the reasoning that follows:
in this world, there is no such thing as an "effect" that could come into being while disregarding the entire circle of causal factors; of this there is no dispute.
And all that is based on volition;

otherwise, the establishment of its definition would be untenable. For instance, the nature of the locus (adhikaraṇa) is based on the object (artha) as conditioned by the efficient cause (kāraka) that is to be placed within it.
Because it is the substratum;
and because the essential nature of the *apādāna* (ablative) is constituted by the causal factors of that which is to be removed and that which removes,
due to its being the limit (*avadhi*).
Because that is intended;
and because the form of action is conditioned by the instrument,
since it is pervaded by it.
And the form of the instrument is superposed by the agent,
because it is the direct object of the agent's activity;
and the form of the agent is superposed by all the case-factors (kārakas).
Because it is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of that [action],
and because the status of being the substratum (*ādhāra*) of knowledge, desire-to-act, and effort is firmly established, there is no fault of circular reasoning (*cakraka-itaretarāśraya*).

This being so, the objection that "if the agent is excluded, then all the *kārakas* whose boundaries are delimited by him would also be excluded, resulting in the production of an effect without a *kāraka*" is a gross error.
This would indeed be the case if there were a pervasion of all factors of action (*kāraka*) by the agent (*kartṛ*). But why is that so?

Why, then, is there no such pervasion? For there is no factor of action other than the six that is not supported by an agent, nor is there a definition for these [six] that is devoid of support by an agent; because if one were to exclude each one individually and yet assume the possibility of the effect arising from the remainder, it would follow that the effect could arise even when all [factors] are excluded.

Furthermore, there can be no subsistence of a universal through the exclusion of all its particulars; for if that were so, even when specific causal factors (*kāraka*) are excluded, one might still expect an effect from the mere category of "causality" (*kārakatvamātra*). However, since they are established in a chain-like connection such that the operation of one entails the operation of all without obstruction, this is not the case.
Now, if you think: "This procedure belongs to you alone; as for us, we say that a cause—whether conscious or unconscious—is that which follows the presence and absence of the effect."
But when combined, everything has itself as its primary [nature]. If it is argued that the distinction between material cause and other factors is established in some way, we say:
no.
Even so, it would follow that there is no material cause (*nirupādānatva*).

If it is argued that this must necessarily be accepted because the cause is restricted by its genus (*jāti*), since it cannot be denied due to being established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say:
no. For if the mere material cause were the cause [of the effect], it would follow that even when the instrumental causes (*nimitta*) vary, the effects would be of a single genus.
Or else, it would follow that [the effect] is causeless, since it arises from such a kind of appropriation alone.
If it is argued that nothing single arises from a single thing, because everything arises from a collection (*sāmagrī*), we say:
no.
Because those two have as their object only that which is being perceived.
If it is argued that its state of being perceived is somehow not intended [to be expressed],
we say no.
"Why should it not be the same for the conscious [agent] as well?

Therefore, just as the causal capacity for an effect resides only when the material cause (*upādāna*) and the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) are mutually associated, so too must it be for the conscious and the unconscious; thus, the cessation of one would entail the necessity of the cessation of the other.

Furthermore, in the case of the lump of clay, the staff, and so forth, dependence upon another in their own operation is invariably observed. Now, consider carefully whether this dependence is connected solely to the nature of being a staff and so on, or to the influence of a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), or to the mere fact of being unconscious (*acaitanya*).
In that regard, it is not the first [alternative],
because it would entail the consequence that the shuttle and other such tools possess independence.
If it is argued that their status as a shuttle and so forth is merely contingent upon [the threads],
we say no; for this would entail the consequence that the staff and other such implements would possess independent status.
Nor is this [dependence] restricted to specific effects, for that would entail the independence of sticks and other tools in cases such as the branding of cattle.
Nor is it the second [alternative],
because if that were not restricted to specific classes [of effects], there would occasionally entail the independence of those very tools even for the purpose of making a jar.
If it were restricted to that [specific object], let that very object be named.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any universal-particular (sāmānyaviśeṣa) residing in jars, cloths, carts, or pots, nor in sticks, looms, hammers, or pincers.
If you argue that such a universal exists, from which the inference of a corporeal creator could proceed, [we reply: no.
No;
for it is precisely potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth that exist in such a manner.
Or, let there be a particular configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*).
Nor is that [the body] itself the basis here,
because even in its absence, water, fire, and so forth are seen to be impelled by a conscious agent.
Furthermore, there is no rule that whatever is operated by a body must necessarily be impelled by a conscious agent.
It has already been largely stated that this would entail the consequence of the body itself possessing independence.

Therefore, this [absence of cognition] is based solely on the lack of sentience; since it exists in such a manner in sticks and the like, as well as in atoms, *adṛṣṭa*, and so forth, its non-existence there is unavoidable.

Thus, this effect is pervaded by its cause; and since that [pervasion] is impossible in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), it excludes its own pervaded [the effect] and comes to rest in the similar example (*sapakṣa*). In this way, the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is twofold.
[ĀtTaViv 863.10–864.2] But what is this "invariable concomitance" (*pratibandha*)? It is an essential connection (*svābhāvika-sambandha*).
What is the meaning of "essential"? It is the state of being without conditions (*nirupādhitva*).

What, then, is a *upādhi*? It is another factor that does not contribute to the probandum (*sādhyaprayojaka*). What is its definition? It is being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) while not being a pervader of the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*).

How, then, is an object characterized by such a definition to be understood or refuted? By means of the absence of contradiction with the opposite case and by means of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*).

What is the subverting [reasoning]? It is the unsurpassed *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) which, by assisting the observation of numerous instances of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), serves as an aid.

Although it is fivefold—distinguished as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), circularity (*cakraka*), infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*)—it functions as an assistant by either excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in some cases or by shaking off the limiting condition (*upādhi*) that is its cause in others; thus, in effect, there is no difference between them.
Their respective examples are to be understood here according to their appropriate application.

[ĀtTaViv 866.11–867.12] Now, if one who is weak in logic employs a *pratibandi* (counter-example), namely: "In this way, even the horn of a hare would be established, because the sublation by perception is restricted solely to what is perceptible; moreover, the cessation of perceptibility does not necessarily entail the cessation of 'horn-ness,' since it is impossible for the non-pervaded to cease when the pervader ceases.

Furthermore, because the pervasion of perceptibility is conditioned by the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) residing in the horn, the cessation of that [perceptibility] does not entail the cessation of a horn that is not an effect."

And that [objection] does not lead to the downfall of one who has accomplished his task through the attainment of the great goal, because its object is purposeless. If it is argued that, nevertheless, an obstacle ought not to be ignored for fear of the ill-repute of one who has been so highly esteemed, then do not fear; this shall be set aside.

For instance, one who is actually engaged in proving the horn of his own head must be asked: "By the word 'horn,' do you intend something entirely different, or a substance belonging to the same class as horns such as hair and the like?"
In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), as well as a contradiction with common worldly usage;
for in the world, the word "horn" denotes precisely the opposite of that [which you claim].

In the second case, however, since the manifestation characterized by conventional usage is an effect of a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*)—as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—how could it possibly occur in atoms and the like, which are devoid of such a configuration?

Or, if it were possible [for a horn to exist on a crow], why would potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth not also exist there? For one who says "yes" to this, how could there not be the consequence of a confusion of universals (*jātisaṅkara*), or the consequence that an effect could arise without a cause? Furthermore, positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the relation of cause and effect; thus, everything is indeed in total disorder for one of disordered intellect. Therefore, a horn that is either beyond the senses or eternal does not exist at all; and whatever is a horn is already contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhita*). How, then, can there be any room for its inference?
If that is so, then even the claim that "knowledge is eternal" is contradictory.

If you argue that this is because the universal property of "knowing" (*jñānatva-sāmānya*) is manifested merely through the manifestation of modifications of the sense organs and other such factors, [we reply as follows].
No;
because it is not of that nature and does not entail that.
For knowledge-ness is not the absence of eternality, just as barrenness is not the absence of motherhood.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even insentient things would possess sentience.
Nor does eternality imply the absence of being knowledge, because there is no contradiction between eternality and being knowledge.

This is because there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opposite view that would establish the root of contradiction; furthermore, perception and non-perception are themselves affected by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of being directed toward an object or not being so directed.

Nor is a modification of the sense organs the cause for the manifestation of cognition, since it is merely the manifestation of being directed toward an object—entirely independent of such modifications—that constitutes [the manifestation of cognition]. For if that [modification] were independent of this [direction toward an object], it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
[ĀtmaViv 872.6–12] Now,
as for the minor objections:
if the universe were the product of a single agent alone, there would be a contradiction regarding its manifold nature, and there would also be the undesirable consequence of constant production.
If one assumes dependence on an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), there is the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*), since its arising would result from that very force alone.
If he were to act for his own sake, it would follow that he is not the Lord (*anīśvaratva*);
if he were to act for the sake of others, it would follow that the creation would not consist of suffering (*aduḥkhamaya-sarga*).
In the same way, there is insentience in the case of the evolving [pradhāna];
there is a lack of evidence for its unity;
and if it were manifold, there would be a lack of omniscience, because it would only cognize specific causal complexes, and so forth.
In that regard, if one were to argue that the rest [of the causal factors] are redundant by taking only one from the circle of causes, it would follow that all [the causes] are redundant.

If it is argued that there is no redundancy for those whose status as causes is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then the same applies to those whose status as causes is merely inferred, since there is no difference in their being established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, if that which is postulated as being conducive to a certain result were rendered fruitless by that very same means, then, since this would apply everywhere, it would follow that all observed results are in vain— assuming the unseen (adṛṣṭa) as the cause.
And in that case, even that [unseen] would not exist,
due to a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
For the unseen is inferred from the seen;
and his activity is for the sake of others, since there is no self-interest [on his part]. Nor does the creation of suffering constitute a refutation of his compassion.
Because there are instances of deviation [from this rule] in the cases of Janaka, teachers, physicians, and so forth.
If it is asked, "Why is it not so simply due to wickedness?"—the answer is: No.
Because of the absence of defects;
and that absence [of defects] is due to the absence of delusion;
and that absence [of delusion] is also due to omniscience.

12] Furthermore, there is no dispute that the agent of a single dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)—who is distinct from the atoms (*paramāṇu*)—perceives the six categories of entities, beginning with substance (*dravya*) and extending from the triad (*tryaṇuka*) which is assisted by them, up to the experience (*bhoga*).
This is because these [categories] constitute the nature of their material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth.

Alternatively, because it is impossible to understand [the nature of] the material cause and so forth without understanding the relationship between the delimited (avacchedya) and the delimiter (avacchedaka), there is a rule that whoever is capable of producing or knowing one thing of a certain kind is capable of [producing or knowing] every instance of that kind;
for capability is restricted by class (jāti). Thus, although [the Lord] is indeed capable, he might not act or know due to the absence of auxiliary causes (sahakārin);
however, in this case, the first [alternative—that he acts] is accepted.
Because the restriction of time and place is observed for an effect,
yet that [cause] is not so [restricted]. If one asks how this is so:
Because when the body perishes, the sense faculties and so forth that depend upon it also perish.
Nor can an effect arise from another cause in the absence of a causal relationship established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),
for that would entail the consequence of causelessness (*nirhetukatva*).
Furthermore, there is no such thing as an effect that is without a cause.

Therefore, His capacity for knowledge, volition, and effort is established by its very nature; and since whatever falls within the scope of that capacity applies to the entire class of objects of that same kind, the proof of omniscience is established.

If it is asked how there can be the destruction of the body itself: because that which is visible is contradicted by direct perception; and even in the case of that which is invisible, since it possesses parts and is corporeal, it cannot enter into a dense stone without being broken when an effect such as a frog must be produced therein.
Nor is that body composed of atoms, for, being without intervals and lacking a mind, it would be impossible for it to serve as a substratum for the sense organs.

Nor is it considered that an external operation is useful for the production of cognition, because that would entail the uselessness of the body; nor is it reasonable that the sun and so forth, being at a great distance, could perform that function, since they lack an agent to direct them, and because effort—which resides in the body—is not all-pervasive. Even if [the soul] were all-pervasive, then, by not conforming to the requirements of a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), it would follow that it has no cause at all, and thus it would be eternal.
Nor can it be the cause of action merely through a connection by way of mere enumeration, for that would entail the consequence that the effort of beings such as ourselves would also be so.
Nor does the presiding occur through conjunction with what is conjoined, because direct presiding is intended here.
If it is asked, "How is this the case in instances such as the removal of poison? [the answer follows].
No;
for in that case, there is no contradiction with the mere effort of persons such as ourselves toward cognition.

However, in cases such as the removal of poison, the effort directed toward that end is caused by something else—either a cooperative factor of that [effort] or an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by it—which serves as the cause of the action.

But at the beginning of creation, there is not even a scent of a body; thus, since the body has entirely departed, it is impossible for the intellect to lack a cause. Therefore, it is unavoidable that the single creator of all things is omniscient.
[ĀtTaViv 881.14–882.7] If it is argued: "Granted that he may be such an omniscient creator, but how can he be a speaker?"—it is not so.
Because, although he possesses the power of speech, his intent is solely directed toward the welfare of others.

For one who knows the distinction between the beneficial and the harmful and whose intention is for the sake of others would certainly instruct an ignorant person when there is proficiency in the organs of articulation (*sthāna*) and the points of production (*karaṇa*), just as an ordinary person might say to a blind man, "Go by the right; do not go by the left. Such is the Blessed One. [Objection: Proficiency in the organs of articulation and the points of production is unestablished, because of the absence of a body.
This is because they consist of the palate and other organs, as well as the states of opening and so forth;
for there is no production of phonemes without them, as their occurrence has been determined.
If it is argued that even the Lord cannot be the agent of those [phonemes] because he does not preside over their causes, we say: no.

Whatever is the cause of a particular effect, as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there is a necessary rule that for the sake of establishing the grossness of that cause and its locus, there must necessarily be a locus for the series of causes consisting of its parts, just as there is a locus for the series of causes of those parts.
Now, it might be objected: "In every case, the body is the cause of the effect"—this was previously set aside.
Or rather, the inference [of a creator] follows from the fact of being a father, as in the case of instruction.
Nevertheless, if it is asked which scripture is established by him, the lion’s roar that puts an end to the fever in the ears of the enemies is: "The Vedas, the *Āyurveda*, and so forth.
For this *Āyurveda* is certainly not invalid, because its correspondence with reality is generally consistent.
Because non-correspondence occurs by chance (*kākatālīya*) due to defects in the agent, the object, or the means;
furthermore, when those [factors] are perfected, the fruit is established from that very same source.
Nor can it be so without a basis.
Because this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor can positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) be its basis, because it is impossible for a person of limited capacity to grasp the infinite variety of yogas through the process of insertion and exclusion (*āvāpodvāpa*).
Furthermore, if one were to apply [yogas] in such a manner to poison and the like, it would result in a great many calamities.

What discerning person, who has not ascertained the true nature of things, would have someone perform—or indeed perform themselves—such acts as sharpening, nourishing, cutting, cauterizing, piercing veins, or leaping, for the sake of training?

Nor is the mere tradition of instruction the source of an instruction; for there is an invariable pervasion (vyāpti) that every instruction must ultimately rest upon some means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Furthermore, an eternal scripture is impossible, because it possesses the nature of a sentence.
Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), this [knowledge of Dharma] must have been preceded by one who perceives supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārthadarśin*).
And thus, by means of this example, it is inferred that the Vedas as well are preceded by an omniscient being (*sarvajña*), because they have been accepted by the great multitude of people.

If it is objected: "If the word 'great' (*mahat*) here refers to the statement of an authoritative person (*prāmāṇika*), then the reason has a qualifier that is doubtful and unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). If, on the other hand, it means 'many,' then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the scriptures of the Sugata and others, since those too must have been preceded by an omniscient being," we reply: No, because what is intended to be expressed is a preponderance of number (*bahutvātiśaya*).
What is the distinction? It is the inclusion within all philosophical systems (*darśana*).

What constitutes their acceptance [of this system]? It is the performance of its prescribed practices, the obligation to maintain the linguistic conventions and grammatical rules it has adopted, and the acceptance of the contents of the authoritative Ayurveda and other sciences which it has accepted as valid.

For indeed, there is no such philosophical system where people, even after asserting that something is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), do not perform Vedic rites ranging from the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) to the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*), nor do they fail to acknowledge the distinction between the touchable and the untouchable, nor do they fail to perform expiations such as sipping water (*ācamana*) or bathing when a transgression occurs.

If it is argued that not every person everywhere acts in this way, let it be so; for the fact that the meaning of Āyurveda is not practiced by all sick people does not mean that it lacks the acceptance of the great multitude (*mahājanaparigraha*). Rather, it is simply because it is accepted by those who belong to all philosophical systems (*sarvadarśanāntaḥpātibhiḥ*).
Even so, if it is argued that not every Vedic meaning is like this, let it be so.
For it is not only the meaning of medical treatises that is thus [accepted by all], but rather, some [meaning] is accepted by someone [in particular].

If that were the case, then even the meaning of the scriptures of the Buddhists and others—such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth—is indeed practiced by some who belong to every philosophical school; therefore, that too would be "accepted by the great multitude" (*mahājanaparigṛhīta*).
No.
Because of doubt:

is this subject matter, such as non-violence and so forth, merely something composed by the followers of Śauddhodana and others to induce faith according to the maxim of the "cat's vow," or is it something actually perceived by [the author] himself? It cannot be the latter, because it is common to the scriptures of the Śramaṇakas and others.

However, that which is unique—such as the circular arrangement [of the body] or the plucking out of hair—is not practiced by all; likewise, the Vedic [practices], such as the *niṣeka* (conception rite) and so forth, are indeed unique.

Furthermore, whether or not there is a distinction between the expressive word (*vācaka*) and its corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*), the practice of them has been accepted without dispute by all non-Buddhist sectarians (*tīrthika*).
The same applies to the meaning of the *Śikṣā*, *Jyotiṣa*, *Chandas*, *Nigama*, *Nirukta*, and so on.
And for them, the preservation of the Vedas alone is the supreme purpose.
It might be argued: "Since grammar and the other [auxiliary sciences] have their purposes accepted by all, let the Vedas also be protected by them."
But how can it be said that "they are those very same [scriptures]"? If it is asked, "Why should the scripture of the Saṃsāramocakas not also be something to be protected by them?", we say: No.
Because its authors did not accept it as such, because they did not explain it, because there is no unique evidence for it, and because there exists contrary evidence.

For their activity does not proceed by conforming to the specific words and meanings of the scriptures of the Sugatas and others, as is the case with the Vedic words and meanings, such that it could be inferred [of them] in this way; on the contrary, there is indeed a contradiction, because they have demonstrated the lack of authority of those [Vedic texts].
Therefore, even the necessity of preserving grammar and other systems of linguistic convention accepted by everyone belongs to the Vedas alone, and not to others.

Furthermore, their meaning is accepted by Āyurveda and other sciences whose authority is universally admitted, because at every step these [texts] provide instructions for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), expiation (*prāyaścitta*), austerity (*tapas*), recitation (*japa*), giving (*dāna*), and fire-offerings (*homa*).
Nor is this portion [of the argument] invalid in that regard,
because it shares the same logical status (*yogakṣema*).
If it is argued that this very point is unestablished (*asiddha*) because the possibility of interpolation (*prakṣepa*) also exists;
No;
because the tradition of the students and teachers has remained uninterrupted.
Furthermore, if there were any alteration of this [text], it would have been prevented by many people.
According to this principle,

such is the acceptance by the great masses (*mahājanaparigraha*) of the Vedas; therefore, this very acceptance by the great masses, being impossible if it were not preceded by an omniscient being, is pervaded (*vyāpyate*) by the state of being preceded by an omniscient being.

For just as there is non-acceptance due to disagreement regarding medical treatises and the like—such as those that contradict previous works or present unprecedented expositions—so it is with a treatise on Dharma of that kind.
Even if such acceptance occurs for some due to delusion, it does not occur for everyone.
