Furthermore, if it does not contradict previous works, even so, if the previous work was not accepted as before or was accepted by only some, how could another work based upon it be accepted by all?

Nor is it the case that the *Dharmaśāstra* did not exist previously at all; for if there were no other means of knowledge regarding this matter, it would follow that no religious practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) could take place.

And thus, in the absence of *dharma*, its effect—happiness—would also be absent; and in the non-arising of passion (*rāga*), the collective activity of the world (*lokasamīha*) would cease, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the destruction of the world.

Therefore, the acceptance by the great multitude [of followers] is due either to its being preceded by successive scriptures accepted by previous generations, or to its eternity as a continuous stream (*pravāha-nityatva*), or, even in the event of interruption at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), to its being preceded by a preeminent person (*puruṣadhaureya*) who is followed by all; it is not, however, due to its being preceded by a mere beast-like person of recent times who disregards previous scriptures.
For in either case—whether the previous scripture is authoritative or not—that [recent teacher] is a deceiver:
for if it is authoritative, his statement of something contrary to it is indeed a deception.

Even if [the scripture] were invalid, for one who does not know the means, there would be either a failure to act or an action based on a mere appearance of that [means]; thus, the instruction of one who is not omniscient would be nothing but deception.
[ĀtTaViv 896.7–897.14] Among these, the first case is not [possible].

Because no tradition of the Vedas is perceived, and because there is no evidence for postulating such a tradition when the continuity of the stream can be accounted for by the mere fact that later individuals depend upon the recitations of their predecessors;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because a diminution of the Vedas is observed.
For even now, the meaning of the Veda—which is no longer heard—is both practiced and codified by Manu and others, and this is also due to the diminishing capacity of human beings.
For just as there is a diminution of the capacity to perform the Aśvamedha, Rājasūya, and other such sacrifices, so too there is a diminution of the capacity for Vedic study.

Nor is it the case that the Rājasūya and other rites were not performed even previously, because that would entail the consequence of the entire corpus of the Veda being rendered useless. Furthermore, the possibility of an eternally inferred Veda does not exist.

Even if the phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal, since their sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) depends upon the [traditional] recitation, and since a word (*pada*) is not merely phonemes devoid of sequence, nor is a sentence (*vākya*) anything other than a collection of words endowed with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, even the Guru [Kumārila] is effectively refuted. Therefore, just as the capacity for ritual performance among men declines according to the succession of the ages (*yuga*), so too does the capacity for Vedic study decline; consequently, there is the disappearance of Vedic branches (*śākhā*), the disappearance of the performance of their meanings, and the collapse of the established order of the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*).

For this very reason, the Blessed Vyāsa, observing the decline in human capacity, uttered such statements as, "People will have short lifespans and little strength"; observing the disappearance of the Vedas, he said, "In every Manvantara, a different Veda is ordained"; and observing the exhaustion of religious practice, he declared, "In the Kali age, charity alone [is the duty]."
Having observed the corruption of conduct, [the scriptures declare]: "In that time, people will be devoted solely to their genitals and bellies," and so forth.

Furthermore, even the Vedas, though currently being heard, will undergo extinction; this follows the logical principle (*nyāya*) that they will perish because they are Vedas or because they are composed of sentences, just like extinct Vedic branches (*śākhā*).
And just as this is the case, even mountains will be reduced to powder because they are composed of earth (*pārthivatva*), like a jar.
Even the oceans will reach desiccation because they are reservoirs of water, like a puddle on dry land;
even the sun will go out because it is composed of fire, like a lamp;
and even Brahmā will pass away because he possesses a body, like ourselves and others—let this be inferred in accordance with scripture.
It might be argued: "The future annihilation has been inferred; but how can it be said that it has already occurred? Because, immediately after annihilation, there must again be a creation.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtahāna*) by transmigrating beings.
For indeed, experience and knowledge are not possible without the emanation of the universe;
nor is the cessation of the stream of karma possible without it. Therefore, just as the future emanation of the universe is preceded by dissolution, so too is this [present one].

The restriction of time (samayaniyama), however, should be understood—despite the inequality of the karma of living beings—as being like the restriction of the rainy season and so forth, or like the restriction of sunrise and sunset;
for such is the very nature of karmas themselves.
It is precisely for this reason that in the Purāṇas, the conventions of day and night are applied to the processes of creation and dissolution.

Nevertheless, if it is asked what proof there is for the simultaneous destruction of the intentions (*āśaya*) of all living beings, the answer is this: even when the palaces of the fourteen worlds (*caturdaśabhūmika*) are destroyed, embodied beings who frequent village huts and marketplaces remain entirely fearless; this is a profound observation.

Therefore, we consider it logical that this [tradition], preceded by its acceptance by the great men of the beginning of creation such as Manu and others, continues uninterrupted until the present day; thus, there is not even the slightest room for the fault of [the tradition being established at] an inappropriate time.

If it is asked, "In that case, how could the Vedas be accepted by Manu and others? [The answer is: Because, like the *Āyurveda*, their status as the word of a reliable authority (*āptoktatva*) is certain.
If it is asked, "How is that certain? [The answer is: Through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they too possess the vision of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*).

If it is asked, "What is the purpose for such persons to accept them? [The answer is: "May our offspring and others be educated through our own conduct, and thus may the tradition of Dharma (*dharma-sampradāya*) continue"—this is compassion for living beings (*bhūtadayā*) and the fulfillment of one's own duty (*svādhikāra*).

Alternatively, when the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) grasped in another creation manifests—as in the case of one who has woken from sleep—they infer his omniscience by observing his creation of various high and low beings, and thus ascertain his reliability through their perception of him as a non-deceptive father figure.

Or rather, the Blessed One himself, intent upon the task of establishing the tradition, manifested thousands of bodies arranged in the roles of teacher and student, and caused the great multitude of that time to accept them, just as a dance instructor performs the dance himself; thus, everything is well-established.
In all three of these positions, there is also the traditional account found in the Purāṇas and other texts.

One might argue: "This very tradition of the Veda, set in motion by the Supreme Lord, depends precisely upon the Vedas of a previous creation"—this would be either the position of the *Seśvara-mīmāṃsā* (Theistic Mīmāṃsā) or the position of Kapila. If this is so, for what purpose is this dependence? It is certainly not for the sake of perceiving the meaning of the Veda for one who dwells in the world during the previous Veda.
Because he is eternally omniscient;
nor for the sake of composition, since,
by virtue of being the creator of all things by his very nature, he has no need for a model.
Nor is it for the purpose of resolving contradictions,
because those to whom it is taught lack the capacity for such investigation;
or, even if they possessed such capacity, all contradictions would already have been dispelled by the author’s own realization of omniscience.

Even so, if it is argued that the non-perception of the Vedas in other previous creations is also within the scope of the Supreme Lord, what doubt could there be? If this alone constitutes the eternal flux of the Veda, then it applies not only to it, but to jars and other things as well; such is the very logic of the matter. Otherwise, where would the Mīmāṃsā be, and where would the "Mīmāṃsā with a Lord" (Seśvara-mīmāṃsā) exist?
Therefore, acceptance in the form described is not possible otherwise; thus, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established.
And thus, its validity is established because it was spoken by a reliable authority (*āpta*). Furthermore,

do not harbor the suspicion that there is no trust in the scriptures of the Sugata and others because they were composed by persons belonging to philosophical systems hostile to the Veda and characterized by a contempt for the Vedas.
Even regarding those works composed by the Victors, such as Jina, Jagadindra, and others, one should proceed with reverence.
For what reason? Because they follow those [scriptures] previously accepted by the great multitude, being non-contradictory to them.
From where, then, [does this objection arise]? From the contradiction with the Vedas, whose authority is established.

How then is it that even a few take up that [Veda]? Because of laziness, cowardice, and aversion toward the innate duties consisting of suffering—like the weaver who strives for the fibers located in the *udumbara* tree.
But it is not so with the Veda, because of the absolute necessity of ritual action (*karman*) therein.
By those excluded from the three castes who lack qualification, [this path is followed] because they have no other resort, as in the cases of Kīrti and Prajñākaragupta;
but it is not so with respect to the Śruti, for even those honored by others are not admitted here, while even those fallen from this [path] are accepted there.

Furthermore, those who take pleasure in the non-duality of food, drink, and so forth, follow out of passion like the *sarabha* and others; but it is not so with the Āmnāya, for its purpose is the establishment of the systematic distinction between them.

And [the objection] raised by those who practice fallacious reasoning out of delusion—like the teacher Kaṇāda and others—is not applicable here, because [the knowledge of Brahman] proceeds from childhood onwards.
Nor is it like those who, through association with heretics, become like vintners and the like; for in the present case, [the knowledge] proceeds through the sequence beginning with the father.

Furthermore, the objection of those who pride themselves on the practice of yoga, based on the intention of remaining undistracted—like Subhūti and others—is not applicable here, because in the context at hand, the first [stage] is enjoined precisely within the Karma-kāṇḍa itself.

It is not like the livelihood of unworthy people, which is common among ordinary ascetics; for in this case, there is no authority for newcomers. Nor is it like the case of fools deceived by impostors who, through false conviction, see hollows in the flame of Dīpaṅkara, for such a thing does not exist here.
Rather, it is like those desiring health [relying on] the science of medicine after inferring the authority of the speaker due to its acceptance by the great multitude.

[ĀtTaViv 909. 17–910. 20] What, then, is the root of these [scriptures]? For such vast masses of texts are not composed for the purpose of deceiving others, nor is it the case that only the ignorant are to be deceived. If this is asked, let there be some root; what is the use of deliberating upon it? However, if one persists in the inquiry, the answer is: the practice of reasoning (*tarka*) that establishes momentariness, selflessness, and so forth.
And it has been established accordingly.
However, those who propound emptiness, mental images, and so forth, have practiced erroneously;
for in the Yoga treatises, it is taught that for one practicing therein, there is only a single object to be cultivated as if empty of its own intrinsic nature.

However, for those who offer gifts such as robes to a *caitya*, there is an aversion toward the positions of other philosophical systems because they disregard the authority of their own tradition and find fault with the positions of others. For those who practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*), however, it is the Vedas alone; yet, even that which is taught in other systems is accepted if it is not contradicted by logic and is established as being conducive [to one's goal], according to careful reflection.

However, for those who expound the treasury of mantras, the classes of seed-syllables (*bīja*) beginning with the *praṇava* are common to all; yet the specific insignia (*āṅka*) of the deities to be invoked is additional. It is a matter of common consensus that the syllable "A" is the deity when embraced by faith. The word of those endowed with truth and austerity is the mantra, and its purpose in contemplation directed toward an object is the stabilization of the mind. Otherwise, how could the great sages possess the power to bestow curses or favors, or how could there be such difficult-to-comprehend forms as four-armed or eight-armed deities?

Or rather, what is there that is not possible? Someone might have composed a small portion for the sake of deceiving a single person, and it was practiced by him; then it was adopted, practiced, explained, and expanded by others who followed him.

Therefore, by the exclusion of contradictory scriptures (*āgama*), the Vedas alone—by the exclusion of the suspicion that they were preceded by recent human authors because they were indeed composed by the Supreme Lord, and by the exclusion of the suspicion of invalidity regarding their portion concerning real entities (*bhūtārtha*)—are established as authoritative. This is the settled rule.

If it is asked, "How does it proceed?"—it proceeds because the grounds for its authority, namely the acceptance by the great multitude, or the fact that what it establishes is preceded by an omniscient being, or the absence of defects in the person [who taught it], are common to both the portions concerning past and future objects.

If it is asked, "What is its fruit?"—it is the communication of its own meaning. If it is asked, "What is the purpose served by that?"—it is the adoption, the avoidance, and liberation, according to each case. In this regard, there is the avoidance of the causes of misfortune through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the adoption of the causes of well-being, and the liberation of the self.
[ĀtmaViv 915.1–916.18] But what is this liberation? It is the absolute cessation of suffering for the self.
What is absoluteness? It is the state of being characterized by the absolute non-existence of that which belongs to the same class [as the suffering].
How is their non-existence [established]? Because of the total abolition of the cause alone.
If it is argued that this is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), we say:
no.
Because that which is unreal, undesirable, impossible, and difficult to terminate exists in such a manner;
however, this [reality] is not like that.
This is real, because it is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because it is accepted by everyone;
and because it is optional, since suffering is to be abandoned by its very nature. If it is argued that its abandonment is for the sake of happiness:
No;
because it is not the cause of that.
If it is argued that this is due to pervasion (*vyāpti*), [we reply: no.
No; because it is unproven.
For the absence of suffering is not pervaded by pleasure.

If it is argued that happiness is first pervaded by it [the desire], then, since the absence of suffering would necessarily exist whenever happiness exists, the pursuit of happiness results in a contradictory consequence.
If it is argued that this [absence of suffering] is not desired because it is not itself experienced,
we say no.
Otherwise, how could those afflicted by suffering abandon even their bodies?

If you argue that they are non-discriminating (avivekin), what does it matter here whether they possess discrimination or not, since the status of something as a human goal (puruṣārtha) is tied solely to its being desired, as in the case of sexual desire regarding women who may or may not be approachable?
It is precisely because they seek to align themselves with the scriptures out of fear of falling into greater misfortune that they are distinguished from others.
Moreover, in this way, even the cessation of suffering produced by thorns and the like would not be a human goal (puruṣārtha),
because it is not an object of cognition (avedyatvāt).
If it is argued that "this [cessation] is first indeed known," then the same applies to liberation (mokṣa) as well.
If it is argued that [the destruction of evil] is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
then it would follow that the performance of ritual action by one who desires the destruction of evil would be purposeless;
for both the absence of that [evil] and the absence of its fruit would likewise not be perceived.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because [the state of liberation] consists in the cessation of the undesirable once it has reached the condition of being perceptible, then the same applies [to pleasure].
If it is argued that this [liberation] is undesirable because, like suffering, pleasure too is annihilated, [we reply: so be it.
No;

for we observe that just as activity proceeds through the concealment of faults by craving, so too does cessation occur through the concealment of virtues by the conviction of sufficiency (*alampratyaya*).
In this regard, food mixed with honey and poison serves as the illustration.
And there are some who possess sufficient grounds for conviction;
yet there is no equality [between pleasure and pain], because of the sheer abundance of suffering.
For even when suffering is not accompanied by a cause of pleasure, pleasure is invariably accompanied by a cause of suffering.

For instance, even regarding objects acquired through righteous means, how small is the mere flicker of pleasure compared to the long-lasting storms of suffering caused by their acquisition, preservation, and so forth?

As for those acquired through unrighteous means, what will happen is impossible even to conceive in the mind. Let the wise discern whether there is even the slightest trace of pleasure attached to sufferings such as those born from thorns and the like.
Moreover, even in the pleasures of heaven and the like, there is an abundant piercing by the thorns of suffering;

therefore, it is impossible [to claim] that these should be enjoyed after being separated [from their suffering], like rice from its husk. Yet this [separation] is possible, because it is something that can be accomplished.
And it is auspicious because there is no further transmigration and because its intention is not conducive to the latent impressions of what is harmful.
However, eternal happiness is not real.
Because it is sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible.
If it is argued that scripture is the authority in this matter,
we say no.
Because there is no room for it when [the object] is sublated by the non-apprehension of what is otherwise fit [to be perceived];
or else, if there were such room, it would follow that even the scriptural statement regarding stones floating would likewise be [authoritative].
Nor is it optional, because it is eternal.
If it is argued that one does not desire what has already been attained by oneself, because such [desire] arises solely from delusion— like the case of gold already around one's neck—
the answer is no;
for [the Self] is self-evident due to its eternality.
Nor is it something to be modified,
because it is unchanging;
nor is it something to be refined, because no excellence can be imparted to it.
It is not something to be attained, because it possesses an eternal connection [with the self].
It is not something to be known, because knowledge itself is eternal;
or, if it were non-eternal, it would not arise once the causes such as the body have ceased to exist.
Or else, if they were to arise [spontaneously], it would follow that they lack a cause;
and if that were so, everyone would be omniscient,
because the conjunction of the self and the mind is no different in all cases.

If it is argued that although both knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) are eternal, their relation is produced, and that—being distinct from the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*)—does not cease even once produced, like a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), we say no;
for there is no other mode of being between existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*).
In this case, that [relation] is not a non-existence.
Because a counter-entity (pratiyogin) is untenable;
for if it were a positive entity (bhāvatva), it would necessarily cease once produced, as there is no other limiting adjunct (upādhi).
If it is argued that its "attainment" is simply the destruction of ignorance (avidyā), we have no dispute with that.
For there is no such thing as ignorance distinct from suffering, which is divided into twenty-one varieties;
and because it is established that the destruction of that [ignorance] is the goal of human endeavor, it is said:
"And that [suffering] is endless."

Because, through that intention, when [the object] arises by way of being accompanied by the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) of pleasure, activity toward even a sensual object is possible for one who desires a specific pleasure;
as it is said in the illustration: "When she was not obtained, desire was seen even among animals for a beautiful woman. Thus.
It might be argued: "But we ask, is the self of the nature of self-luminous bliss, or otherwise?
If you are faithful, then ask the Upaniṣads.
If you are impartial, then inquire of experience.

If you are a Naiyāyika, you should determine that [the self] does not have the nature of the cognition of sensory pleasure; for there is no basis for the conventional usage of the term "pleasure-cognition" apart from that [sensory pleasure], and thus such usage would be absent. For the effect characterized by favorability (*anugraha*), attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*), clarity of the senses (*indriyaprasāda*), and so forth, is the basis for the conventional usage of that [pleasure]; and in the world, the state of being directed toward an object (*arthapravaṇatva*) and the effects such as memory and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are the bases for the conventional usage of [the term] "cognition. And both of these are absent in the case of the self.
Therefore—
having heard the Self from the Śruti, and thereafter having followed its manifested form...
Having thus determined through reasoning that the cycle of what is to be abandoned has been destroyed,

one should— possessing faith, tranquility, self-control, and the cessation [of worldly activity] as one's sole wealth— practice for the sake of ending cyclic existence by means of the methods of yoga prescribed through the mental resolve.

And while that [Self] is being meditated upon, first of all external objects themselves appear; depending upon these, there is the conclusion of the *Karma-mīmāṃsā* and the emergence of the Cārvākas, as well as the scriptural passage beginning with "The senses are directed outward" (*parāñci khāni*) for the purpose of explaining those [objects]. Then, for the abandonment of those [objects], there is the passage beginning with "Beyond ritual actions" (*paraṃ karmebhyaḥ*). Next, the form of the object appears, depending upon which there is the conclusion of the *Tridaṇḍika* [sect] and the emergence of the Yogācāras; for the purpose of explaining that [subjective form], there is the passage beginning with "All this is indeed the Self" (*ātmaivedaṃ sarvam*), and for the purpose of abandoning that [form], there is the passage beginning with "without smell, without taste" (*agandham arasam*).

Now, there is the non-existence of objects (*arthābhāva*), depending upon which there is the summary of the Vedānta and the emergence of the doctrine of emptiness and selflessness; for the purpose of establishing that, [the text says] "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" and so forth; and for the purpose of abandoning that [view], [it says] "Those people who destroy themselves enter into odorless darkness" and so forth. Then, there is the discernment (*viveka*), depending upon which there is the summary of Sāṃkhya and the emergence of the doctrine of power (*śakti*) and existence (*sattva*); for the purpose of establishing that, [the text says] "Beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*)" and so forth; and for the abandonment of that [view], [it says] "There is nothing else that exists" and so forth.

Thereupon, the absolute Self shines forth; having relied upon that [Self], non-duality (advaita) is concluded. To demonstrate that state, it is said: "from which words turn back, unable to reach it with the mind. And that state is not to be abandoned.

To demonstrate it, they say, "it does not see," "it becomes one," and so forth; and for the purpose of relinquishing even that [notion of its own realization], it is said, "neither non-duality nor duality," and so on.

Then, because all mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been overcome, even that which is absolute is not conceptualized—that which serves as the basis for the concluding summary of the final Vedānta texts. Since it acts like a gateway to the city of liberation, its own extinction (*nirvāṇa*), however, is self-evident; this serves as the basis for the concluding summary of the Nyāya system. To explain that [extinction], there are such passages as: "Now, he who is free from desire, whose desire is the Self, whose desire is fulfilled—he, being Brahman itself, attains Brahman; his vital breaths do not depart, they are absorbed right there," and so forth.

Therefore, even one who desires to practice should enter only by the gates, avoiding side-entrances; for it is said by those fearing confusion between the path and the non-path that "the application of bows is by means of the target. [One who is] terrified by the dense darkness of the wilderness, which is largely dependent on others...
By Udayana, acting as a caravan leader who diligently protects weary travelers,
this path to liberation has been revealed after he had dispelled the contradictions between logic, worldly experience, and scripture. (1)

No one who lacks discerned virtues, while praising him, can bring us joy; for what excellence could a blind man possess in the art of composing hundreds of eulogies? Let people instead spread only censure, having first scrutinized his faults.
To those who are discerning, the speaking of even a truth that deviates from the facts will surely bring further delight. ||2||
Thus ends the *Ātmatattvaviveka* composed by the teacher Udayana.
